## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Open strings and names, 2 minutes
1. C major and A minor scales, 5 times each
1. Keep your fingers close to the strings
1. **With a tool —** Find the song on YouTube and use the playback-speed control (or a free slow-downer app) to take it to 0.5× without changing the pitch. Learn it slowly and correctly, then step the speed back up.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Instrument care:** wipe the strings after playing, store the guitar in its bag or on a stand, never leave it in the sun.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

You will strum a chord solid (all strings together)
You will pick a chord broken (one string at a time)
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C major scale
- Finger stretch

## Learn (30 minutes)

The **tonic chord** is the home chord of a key — C in C major, Am in A minor. **Solid** means strumming all the strings together; **broken** means picking them one at a time (an arpeggio). Press with fingertips so no string buzzes or is muted — check by picking each string one at a time.

## Understand it

Every key has a **tonic** — the home note — and a **tonic chord** built on it: **C** in C major, **Am** in A minor. Music feels finished when it returns there.

**Two ways to play any chord:**

- **Solid (strummed)** — all strings sounded together with a sweep of the pick or thumb. Full and rhythmic.
- **Broken (arpeggiated)** — strings picked **one at a time**, usually bass string first. Gentle and flowing — the sound of ballads and finger-style songs.

**Chord shapes in open position:**

- **C**: ring finger A string fret 3; middle finger D fret 2; index B fret 1. Strum from the **A string** down — the low E is not part of the chord.
- **Am**: middle finger D fret 2; ring finger G fret 2; index B fret 1. Strum from the A string.

Am and C share two fingers (index on B1, middle on D2) — move only the **ring finger** to change between them. Finding these **anchor fingers** makes changes faster.

**The clean-chord check:** after fretting a chord, pick **each string separately**. Every note should ring. A **buzz** means the finger is too far from the fret or not pressing firmly; a **dead (muted)** note means another finger is touching that string — arch the fingers more.

Strum in **steady quarter notes** at 60 bpm, changing between C and Am every bar. Aim to arrive on beat 1 on time, even if a string is imperfect — then clean it up.

## Key words

- **Tonic:** the home note of a key
- **Arpeggio:** a chord played one note at a time
- **Anchor finger:** a finger that stays put between two chords
- **Buzz:** a rattling note from poor fretting

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Acoustic guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/acoustic_guitar/) — Yamaha

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E F G A B
```

```keys A B C5 D5 E5 F5 G5
```

```chord C Am
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- C and Am chord shapes; check each string rings
- Strum down on each beat, 4 beats per chord
- Broken: pick bass note, then the top strings one by one

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Change C ↔ Am 30 times a day
1. Strum 4 beats each for 2 minutes
1. Broken chord pattern, slowly

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Practice habits:** practise little and often — 20 focused minutes every day beats two hours on Friday. Keep a practice log: date, what, how long, what improved.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play C and Am solid and broken, changing between them without stopping for one minute.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.summary: C, F (easy shape) and G — the three chords of countless songs, played as a progression.

You will play I–IV–V–I in C
You will keep a steady strumming pattern while changing
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C ↔ Am changes

## Learn (30 minutes)

**I–IV–V–I** in C is **C–F–G–C**. Use the easy F (the top four strings) until your barre strength grows. Change chords on the **last beat** of the bar so the new chord lands on beat 1. Strum pattern: Down, Down-Up, Up-Down-Up.

## Understand it

**I–IV–V–I** — built on the 1st, 4th and 5th notes of a key — is the most important progression in popular, church and folk music. In C it is **C – F – G – C**; in G it is **G – C – D – G**.

- **I** is home; **IV** moves away; **V** builds tension that wants to return; **I** resolves it.

**The F problem.** The full F chord is a **barre** (week 13). For now, use the **easy F**: index finger across the **B and high E strings** at fret 1 (a mini-barre), middle finger G fret 2, ring finger D fret 3; strum the top four strings only.

**Changing chords on time** is the core skill:

- **Change on the last beat**: while you strum beat 4 (or the last "and"), the fretting hand is already moving. The new chord lands exactly on **beat 1**.
- **Lift fingers together** and place them as a shape, not one at a time.
- **Practise only the change**: C to F to C to F, slowly, 1 minute at a time — a "one-minute change" exercise. Count your successful changes and try to beat it each day.
- **Keep the strumming hand moving** even if the chord is not ready — the rhythm must not stop.

**Strum pattern: D – DU – UDU** (down, down-up, up-down-up) over "1, 2 and, and 4 and" — the "missing" down on beat 3 is a strum in the air. It is the backbone of thousands of songs.

## Key words

- **I–IV–V–I:** home, away, tension, home
- **Easy F:** a four-string F chord for beginners
- **Strum pattern:** a repeating sequence of down and up strokes
- **Chord change:** moving from one shape to the next in time

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```chord C Am F G
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- F and G chord shapes
- C–F–G–C, 4 beats each
- Add the D DU UDU strumming pattern

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. I–IV–V–I 10 times a day
1. Strumming pattern on one chord, then two

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** the musical alphabet is only A to G, then it repeats. A sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone, a flat (♭) lowers it.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play I–IV–V–I in C with the strumming pattern for two minutes without stopping.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Diatonic scales: G major and E minor, one octave
lessons.summary: The scale of G major and its relative minor, E minor, with alternate picking.
objectives: You will play G major and E natural minor one octave
You will use alternate picking evenly at 80 bpm
You will explain why E minor is G's relative minor
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C major and A minor scales

## Learn (30 minutes)

**G major** has one sharp, **F♯**. **E minor** uses the same notes starting on E — it is G's **relative minor**. Alternate picking (down-up-down-up) keeps the rhythm even; use a metronome and start slowly.

## Understand it

**G major** — G A B C D E **F♯** G — has **one sharp, F♯**. Every major scale uses the pattern **tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone**; starting on G, the 7th note must be F♯ to keep the pattern.

**E minor** uses the **same seven notes**, starting on E: E F♯ G A B C D E. It is G major's **relative minor** — same key signature, different home note, darker mood. Every major key has one, starting on its **6th note**.

**One octave of G major in open position:** G (low E string, fret 3), A (A open), B (A, fret 2), C (A, fret 3), D (D open), E (D, fret 2), F♯ (D, fret 4), G (G open).

**Alternate picking** — strictly **down, up, down, up** — whatever the string. It keeps rhythm even and becomes essential at faster tempos. Picking only downstrokes works slowly but cannot keep up later.

**Using a metronome well:**

1. Start at a speed where every note is clean — perhaps **60 bpm**, one note per click.
2. Play the scale up and down **three times perfectly**.
3. Raise the tempo by **4–5 bpm**. Repeat.
4. When mistakes start, drop back 10 bpm.

Watch for **economy** — fingers staying close to the strings, only the fingers that need to move moving. Wasted motion is what limits speed later.

## Key words

- **Key signature:** the sharps or flats that define a key
- **Relative minor:** the minor key sharing a major key's notes
- **Metronome:** a steady click for practising in time
- **Economy of motion:** moving only as much as needed

## Read and watch

- [Minor scales](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/notes-and-scales/minor-scales.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys G A B C5 D5 E5 F#5
```

```keys E F# G A B C5 D5
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- G major one octave from the low G (3rd fret, E string)
- E minor one octave from the open low E
- Both at 60, then 80 bpm

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. G major and E minor daily at 80 bpm
1. Say the note names as you play
1. **With a tool —** Find the song on YouTube and use the playback-speed control (or a free slow-downer app) to take it to 0.5× without changing the pitch. Learn it slowly and correctly, then step the speed back up.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Listening:** listen to one song this week and name the instruments you hear. Drums, bass, keys, guitar, voice — where does each sit?

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play G major and E minor one octave at 80 bpm with alternate picking.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- G major scale

## Learn (30 minutes)

The tonic chords in this key are **G** (major) and **Em** (minor). The D chord is new: three fingers on the top strings, strum only the top four. I–IV–V–I in G is **G–C–D–G**.

## Understand it

In the key of **G**, the tonic chords are **G** (major, home) and **Em** (its relative minor). Add **C** and **D** and you have **G – C – D – Em**: enough to play a huge number of songs.

**The shapes:**

- **G**: middle finger low E fret 3; index A fret 2; ring (or little) finger high E fret 3. Strum all six strings.
- **Em**: middle finger A fret 2; ring finger D fret 2. All six strings — one of the easiest, fullest-sounding chords.
- **D**: index G fret 2; middle high E fret 2; ring B fret 3 — a small triangle. Strum the **top four strings** only (from the open D). Hitting the low E or A makes D sound muddy.
- **C** (from week 2).

**I–IV–V–I in G** is **G – C – D – G**. The relative minor gives an emotional variation: **G – Em – C – D**.

**Strumming only some strings** is a key skill: aim the strum to start at the right string. Watch your pick for a few strums, then try with eyes closed.

**Smooth changes in G:**

- **G to C**: index moves from A2 to B1, middle from E3 to D2, ring from E3 to A3 — practise as one movement.
- **G to Em**: lift all, place middle and ring fingers on A2 and D2.
- **D to G**: pivot from the D triangle to the G shape.

Use the **one-minute change** drill for each pair, and record your score each day.

## Key words

- **Tonic chord:** the chord built on the home note
- **Partial strum:** strumming only some strings
- **Chord family:** the chords that belong to a key

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Acoustic guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/acoustic_guitar/) — Yamaha

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys G A B C5 D5 E5 F#5
```

```chord G C D Em
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- G, Em, D chord shapes
- Broken and solid G and Em
- G–C–D–G with strumming

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. G ↔ Em ↔ D changes 20 times
1. G–C–D–G, 2 minutes

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** the treble clef (𝄞) curls round G; the lines are E G B D F (Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit), the spaces F A C E.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play G–C–D–G with the strumming pattern, and G and Em broken, without stopping.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.summary: Two-octave pentatonic shapes and playing them over the progression.
objectives: You will play the A minor pentatonic scale (shape 1)
You will play C major pentatonic
You will play pentatonic phrases over I–IV–V–I
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- I–IV–V–I in C

## Learn (30 minutes)

The **minor pentatonic** (A–C–D–E–G) is the guitar's most-used scale. Shape 1 sits at the 5th fret: fingers 1 and 4 on every string except G and B (1 and 3). The same notes from C make **C major pentatonic**. Every note fits over C–F–G, so it is safe for melodies and solos.

## Understand it

The **pentatonic scale** has five notes per octave. The **minor pentatonic** — on A: **A C D E G** — is the most used scale on the guitar, in blues, rock, gospel, highlife and Afrobeats solos.

**Shape 1 at the 5th fret (A minor pentatonic):**

- Low E: frets **5, 8**
- A: **5, 7**
- D: **5, 7**
- G: **5, 7**
- B: **5, 8**
- High E: **5, 8**

Use finger 1 for fret 5, finger 3 for fret 7, finger 4 for fret 8. The **root notes** (A) are on the low E fret 5, the D string fret 7 and the high E fret 5 — mark them in your mind; phrases sound resolved when they land there.

**Major pentatonic** uses the **same five notes** starting from C: **C D E G A** — C major pentatonic. Same shape, different home note.

**Why it is "safe":** the pentatonic leaves out the two notes (the 4th and 7th of the major scale) most likely to clash with chords. Over C – F – G, almost every note works.

**Start improvising:**

1. Loop C – F – G – C on a phone recording, or play with a partner.
2. Play **one note** in different rhythms. Then two notes. Then three.
3. Make **short phrases** with **gaps** between them — like speaking.
4. **Repeat** a good phrase, then vary it.
5. End phrases on **C, E or G** for a resolved sound.

## Key words

- **Pentatonic scale:** a five-note scale
- **Box shape:** a fretboard pattern for a scale in one position
- **Root:** the scale's home note
- **Phrase:** a short musical sentence

## Read and watch

- [Make melodies](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-melodies/make-melodies.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E G A
```

```keys A C5 D5 E5 G5
```

```chord C F G
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- A minor pentatonic shape 1, up and down
- Short phrases over a C–F–G–C backing
- Call and response with the instructor

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Pentatonic shape 1 daily
1. Make up a 4-note phrase and repeat it
1. **With a tool —** Find the song on YouTube and use the playback-speed control (or a free slow-downer app) to take it to 0.5× without changing the pitch. Learn it slowly and correctly, then step the speed back up.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Body:** warm up your hands and wrists before playing, and stop if anything hurts. Pain is a signal, not a challenge.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play the A minor pentatonic up and down at 80 bpm and record a short phrase over C–F–G–C.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Playing from a fakebook: "Holy Are You Lord"
lessons.summary: Reading chord symbols on a lead sheet and strumming a full worship song.
objectives: You will read chord symbols and change on time
You will choose a strumming pattern that fits the song
You will perform "Holy Are You Lord" from start to finish
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- G–C–D–G changes

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **fakebook** shows the melody with chord symbols above. You play the chord named above each bar, changing exactly where it is written. If a chord is new to you, learn its shape before the song, not during it.

## Understand it

A **fakebook** is a collection of **lead sheets**: the melody in notation, **chord symbols** above it, and the lyrics. Church musicians and band players use them constantly — you create your own part from the chord names.

**Reading chord symbols:**

- **G** = G major; **Em** or **E-** = E minor.
- **D7** = D dominant seventh; **Cmaj7** = C major seventh.
- **Dsus4**, **Dsus2** = the 3rd replaced by the 4th or 2nd.
- **G/B** = G chord with **B as the bass note** (on guitar, play B on the A string fret 2 as the lowest note).
- A symbol lasts until the next one. If a bar has two chords, each usually takes half the bar.

**Structure markings:** repeat signs (‖: :‖), **first and second endings** (1. and 2. brackets), **D.C.** (go back to the start), **D.S.** (go back to the sign 𝄋), **Coda** (jump to the ending 𝄌). Map the route through the song before playing.

**Learning a song from a lead sheet:**

1. **List every chord** and learn any new shape **before** playing the song.
2. **Practise the changes** in the order they appear, slowly.
3. **Choose a strum or picking pattern** to suit the mood.
4. Play through with a metronome, **never stopping** at a change — late is better than stopping.
5. **Sing or hum** the melody while you play — it keeps you in the right place.

Worship songs like "Holy Are You Lord" have few chords and clear repeats — ideal first lead-sheet practice.

## Key words

- **Lead sheet:** melody, chord symbols and lyrics
- **Chord symbol:** a short chord name like Em or D7
- **Slash chord:** a chord with a named bass note, like G/B
- **D.C. / D.S.:** go back to the start / to the sign

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [MuseScore handbook](https://musescore.org/en/handbook) — MuseScore

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```chord G C D
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Name every chord in the lead sheet
- Chords only, in time, with a simple strum
- Sing or hum the melody while strumming

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Play the song through daily
1. Practise the hardest change on its own 20 times

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Performance:** an audience remembers the feeling, not the mistakes. Practise starting and finishing confidently.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Perfect "Holy Are You Lord" — play it through with no stops, and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Harmonic and melodic minor: A and E
lessons.summary: The two other forms of the minor scale and how they sound.
objectives: You will play A and E harmonic minor
You will play A and E melodic minor (up and down)
You will describe how each form sounds
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- A natural minor, E natural minor

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Harmonic minor** raises the 7th: A harmonic minor has **G♯**; E harmonic minor has **D♯**. **Melodic minor** raises the 6th and 7th going up (A: F♯ and G♯) and returns to natural minor coming down.

## Understand it

The **natural minor** scale (A B C D E F G A) has a weak pull home: its 7th note (G) is a whole tone below the tonic. Two variations fix that.

**Harmonic minor — raise the 7th.**

- **A harmonic minor**: A B C D E F **G♯** A.
- **E harmonic minor**: E F♯ G A B C **D♯** E.

The raised 7th becomes a **leading note**, a semitone below the tonic, pulling strongly home. It also creates a gap of **three semitones** (F to G♯) — the exotic sound heard in classical, flamenco and Middle-Eastern-influenced music. It is called "harmonic" because it creates the **major V chord** (E–G♯–B in A minor) that makes minor-key chord progressions resolve strongly: **Am – Dm – E – Am**.

**Melodic minor — raise the 6th and 7th going up.**

- **A melodic minor ascending**: A B C D E **F♯ G♯** A; descending, it returns to the **natural** minor (G, F).
- It removes the awkward three-semitone gap, so melodies flow smoothly upward.

**On the guitar:** play A natural minor in open position, then change only the G to **G♯** (G string, fret 1) for harmonic minor. For melodic, also change F to **F♯** (D string, fret 4) going up.

Play all three back to back and listen to the mood of each — a skill that helps you choose notes when soloing over minor songs.

## Key words

- **Natural minor:** the minor scale without alterations
- **Harmonic minor:** the minor scale with a raised 7th
- **Melodic minor:** raised 6th and 7th going up, natural coming down
- **Leading note:** the note a semitone below the tonic

## Read and watch

- [Minor scales](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/notes-and-scales/minor-scales.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys A B C5 D5 E5 F5 G5
```

```keys E F# G A B C5 D5
```

```chord Am Dm E
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- A harmonic and melodic minor
- E harmonic and melodic minor
- Listen: natural vs harmonic vs melodic

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Each scale form daily, slowly
1. Play Am–Dm–E–Am (i–iv–V–i)
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to turn this week's material into a 20-minute daily practice plan, then change it to fit your actual week. A plan you will not follow is worse than a shorter one you will.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** the bass clef (𝄢) dots surround F; its lines are G B D F A (Good Boys Do Fine Always), the spaces A C E G.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Play A and E harmonic and melodic minor, and play the progression Am–Dm–E–Am.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Revision
lessons.summary: Weeks 1–8 together: scales, chords, progressions and the song, ready for the test.
objectives: You will play each scale and chord from memory
You will find your weakest skill and practise it
You will play your test song cleanly
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- All scales so far at 80 bpm

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: open strings; C, G major; A, E minor (natural, harmonic, melodic); chords C, Am, F, G, Em, D; I–IV–V–I in C and G; strumming pattern; A minor pentatonic; "Holy Are You Lord".

## Understand it

Revision turns what you have **met** into what you can **do on demand**. The test next week checks the second.

**Test yourself rather than just playing through.** Research on learning shows **retrieval** — doing something from memory — strengthens it far more than repeating with the answer in front of you.

**A revision routine (repeat daily this week):**

1. **Tune** the guitar.
2. **Warm up** — chromatic exercise (frets 1-2-3-4 on each string) slowly, alternate picking.
3. **Scales from memory** — C and G major; A and E minor (natural, harmonic, melodic); A minor pentatonic. Metronome on.
4. **Chords on request** — have someone (or a random list) call chords: C, Am, F, G, Em, D. Count how long each takes to sound cleanly.
5. **Progressions** — I–IV–V–I in C and G, with the D–DU–UDU strum.
6. **The song** — "Holy Are You Lord" from the lead sheet, without stopping.

**Rate each item** green (secure), amber (shaky), red (cannot do). Spend **most time on amber**; ask the instructor about red.

**Fix weak spots with slow practice:** isolate the problem (one change, one bar), slow it down, repeat correctly five times, speed up gradually, then put it back.

**Mix topics** in each session (interleaving) — harder, but it sticks better.

Keep your practice log: what you did, for how long, what improved.

## Key words

- **Retrieval practice:** doing something from memory to strengthen it
- **Chromatic exercise:** playing every fret in order to train the fingers
- **Interleaving:** mixing topics in one practice session

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys G A B C5 D5 E5 F#5
```

```keys E F# G A B C5 D5
```

```chord C Am F G Em D
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Self-test the checklist with a partner
- Most time on the two weakest items

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Your own warm-up

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical** (instructor marks): one major and one minor scale; chords on request; I–IV–V–I in C or G; the pentatonic; "Holy Are You Lord". **Written**: the check below. Steady and clean beats fast and messy.

## Understand it

The term test checks what you can play **cleanly, steadily and from memory**, plus what you understand.

**Practical — how instructors usually mark:**

- **Accuracy** — right notes and chords, clean (no buzzing or muted strings).
- **Pulse** — steady tempo, no stopping at chord changes. A slower, steady performance scores higher than a fast one that stops.
- **Technique** — correct fingering, alternate picking, relaxed posture.
- **Musicality** — dynamics, shape, feel.

**Written check — what to know:**

- The open strings (E A D G B E).
- Notes of C and G major; key signatures (G has F♯).
- Relative minor (Am for C, Em for G).
- Harmonic minor raises the 7th; melodic raises 6th and 7th going up.
- I, IV, V in C and G.
- Pentatonic: five notes; A minor pentatonic = A C D E G.
- Chord symbols (Em, D7, G/B).

**On the day:**

1. **Tune** carefully — ask for time if needed.
2. **Warm up** quickly — a scale, a few chord changes.
3. **Breathe** and set your tempo in your head before starting.
4. **Keep going** after a slip — never restart.
5. In the written part, **read each question twice**.

Afterwards, get your marks and **specific feedback** — they set your goals for the next term.

## Key words

- **Practical:** the playing part of a test
- **Pulse:** the steady beat
- **Clean chord:** every note ringing clearly

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

```chord G
```

- Practical test
- Theory check

1. Note what went well and what to improve

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Mindset:** a test shows where you are today, not who you are. Mistakes are information.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Rhythm: strumming patterns and reading rhythm
lessons.summary: Counting in 4/4 and 3/4, eighth-note strumming and accents.
objectives: You will count and strum in 4/4 and 3/4
You will play eighth-note strumming with accents
You will read a simple rhythm chart
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Down-strums on G, counting 1-2-3-4

## Learn (30 minutes)

Keep your strumming hand moving down-up all the time, like a pendulum; only touch the strings when the rhythm says so. In **3/4** (waltz) count 1-2-3 and accent beat 1. **Accents** make a groove: try accenting beats 2 and 4.

## Understand it

Great rhythm guitar is about **time and feel**, not chord shapes. The secret is the **pendulum**:

**Keep the strumming hand moving down-up all the time** — **down on the beat** (1, 2, 3, 4), **up on the "and"** — like a pendulum, whether or not you hit the strings. To create a rhythm, you simply **miss** the strings on some strokes. This keeps your time steady and makes complex patterns easy.

Pattern **D – DU – UDU** in 4/4: count "**1**, **2** and, (3) **and**, **4 and**":

- 1: down (hit)
- 2: down (hit), and: up (hit)
- 3: down (**miss**), and: up (hit)
- 4: down (hit), and: up (hit)

**Reading rhythm** — the same note values as all music: whole (4 beats), half (2), quarter (1), eighth (½), with rests. Rhythm slashes (/) in charts show strums; noteheads on stems show rhythms.

**Time signatures:**

- **4/4** — four beats; most pop, gospel, Afrobeats.
- **3/4** — three beats, **accent beat 1** ("**1**-2-3"): waltzes, some hymns. Strum "**D** D D" or "**D** DU DU".
- **6/8** — two groups of three ("**1**-2-3-**4**-5-6"): a rolling feel, common in African and gospel music.

**Accents** make a groove: hit beats **2 and 4** harder (the backbeat). Use **palm muting** (the side of the strumming hand resting on the strings near the bridge) for a percussive, tight sound.

## Key words

- **Pendulum strumming:** keeping the hand moving down-up continuously
- **Ghost strum:** a strum that deliberately misses the strings
- **Backbeat:** accents on beats 2 and 4
- **Palm muting:** damping the strings with the side of the hand

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons: rhythm and meter](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```chord G C D
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Pendulum strumming at 70 bpm
- 3/4 waltz pattern on G–C–D
- Accents on 2 and 4

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. One strumming pattern a day at a steady tempo
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it for four short sight-reading exercises at your level. Check each one BEFORE you play it: are the notes inside the key, do the bars add up to the time signature? Models get notation wrong, and finding the bad bar is the real exercise. Play each sound one ONCE. Sight-reading only improves on music you have not seen before.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** dotted notes add half their value — a dotted half note lasts 3 beats; a tie joins two notes into one longer sound.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Learn two new strumming patterns and play a song with each.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Run your pieces once, slowly

## Learn (30 minutes)

Introduce, perform (keep going through slips), bow. Choose one song from this term and one in a different style or tempo.

## Understand it

The term showcase is a short performance for an audience — the point of all the practice.

**Choosing two contrasting songs** keeps listeners interested and shows range: one strummed and one picked; or one slow and one fast; or one worship song and one pop or highlife song.

**Preparing:**

- **Play it through without stopping** every day this week — performance practice, not fixing practice.
- **Practise the start and the end** most. A confident start settles your nerves; a clean ending leaves a good impression.
- **Plan recovery points** — if you lose your place, where will you jump back in? (Usually the next chord change or the next chorus.)
- **Rehearse your introduction**: "This is ___ by ___."
- **Check your gear**: strings in good condition, spare pick, tuner, capo if needed, a strap if standing.

**On the day:**

1. **Tune** just before playing (strings drift with temperature and handling).
2. **Sit or stand comfortably**; adjust the strap or footstool.
3. **Introduce** the song, breathe, hear the tempo in your head, start.
4. **Keep going** through slips — keep the strumming hand moving and rejoin at the next chord.
5. **End cleanly** — let the last chord ring, then mute it with your palm; **bow**.

Afterwards: one thing that went well, one to improve. Then celebrate — performing takes courage.

## Key words

- **Showcase:** a short public performance
- **Recovery point:** a place to rejoin after losing your place
- **Contrast:** differences in style, tempo or mood

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

1. Perform for family twice before Saturday

**Performance etiquette:** walk on, acknowledge the audience, settle before you play, bow at the end, thank the people who helped.

lessons.title: The barre chord: F and B♭
lessons.summary: Building the strength and technique for barre chords.
objectives: You will play a full F barre chord
You will move the shape to play other major chords
You will play C–F–G–C with a barre F
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Finger stretch; easy F

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **barre** lays the first finger across all the strings. Roll the finger slightly onto its side, keep the thumb low behind the neck, and press just behind the fret. The E-shape barre at fret 1 is **F**; slide it to fret 3 for **G**, fret 6 for **B♭**.

## Understand it

A **barre chord** uses the index finger as a **movable nut**, pressed across all six strings, while the other fingers form a chord shape above it. Once learnt, one shape plays **every** major chord — you just slide it to a different fret.

**The E-shape barre:**

- Index finger flat across **all six strings** at the barre fret.
- Ring finger on the **A string**, two frets higher; little finger on the **D string**, two frets higher; middle finger on the **G string**, one fret higher — exactly the open E-major shape, moved up.
- At **fret 1** this is **F**; **fret 3** = **G**; **fret 5** = **A**; **fret 6** = **B♭**; **fret 8** = **C**. The chord is named after the note on the **low E string** under your index finger.
- Remove the middle finger to get the **minor** version (Fm, Gm, Am…).

**Making it ring:**

- **Roll the index finger slightly onto its bony side** (towards the headstock) — the side is harder and presses more evenly than the soft middle.
- Press **just behind the fret**.
- **Thumb low** behind the neck, roughly behind the middle finger — not hooked over the top.
- Use **arm weight** (gently pull back with the arm) rather than squeezing with the thumb. Squeezing tires the hand fast.
- Check each string one by one; adjust until they ring.

Barre chords take **weeks** of short daily practice. Practise at **fret 5** first (less tension than fret 1), then work down to F. Rest if the hand hurts.

## Key words

- **Barre chord:** a chord with the index finger across all strings
- **Movable shape:** a chord shape that can slide to any fret
- **E-shape barre:** the open E chord shape moved up the neck

## Read and watch

- [Electric guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/electric_guitar/) — Yamaha
- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```chord C F G
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Barre at fret 1, string by string check
- Move the shape: F, G, A, B♭
- C–F–G–C with barre F

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Barre F for 30 seconds a day, then rest — strength builds slowly
1. Change C → barre F 20 times

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** sharps in key signatures always appear in the order F C G D A E B; flats in the order B E A D G C F.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

objectives: You will use p-i-m-a fingering

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C and G chords

## Learn (30 minutes)

Fingers are named **p** (thumb), **i** (index), **m** (middle), **a** (ring). The thumb plays the bass strings, fingers play the top three. Pattern: p–i–m–a–m–i. The **alternating bass** moves the thumb between two bass strings.

## Understand it

**Finger-picking** (finger-style) means plucking the strings with the fingers instead of a pick. It lets one guitarist play **bass, chords and melody at once** — the sound of folk, ballads, classical, palm-wine and much worship music.

**Finger names** (from Spanish, used in classical notation):

- **p** (pulgar) — thumb: plays the **bass strings** (E, A, D).
- **i** (índice) — index: usually the **G** string.
- **m** (medio) — middle: usually the **B** string.
- **a** (anular) — ring: usually the **high E**.

**Hand position:** wrist slightly arched, hand relaxed over the sound hole (or just behind it), fingers resting near their strings. Pluck **through** the string with the fingertip (and nail, if you have short nails), moving from the knuckle — not pulling outwards.

**Pattern p–i–m–a–m–i** over a C chord: thumb plays the bass (A string), then index–middle–ring–middle–index on G, B, E, B, G — six even notes. Fits 6/8 or a steady eighth-note feel.

**Alternating bass (Travis picking):** the thumb alternates between **two bass strings** on every beat (for C: A string, then D string; for G: low E, then D) while the fingers add notes in between. It creates a full, rolling sound and needs **thumb independence** — the thumb keeps a steady beat no matter what the fingers do.

**Practise slowly** — the thumb alone until steady, then add one finger at a time.

## Key words

- **p i m a:** thumb, index, middle, ring — the picking fingers
- **Finger-style:** playing with the fingers instead of a pick
- **Alternating bass:** the thumb switching between two bass strings on each beat
- **Thumb independence:** the thumb keeping steady time on its own

## Read and watch

- [Classical guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/classical_guitar/) — Yamaha
- [The Guitar School](https://www.classical-guitar-school.com/) — Classical Guitar School


lessons.title: The pop progression and Afrobeats guitar
lessons.summary: I–V–vi–IV and the bright, syncopated picking of Afrobeats guitar.
objectives: You will play I–V–vi–IV in G and C
You will play short Afrobeats picking patterns on the high strings
You will identify the progression in songs
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- G–D–Em–C changes

## Learn (30 minutes)

**I–V–vi–IV** in G is **G–D–Em–C**. Afrobeats guitar often plays short, bright, repeating **single-note or two-note riffs** high on the neck, muted between notes, locking with the drums rather than strumming full chords.

## Understand it

**I–V–vi–IV** — the "pop progression" — runs under countless hits. In G: **G – D – Em – C**. In C: **C – G – Am – F**. Starting at **vi** (Em – C – G – D) gives a more emotional colour.

**Afrobeats guitar** usually does **not** strum big open chords. Instead, guitarists play:

- **Short, bright riffs** — single notes or **two-note shapes (double stops)**, often high on the neck (frets 7–12) on the **B and high E strings**.
- **Muted between notes** — lift the fretting finger slightly or rest the strumming hand to stop notes ringing; this gives a clean, **staccato**, percussive sound.
- **Syncopated rhythms** that lock with the drums and percussion, often on the off-beats ("and"s and the sixteenth notes in between).
- **Repetition** — a one- or two-bar riff looped through a section, with small variations.
- A **clean electric tone**, sometimes with a little chorus or delay.

This tradition goes back through **highlife** and **jùjú** guitar, where interlocking guitar lines were central.

**Try it:** play the pop progression using only **two notes** per chord — e.g. the top two notes of each chord shape on the B and E strings — in a syncopated rhythm, muting between notes. Play along with an Afrobeats track at 100–110 bpm and copy the riff's **rhythm** before its notes.

## Key words

- **Pop progression:** I–V–vi–IV
- **Riff:** a short repeated musical phrase
- **Double stop:** two notes played together
- **Muting:** stopping strings from ringing for a short, percussive sound

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Search: jùjú music](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=juju%20music) — Google Arts & Culture

```chord G D Em C
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- G–D–Em–C strummed
- Afrobeats riff on the B and high E strings
- Play along to a track

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Loop the riff to a metronome for 3 minutes

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Instrument care:** learn to tune by ear and with a tuner; change strings when they sound dull or won't stay in tune.

- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

lessons.title: Highlife guitar
lessons.summary: The bright, interlocking palm-wine and highlife guitar style of West Africa.
objectives: You will play a highlife picking pattern
You will combine bass notes and treble melody
You will play a highlife song
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- C–F–G–C finger-picked

## Learn (30 minutes)

Highlife guitar (and its ancestor, **palm-wine**) combines a bass line on the thumb with a sweet, repeating melody on the treble strings, often in thirds. It is played light and lilting, over I–IV–V progressions.

## Understand it

**Highlife** grew in Ghana and Nigeria in the early 20th century, and its guitar style came largely from **palm-wine music** — informal guitar music played by sailors and workers in West African port towns, mixing local melodies with influences from Caribbean and Western guitar.

**The palm-wine and highlife guitar style:**

- **The thumb plays a steady bass line** — often alternating between the root and the fifth of the chord.
- **The fingers play a sweet, repeating melody** on the treble strings, often in **thirds** or **sixths** (two notes moving together in parallel).
- **Interlocking parts** — in bands, two or more guitars play different patterns that fit together like a puzzle, each simple on its own.
- **I–IV–V harmony**, mostly major keys — bright and joyful.
- **Light, lilting feel** — relaxed, never heavy; it should make people want to dance.

**Listen to the masters:** Nigerian highlife guitar includes players and bandleaders such as **Victor Uwaifo**, **Rex Lawson**'s bands and **Osita Osadebe**; Ghanaian highlife includes **E. T. Mensah** and **Koo Nimo** (palm-wine). Jùjú guitar (King Sunny Adé, Ebenezer Obey) developed from the same roots.

**Try:** play C – F – G – C with the thumb alternating bass notes (C–G for C; F–C for F; G–D for G) while the fingers pick a simple melody in **thirds** on the G and B strings. Keep it light and steady.

## Key words

- **Highlife:** West African dance music with melodic guitar and horns
- **Palm-wine music:** an acoustic guitar style from West African ports
- **Thirds:** two notes three scale-steps apart, played together
- **Interlocking:** separate parts that fit together into one pattern

## Read and watch

- [Search: highlife](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=highlife) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Search: King Sunny Adé](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=king%20sunny%20ade) — Google Arts & Culture

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E F G A B
```

```chord C F G
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Thumb bass + treble thirds on C–F–G
- Learn a classic highlife riff
- Play with a partner on chords

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Highlife pattern daily
1. Listen to two highlife recordings
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Nigerian music history:** Afrobeats grew from Afrobeat (Fela Kuti, 1970s), highlife and hip-hop. Listen to one track from each and spot what was carried forward.

## Make it fit you

lessons.title: Gospel and worship guitar
lessons.summary: Leading worship: capo use, sus chords and dynamics.
objectives: You will use a capo to change key
You will add sus2 and sus4 colours
You will build dynamics from verse to chorus
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- G–C–D–G

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **capo** clamps across the frets so the same shapes sound higher — G shapes with a capo at fret 2 sound in A. **Sus** chords (Dsus4, Dsus2) replace the 3rd with a 4th or 2nd for a floating sound. Worship guitar builds from soft picking in verses to full strumming in choruses.

## Understand it

Worship guitar serves the congregation: it must support singing, follow the worship leader, and match the mood of each moment.

**The capo** clamps across all the strings at a fret, raising every string's pitch. It lets you use **familiar open-chord shapes in any key**:

- **Capo 2 + G shapes** (G – C – D – Em) sounds in **A** (A – D – E – F♯m).
- **Capo 3 + G shapes** sounds in **B♭**.
- **Capo 2 + C shapes** sounds in **D**.

To find where to put it: count the semitones from your shape key to the song's key. Chord charts often say "Capo 2, play G shapes".

**Sus chords** — **suspended** — replace the 3rd of a chord with the **4th (sus4)** or **2nd (sus2)**. Without a 3rd, the chord is neither major nor minor: it sounds open and floating, then **resolves** when the 3rd returns. **D → Dsus4 → D** (add the little finger on high E fret 3, then lift it) is a classic worship move. **Dsus2**: lift the finger off the high E.

**Dynamics follow the worship:**

- **Verses / reflective moments** — soft finger-picking, single strums, or palm-muted eighths.
- **Build** — gradually fuller strumming, adding beats.
- **Choruses** — full, driving strumming.
- **Watch the worship leader** — songs repeat, slow down, or stop according to the moment.

Tune carefully, and agree keys in advance with the singers.

## Key words

- **Capo:** a clamp raising the pitch of all strings
- **Sus chord:** a chord with the 3rd replaced by a 2nd or 4th
- **Resolution:** tension moving to stability
- **Dynamics:** changes in loudness

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Acoustic guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/acoustic_guitar/) — Yamaha

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E F G A B
```

```chord G C D
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Capo on 2: play G shapes, name the real key
- Dsus4 → D, Csus2 → C
- Verse soft, chorus full

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Play a worship song with a capo
1. Add sus chords to it
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Nigerian music history:** highlife began in Ghana and Nigeria in the early 1900s; Nigerian greats include Victor Olaiya, Rex Lawson and Osita Osadebe. Gospel and church music trained many of Nigeria's best musicians.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Ear training: chords and riffs by ear
lessons.summary: Telling major from minor and working out simple songs by ear.
objectives: You will tell major and minor chords apart by ear
You will find a song's first chord by ear
You will work out a short riff
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Strum G, then Em — listen to the difference

## Learn (30 minutes)

Hum the lowest note you hear in the song — that is usually the chord's root. Try the major and minor chord on that root; your ear will tell you which fits. Riffs: find the first note, then move one fret at a time.

## Understand it

Playing by ear — working out songs from recordings — is how most guitarists learn their favourite music, and it trains your ear for everything else.

**Finding the chords:**

1. **Find the key** — the note that feels like "home" at the end of a chorus. Hum it; find it on the low E or A string.
2. **Hum the lowest note** in each section — the bass note is usually the **root** of the chord.
3. **Try the major and minor chord** on that root; your ear will tell you which fits.
4. **Use the key's chord family** — in G, the likely chords are G, C, D, Em (and Am, Bm). Most songs use only these.
5. **Note where chords change** — count the beats in each.

**Finding a riff or melody:**

1. **Sing it** until you know it exactly.
2. **Find the first note** — try notes on one string until one matches.
3. For each next note: **higher or lower? a little or a lot?** Move one fret at a time.
4. Work in **short chunks** — three or four notes.
5. Check the **rhythm** as well as the notes.

**Tools:** slow the recording down (YouTube's playback speed, or a slow-downer app) without changing the pitch. Loop the hard part.

**Check chord sites critically** — online chord charts are often wrong by a chord or a key. Use your ear to check them.

## Key words

- **Playing by ear:** working music out by listening
- **Chord family:** the chords belonging to a key
- **Root:** the note a chord is named after
- **Transcribe:** work out and write down music from a recording

## Read and watch

- [Ear training exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web: ear training](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

## Play (40 minutes)

- Major or minor? (instructor plays)
- Find the key of a song by ear
- Work out a riff

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. 10 minutes of ear practice daily
1. Work out the chords of a simple song
1. **With a tool —** Use an ear-training app to drill the intervals in this lesson for five minutes. Sing or hum the interval before you answer; an app that only tests recognition trains your eyes, not your ear.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Ear:** sing before you play. If you can sing it, you can find it on your instrument.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Improvising lead guitar
lessons.summary: Using the pentatonic with bends, slides and hammer-ons to build solos.
objectives: You will use hammer-ons, pull-offs and slides
You will play a half-step and whole-step bend
You will improvise a 12-bar solo
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- A minor pentatonic shape 1

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Hammer-on**: pick a note, then press a higher fret without picking. **Pull-off**: the reverse. **Slide**: move one finger along the string. **Bend**: push the string up to raise the pitch — check it reaches the target note. A solo is a conversation: short phrases, then space.

## Understand it

**Articulation techniques** make lead guitar sound like singing rather than a typewriter. Four are essential:

- **Hammer-on** — pick a note, then bring another finger down **hard** on a higher fret of the same string **without picking**. The second note sounds from the force of the finger.
- **Pull-off** — the reverse: with two fingers fretted, pick the higher note, then **pull** the finger **sideways** off the string (slightly plucking it) so the lower note sounds.
- **Slide** — pick a note and **slide** the same finger along the string to another fret, keeping pressure. Glides between notes.
- **Bend** — push (or pull) the string **across** the fretboard to raise the pitch. Use **two or three fingers** together for strength. A **whole-step bend** must reach the pitch of the note two frets higher — check by playing that note first. Out-of-tune bends are the commonest lead-guitar fault.
- **Vibrato** — small repeated bends that make a held note sing.

**Phrasing — a solo is a conversation:**

- **Short phrases with space** between them — like sentences with pauses. Beginners often play constantly; good players leave room.
- **Call and response** — play a phrase, then answer it.
- **Repeat and vary** an idea rather than always playing something new.
- **Target chord tones** at the start of each chord — it makes the solo fit.
- **Tell a story** — start simple and low; build up; finish strongly.

Use the A minor pentatonic (week 6) as your note set.

## Key words

- **Hammer-on / pull-off:** sounding notes with the fretting hand alone
- **Bend:** pushing a string to raise its pitch
- **Vibrato:** small repeated bends for a singing sound
- **Phrasing:** shaping a solo into musical sentences

## Read and watch

- [Electric guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/electric_guitar/) — Yamaha
- [Make melodies](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-melodies/make-melodies.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys A C5 D5 E5 G5
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Each technique on the pentatonic
- Solo over a 12-bar blues in A
- Trade 4 bars with a partner

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. 5 minutes of improvisation daily over a backing track
1. Record one solo
1. **With an AI assistant —** use it for ideas — a chord progression, a rhythm, a title — then make them yours at the instrument. Hand in what YOU played. A piece you cannot perform is not your piece.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Creativity:** improvising is composing in real time — there are no wrong notes, only notes you haven't resolved yet.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

Record a one-minute improvised solo using at least two techniques (bend, slide, hammer-on or pull-off).

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Accompanying a singer
lessons.summary: Intros, steady patterns, dynamics and following the voice.
objectives: You will play an introduction
You will keep a steady pattern while someone sings
You will use dynamics to support the song
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Finger-picking pattern

## Learn (30 minutes)

Lead in with a short intro, keep time, listen. Play softer in verses (pick or light strum) and fuller in choruses. Watch the singer at the start of each line.

## Understand it

When you accompany a singer, the singer is the centre of the music — your job is to **support, follow and frame** them.

**Before the performance:**

- **Agree the key** — the singer's comfortable range decides it. Use a **capo** to move a song into their key while keeping easy shapes.
- **Agree the structure** — intro, verses, choruses, any repeats, the ending.
- **Agree the tempo** — play a bar so the singer can check it.

**The introduction:** usually the last line's chords or a short riff — enough to set **key**, **tempo** and **feel**, ending clearly so the singer knows when to come in. A slight pause or held chord before their entry helps.

**While they sing:**

- **Play softer in verses** — light picking or gentle strumming — and **fuller in choruses**. The guitar should never cover the words.
- **Keep steady time** — singers lean on your rhythm.
- **Watch the singer** at the start of each line — they may hold a note, breathe longer, or skip ahead.
- **Fill the gaps** — small riffs or a strum pattern change when they breathe, never over the lyrics.
- **Follow them** if they speed up or slow down; do not drag them back.

**If something goes wrong** (they come in early, forget a verse), **adjust instantly** and keep going — the audience should never know. Rehearse the **ending** together: a held chord with a nod is the simplest.

## Key words

- **Accompaniment:** music that supports a soloist
- **Intro:** the opening that sets key and tempo
- **Range:** the span of notes a singer can sing comfortably
- **Cue:** a visual signal between performers

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize
- [Taking care of your voice (for singers you accompany)](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/taking-care-your-voice) — US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E F G A B
```

- Write and play a 4-bar intro
- Accompany a classmate
- Mark soft and loud sections

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Accompany someone at home twice
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Teamwork:** in music, listening is half of playing. Watch the leader and the singer; agree endings before you start.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Ensemble: guitar in a band
lessons.summary: Rhythm and lead roles, leaving space and locking with bass and drums.
objectives: You will play rhythm guitar under a lead part
You will follow an arrangement
You will lock to the drums
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- I–V–vi–IV in G

## Learn (30 minutes)

Two guitars should **not** play the same thing: one strums lower, the other plays higher riffs or a capo shape. Agree the arrangement — intro, verse, chorus, ending — and watch the drummer for the count-in.

## Understand it

In a band, a guitarist must **fit in**, not fill everything. Too many instruments playing the same notes in the same range makes a band sound muddy and small.

**Two guitars:**

- **Different roles** — one plays **rhythm** (chords, strumming, lower and fuller), the other plays **lead** or **riffs** (single notes, higher, more sparse).
- **Different registers** — one in open position, the other higher on the neck or with a **capo** (e.g. one plays G shapes open, the other plays D shapes with capo 5 — same chords, different voicings and range).
- **Different rhythms** — one strums eighths, the other plays syncopated stabs.

**With bass and keys:**

- The **bass** owns the low end — the guitar rarely needs to hammer the low E string.
- If the **keys** play full chords, the guitar can play **small two- or three-note shapes** on the top strings.

**Locking with the drums:** strum with the **hi-hat pattern**; accent with the **snare** on 2 and 4. Watch the drummer for the **count-in** ("1, 2, 3, 4") and fills that signal section changes.

**Agree the arrangement:** who plays in the intro? Which section is quiet? Who takes a solo? How does it end? Write a simple **chart** and rehearse **transitions** and **endings** most.

**Volume:** on electric guitar, set your amp so you can hear yourself **and** the singer. If you cannot hear the vocals, you are too loud.

## Key words

- **Rhythm guitar:** the chordal, timekeeping guitar part
- **Lead guitar:** melodic lines, riffs and solos
- **Voicing:** the particular arrangement of a chord's notes
- **Arrangement:** the plan of who plays what, when

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Electric guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/electric_guitar/) — Yamaha

```keys C D E F G A B
```

- Class band: one song, rotate rhythm and lead
- Capo version vs open version together

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Describe the guitar parts in two band recordings
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Teamwork:** a band is a team — arrive on time, know your part, respect other musicians' instruments, and never play over someone's solo.

lessons.summary: A chord progression, a melody, lyrics and a verse–chorus form.
objectives: You will choose a key and progression
You will write a verse and a chorus
You will perform your song
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Pentatonic improvisation

## Learn (30 minutes)

Most songs use **verse–chorus** form: verses tell the story, the chorus repeats the main idea. Start with a progression, hum a melody over it, then fit words. Record ideas on your phone so you don't lose them.

## Understand it

Writing a song is where everything you have learnt becomes **yours**.

**Song form.** Most popular songs use **verse–chorus** form:

- **Verses** — tell the story; the lyrics change each time; the music is usually calmer and lower.
- **Chorus** — the main idea or **hook**; the same words each time; bigger, higher, more memorable.
- Optional **pre-chorus** (builds into the chorus) and **bridge** (a contrasting section near the end).
- A common order: **Verse – Chorus – Verse – Chorus – Bridge – Chorus**.

**A practical method:**

1. **Choose a progression** — I–IV–V–I, I–V–vi–IV, or two chords in a groove. Use a different progression (or rhythm) for verse and chorus to create contrast.
2. **Hum a melody** over it — record many ideas on your phone; most will be thrown away, which is normal.
3. **Find the hook** — a short, catchy phrase (words and melody) that sums up the song. Build the chorus around it.
4. **Fit the words** — write what you actually mean, in your own voice and languages. Concrete images ("the generator noise at midnight") beat vague ones ("I feel so sad").
5. **Match word stress to the beat** — stressed syllables on strong beats.
6. **Write it down** — lyrics with chord names above the words, and a voice recording.

Play it for someone; ask what they remember — if they remember the chorus, it is working.

## Key words

- **Verse–chorus form:** verses that change, a chorus that repeats
- **Hook:** the catchiest, most memorable part
- **Bridge:** a contrasting section before the last chorus
- **Lyric sheet:** lyrics with chord names written above

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Make melodies](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-melodies/make-melodies.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## Play (40 minutes)

- Choose a progression for verse and chorus
- Write the chorus first
- Add one verse

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Finish your song and give it a title

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Copyright:** a song belongs to its writer. Performing covers in class is fine; posting them online or selling them needs permission. Your own compositions are yours — keep dated recordings.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play everything above at a faster tempo (add 10 bpm), from memory, and teach one part of it to a classmate.

lessons.title: Revision
lessons.summary: The whole year together: barre chords, picking, styles, ear and performance.
objectives: You will self-test the Term 2 checklist
You will polish your test pieces
You will plan your final week
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Barre F and B♭; pentatonic

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: barre F and B♭; finger-picking pattern; I–V–vi–IV; an Afrobeats, highlife or worship part; bends and slides; ear-worked song; your original song.

## Understand it

The final revision covers the whole year — plan it, rather than playing only what you enjoy.

**The year's skills:**

- **Technique** — open strings and tuning; C and G major; A and E minor (natural, harmonic, melodic); A minor pentatonic; alternate picking.
- **Chords** — C, Am, F (easy and barre), G, Em, D, barre F and B♭; sus chords; capo use.
- **Rhythm** — pendulum strumming; D–DU–UDU; 3/4 and 6/8; palm muting.
- **Finger-picking** — p–i–m–a patterns; alternating bass.
- **Progressions** — I–IV–V–I; I–V–vi–IV.
- **Styles** — Afrobeats riffs; highlife; worship.
- **Lead** — hammer-ons, pull-offs, slides, bends, phrasing.
- **Ear** — chords and riffs by ear.
- **Your song**.

**Daily plan this week:** tune → warm up → a technique item → a chord/rhythm item → a style item → your recital pieces → your song. Rotate the items so everything gets covered twice.

**Barre chords** need special attention: practise them in short bursts several times a day — strength builds with frequency, not long sessions.

**Recital pieces:** daily performance runs, start to finish. Record one and listen for steady time, clean chords and dynamics.

**Look after your hands** — warm up, rest when tired, and never play through pain. Change old strings a few days before the recital so they settle in tune.

## Key words

- **Revision plan:** a structured schedule covering all topics
- **Performance run:** playing straight through without stopping
- **String change:** replacing worn strings for better tone and tuning

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Acoustic guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/acoustic_guitar/) — Yamaha

## Play (40 minutes)

- Self-test with a partner
- Fix the two weakest items
- Run your test pieces

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Checklist once a day; 10 minutes on the weakest item

## Essentials (10 minutes)

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical**: a major and a minor scale; barre chords; a progression with a strumming or picking pattern; one style part; a prepared piece; your song. **Written**: the check below. **Recital**: perform for families and friends.

## Understand it

The final test and graduation recital close Year 1 — from your first open strings to barre chords, finger-picking, lead playing, several styles and a song of your own.

**The test:** scales, barre chords, a progression with a strumming or picking pattern, a style part, a prepared piece and your song, plus a written check. Remember: **clean and steady beats fast and messy**; **never restart**; tune carefully before you begin.

**The recital:**

- **Build a short programme with contrast** — perhaps a finger-picked piece, a strummed song, a style piece (highlife, Afrobeats, worship) and your own song.
- **Introduce each piece** in one sentence. For your own song, say what it is about.
- **Stage routine** — walk on, tune quietly, settle, introduce, breathe, play, let the last chord ring and mute it, bow.
- **If a string breaks** (it happens!) — stay calm; finish the song if you can, or pause, change guitar or string, and continue. Keep a spare set of strings and a tuner in your case.

**Your portfolio** — recordings of your recital, your song's lyric sheet and recording, and your practice log. Compare with your first recordings from week 1.

**Reflect and plan Year 2:**

- What are you most **proud** of?
- What is still **hardest**?
- Which **style** do you want to go deeper into?
- Which **practice habits** worked?

Write down two specific goals for next year.

- **Programme:** the order of pieces in a recital
- **Portfolio:** recordings and materials showing your progress
- **Contrast:** variety of style, tempo and mood

**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo

## Learn (30 minutes)

Year 2 builds **independence, reading and harmony**. Today the instructor checks each player on scales, chords, reading and a piece, and you set your own goals. Players who are ahead take the stretch work every week; players who need more time revisit Year 1 skills listed in their plan.

## Understand it

Year 2 builds on the foundation with three big themes: **independence** (each hand doing a different job well), **reading** (both clefs, fluently), and **harmony** (the full chord family, sevenths, minor keys).

**Why a technique check first?** Over a break, skills fade unevenly — scales may survive while reading slips. A quick check of **scales, chords, reading and one piece** shows where each player really is, so practice time goes where it matters.

**Setting good goals** — make them **specific, measurable and time-bound**:

- Weak: "Get better at piano."
- Strong: "Play all major scales hands together, two octaves, at 80 bpm in quavers, by week 11."
- Strong: "Sight-read a Grade 2 piece with no stops by the end of term."

Write **three goals** — one technique, one reading or theory, one musical (a piece or style you want to play) — and check them at mid-term.

**Practice planning for Year 2:** with more material, structure matters:

1. **Warm-up** (5 min) — scales or arpeggios.
2. **Technique** (5–10 min) — the current focus.
3. **Reading** (5 min) — a short sight-reading piece every day.
4. **Repertoire** (10–15 min) — slow work on hard bars, then a run.
5. **Creative** (5 min) — improvise, play by ear, or style work.

Keep the **practice log**: it shows patterns (which days you skip, what improves fastest) and is evidence of progress.

## Key words

- **Technique check:** a quick assessment of current skill level
- **SMART goal:** Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
- **Practice plan:** a structured order for each practice session

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Hands-together scales need the thumbs to cross at different moments — say the finger numbers aloud. Learn the groups: C, G, D, A, E share one fingering (RH 123 1234); F starts on 1 but turns after 4 (RH 1234 123); black-key scales start on finger 2 or 3.

## Understand it

Playing **hands together** in scales is hard because the two thumbs cross at **different moments** — the hands are mirror images. Fluency comes from knowing the fingering groups thoroughly, hands separately first.

**Fingering groups:**

- **C, G, D, A, E major** — the same pattern. Right hand up: **1 2 3 1 2 3 4 (5)**. Left hand up: **5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1**. In two octaves the right hand's 4th finger plays the 7th note, and the thumb continues.
- **F major** — right hand **1 2 3 4 1 2 3 (4)** (finger 4 on B♭); left hand as normal.
- **B major** — right hand normal; left hand **4 3 2 1 4 3 2 1**.
- **Black-key scales** (B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭/F♯) — the thumbs play only **white keys**; fingers 4 often fall on B♭. Learn each from a fingering chart.

**The general rule:** the **thumb never plays a black key** in standard scale fingering; finger 4 plays a given note **once per octave** — find where your 4 goes and the rest follows.

**Practising hands together:**

1. Each hand alone, fluent, **saying the finger numbers**.
2. Together **very slowly** — one note per beat at 60 bpm.
3. Notice **where each thumb crosses** — they are almost never together.
4. Play in **contrary motion** (hands moving apart from the same note) — for many players it is easier, since the fingering mirrors.
5. Increase speed by small steps; **evenness first**.

Listen for **both hands landing exactly together** on every note.

## Key words

- **Hands together:** both hands playing at once
- **Fingering group:** scales that share the same fingering
- **Contrary motion:** hands moving in opposite directions
- **Parallel motion:** hands moving in the same direction

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons: scales](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Piano](https://www.classicfm.com/discover-music/instruments/piano/) — Classic FM

