lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

An **arpeggio** is a chord played one note at a time across octaves. Fingering for C major root position: RH 1 2 3 1 2 3 5, LH 5 4 2 1 4 2 1. Arpeggios train the hand to stretch and the thumb to pass smoothly — the basis of flowing accompaniment.

## Understand it

An **arpeggio** is a chord played **one note at a time**, usually across more than one octave: C–E–G–C–E–G–C. Arpeggios build **stretch**, **thumb passing** and **evenness** — and they are everywhere in piano music, from classical to gospel to ballads.

**C major arpeggio, root position, two octaves:**

- **Right hand up**: 1 2 3 – 1 2 3 – 5. The thumb passes under after finger 3, stretching from G to the next C.
- **Left hand up**: 5 4 2 – 1 4 2 – 1. Finger 4 crosses over the thumb.

(For some hands, 1 2 4 is more comfortable than 1 2 3 — your teacher will advise.)

**Technique for smooth arpeggios:**

- **The wrist and arm travel sideways** with the notes — do not stretch the hand and leave the arm behind.
- **The thumb moves early** — it starts travelling under the hand as soon as it has played.
- **No bumps** at the thumb crossing — listen for an even line.
- **Relax** between notes; stretch only as needed.

**Broken-chord accompaniment patterns** use the same notes in repeating shapes:

- **Alberti bass** — low–high–middle–high.
- **Rolling arpeggios** — root–fifth–tenth (C–G–E above).
- **Root–fifth–octave–fifth** — a spacious ballad pattern.

Practise major and minor arpeggios in C, G, F, A minor and D minor, then apply them as accompaniment under a melody.

## Key words

- **Arpeggio:** a chord played one note at a time across octaves
- **Thumb passing:** moving the thumb under smoothly
- **Broken-chord pattern:** a repeated arrangement of chord notes

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Piano](https://www.classicfm.com/discover-music/instruments/piano/) — Classic FM


- Alberti bass (1-5-3-5) on C–F–G–C
- Accompany a ballad with arpeggios

1. Work on: Arpeggios hands separately, then together
1. Then: Accompany a ballad with arpeggios
1. Record one take and listen back

**Reading:** ledger lines extend the stave above and below; practise reading notes two ledger lines out.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

The **grand staff** joins treble and bass with a brace; middle C sits between them. Read vertically: find the bass note, then the treble, and look for chord shapes rather than single notes. Keep going — sight-reading is about rhythm first, notes second.

## Understand it

Piano music uses the **grand staff**: two staves joined by a **brace**. The **treble clef** (top) usually shows the right hand; the **bass clef** (bottom) the left. **Middle C** sits on a ledger line exactly between them.

**Bass clef notes:**

- **Lines** (bottom to top): **G B D F A** — "Good Boys Do Fine Always".
- **Spaces**: **A C E G** — "All Cows Eat Grass".
- The bass clef's two dots surround the **F line** — it is also called the F clef.

**Treble clef:** lines **E G B D F**; spaces **F A C E**.

**Landmark notes** speed up reading: find a few you know instantly — middle C, treble G (second line), bass F (fourth line), the Cs an octave above and below middle C — and read other notes by **interval** from them ("one line up" = up a third).

**Reading both hands together:**

- **Read vertically** — notes stacked above each other are played together.
- **See shapes, not single notes** — a stack of three notes on lines is a triad; a repeated pattern is the same shape.
- **Read ahead** — the eyes should be a beat or two ahead of the hands.

**Sight-reading rules:**

1. Before playing, scan **key signature**, **time signature**, the **highest and lowest notes**, and tricky **rhythms**.
2. Choose a **slow tempo** you can keep.
3. **Never stop** — keep the pulse even if you miss notes. Sight-reading is about **rhythm and continuity** first.
4. Practise **a little every day** with easy material.

## Key words

- **Grand staff:** treble and bass staves joined by a brace
- **Bass clef:** the F clef, used mainly for the left hand
- **Landmark note:** a note recognised instantly, used to read others
- **Sight-reading:** playing music on first sight

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons: clefs and the staff](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Note identification exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- Note-reading drill on both clefs
- Sight-read three Grade 1–2 pieces
- Clap the rhythm before playing

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Note-reading drill on both clefs
1. Then: Clap the rhythm before playing
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it for four short sight-reading exercises at your level. Check each one BEFORE you play it: are the notes inside the key, do the bars add up to the time signature? Models get notation wrong, and finding the bad bar is the real exercise. Play each sound one ONCE. Sight-reading only improves on music you have not seen before.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** the primary chords are I, IV and V; the secondary chords are ii, iii and vi — all six come from the scale.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Sight-read a Grade 3 piece at a steady tempo.

## This week's assignment

Sight-read one new short piece a day and log which you found hardest.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: The full chord family: I ii iii IV V vi
lessons.summary: Every chord in the key, and the progressions built from them.
objectives: You will build all chords in C, G and F
You will play ii–V–I and I–vi–ii–V
You will find these progressions in songs
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Build a triad on every scale note: in C they are **C Dm Em F G Am** (and B°). Major chords on I, IV, V; minor on ii, iii, vi. Now you can play ii–V–I (Dm–G–C), the most important progression in gospel and jazz, and I–vi–ii–V (C–Am–Dm–G).

## Understand it

Build a triad on **every note** of a major scale, using only notes of that scale, and you get its full **chord family** — the chords that sound "at home" in that key.

In **C major**:

| Degree | I | ii | iii | IV | V | vi | vii° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chord | C | Dm | Em | F | G | Am | B° |
| Quality | major | minor | minor | major | major | minor | diminished |

This pattern — **major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished** — is the same in **every** major key. In G: G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F♯°. Upper-case numerals are major chords; lower-case are minor; ° is diminished (two minor thirds, a tense sound).

**Thinking in numbers** lets you play any song in any key: "I–vi–IV–V" is C–Am–F–G in C and G–Em–C–D in G.

**Key progressions:**

- **ii–V–I** (Dm–G–C) — the most important progression in **gospel and jazz**. The ii prepares the V, which resolves to I. The roots move in fourths (D up to G up to C), which sounds strong and natural.
- **I–vi–ii–V** (C–Am–Dm–G) — the "doo-wop" or "rhythm changes" turnaround; loops back to I.
- **I–V–vi–IV** — the pop progression.
- **vi–IV–I–V** — its emotional cousin.

**Practise:** play each progression in C, G and F, with smooth voice leading (right hand) and roots (left hand). Then find them in songs you know.

## Key words

- **Chord family:** the triads built on each note of a key
- **Scale degree:** a note's position in the scale (1–7)
- **Diminished chord:** a triad of two minor thirds
- **ii–V–I:** the key progression of gospel and jazz

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons: diatonic triads](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- Chords of the key, up and down
- ii–V–I in C, G and F
- I–vi–ii–V loop with inversions

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Chords of the key, up and down
1. Then: I–vi–ii–V loop with inversions
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Listening:** listen to a full song and map its form: intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, outro. Time each section.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play ii–V–I in all twelve keys round the circle of fifths.

## This week's assignment

Play ii–V–I in three keys and find one song using I–vi–ii–V.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

objectives: You will balance melody over accompaniment

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Voicing** means making one part louder than another. The right-hand melody should sing with weight from the arm; the left-hand accompaniment stays light. Practise each hand alone at its correct volume, then together.

## Understand it

In most music, the **melody** must be heard clearly above the **accompaniment**. On the piano — where one player plays both — this needs **hand independence**: each hand playing different notes, rhythms and **volumes** at the same time.

**Voicing** (in this sense) means **balancing** parts — making one louder than another. Typically:

- **Melody** (right hand): **singing**, with weight from the arm — around *mf*.
- **Accompaniment** (left hand): **light**, supportive — around *p*.

When both hands play at the same volume, the melody gets lost.

**How to produce different volumes at once:**

- **Volume comes from speed of key descent**, not from pressing harder after the key is down. A melody note is played with a **faster** key stroke, using **arm weight** through a firm fingertip.
- The accompaniment hand plays **closer to the keys**, with **less movement**.
- Within one hand (e.g. melody on top of right-hand chords), **lean towards the top finger** (usually 4 or 5) so the top note sings.

**Practice steps:**

1. Each hand **alone** at its **correct** volume.
2. Right hand loud, left hand **silent** (just touching keys) — feel the different roles.
3. Together, very slowly, listening for the balance.
4. Record yourself — balance is hard to judge while playing.

Independence also means **different rhythms**: e.g. left hand steady crotchets while right hand plays a syncopated melody. Practise by **tapping** the two rhythms on your knees first.

## Key words

- **Hand independence:** each hand playing different material well at once
- **Balance (voicing):** making the melody louder than the accompaniment
- **Arm weight:** using the arm's weight for a full tone

lessons.title: Compound time and swing
lessons.summary: 6/8, 12/8 and the swing feel of blues, gospel and highlife.
objectives: You will count and play in 6/8 and 12/8
You will swing eighth notes
You will play a 12/8 gospel ballad pattern
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

In **6/8** there are two big beats, each split into three. **Swing** plays pairs of eighth notes long–short (like triplets: 'doo-ba'). Slow gospel ballads are often in 12/8 — four beats each split in three.

## Understand it

**Simple time** divides each beat into **two** (4/4: "1 and 2 and"). **Compound time** divides each beat into **three**.

- **6/8** — **two** big beats per bar, each a **dotted crotchet** split into three quavers: "**1** 2 3 **4** 5 6". It rolls and sways — very common in African, gospel and folk music, and in lullabies.
- **9/8** — three big beats, each split into three.
- **12/8** — **four** big beats, each split into three: "**1** 2 3 **2** 2 3 **3** 2 3 **4** 2 3". The feel of **slow gospel ballads**, soul and blues.

The top number counts the **small** beats (quavers); feel the **big** beats. A 6/8 piece is felt in two, not six.

**Swing** is a way of playing pairs of quavers **unevenly**: **long–short** ("doo-ba, doo-ba"), roughly like the first two thirds and last third of a triplet. Written music often shows straight quavers with the instruction **"Swing"** or a symbol (♫ = ♩♪ in triplet brackets). Swing is the basic feel of **jazz, blues, many gospel songs** and some hip-hop.

**Straight vs swung** — play the same melody both ways: straight sounds square; swung sounds relaxed and bouncy.

**Practise:**

- Count 12/8 aloud while playing slow gospel chords (one chord per big beat, with the triplet feel in the right hand).
- Swing a C major scale in quavers with a metronome on beats 2 and 4.

## Key words

- **Simple time:** beats divided into two
- **Compound time:** beats divided into three, e.g. 6/8, 12/8
- **Swing:** pairs of quavers played long–short
- **Triplet:** three notes in the time of two

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons: time signatures](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Rhythm exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues
lessons.summary: The form behind blues, rock'n'roll and jazz, with left-hand boogie patterns.
objectives: You will play the 12-bar blues form
You will play a boogie-woogie left hand
You will improvise with the blues scale
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

The **12-bar blues** in C: C C C C | F F C C | G F C G. Left hand: a boogie pattern (C–E–G–A–B♭–A–G–E). Right hand: chord stabs or the blues scale (C E♭ F F♯ G B♭).

## Understand it

The **12-bar blues** is one of the most influential forms in popular music — the root of jazz, rock and roll, R&B and soul. It is a 12-bar chord pattern repeated for every verse and solo.

**In C:**

| C | C | C | C |
| F | F | C | C |
| G | F | C | G |

(I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V) — the last bar's V (the **turnaround**) leads back to the start. Variations use the IV in bar 2 ("quick change") or seventh chords throughout (C7, F7, G7).

**Boogie-woogie left hand:** a walking pattern on each chord, e.g. for C: **C–E–G–A–B♭–A–G–E** in quavers (swung). Move the same shape to F and G. It drives the groove.

**The blues scale** — the minor pentatonic plus the **flattened 5th**: on C, **C E♭ F F♯(G♭) G B♭ C**. The **"blue notes"** (E♭, G♭, B♭) clash beautifully against the major chords — the essential blues sound. Slide from E♭ to E (a "crushed" note) to imitate a singer or guitarist bending.

**Right hand:**

- **Chord stabs** — short C7 or F7 chords on off-beats.
- **Riffs** — a short blues-scale phrase repeated over each chord change.
- **Call and response** — a phrase, a rest, an answer.

Play with a **swing** feel. Count bars carefully — losing your place in the 12 bars is the commonest blues mistake.

## Key words

- **12-bar blues:** a 12-bar chord pattern based on I, IV and V
- **Blues scale:** minor pentatonic plus the flattened 5th
- **Boogie-woogie:** a driving walking left-hand blues style
- **Turnaround:** the final bars leading back to the start

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- 12-bar chords in the left hand
- Boogie pattern on C, F, G
- Right-hand blues-scale riffs

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: 12-bar chords in the left hand
1. Then: Right-hand blues-scale riffs
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Nigerian music history:** juju music (King Sunny Adé, Ebenezer Obey) mixed talking drums, guitar and steel guitar. Listen for how the guitars interlock.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play the blues in F and G.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Seventh chords
lessons.summary: Major 7, minor 7 and dominant 7 — the colours of gospel, jazz and neo-soul.
objectives: You will build maj7, m7 and 7 chords
You will play ii7–V7–Imaj7 in C and F
You will reharmonise a simple song with 7th chords
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Add the 7th above the root: **Cmaj7** C–E–G–B, **Am7** A–C–E–G, **G7** G–B–D–F, **Dm7** D–F–A–C. Now ii–V–I becomes Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 — hear how much richer it sounds.

## Understand it

A **seventh chord** adds a fourth note to a triad: the note a **seventh** above the root. Sevenths add **richness, colour and direction** — they are the everyday chords of gospel, jazz, R&B, neo-soul and much Afrobeats.

**The main types (on C):**

- **Major 7th (Cmaj7)** — C–E–G–**B**. Major triad + major 7th. Dreamy, soft, sophisticated.
- **Dominant 7th (C7)** — C–E–G–**B♭**. Major triad + minor 7th. Bluesy, tense — wants to resolve (C7 → F).
- **Minor 7th (Cm7)** — C–E♭–G–**B♭**. Minor triad + minor 7th. Smooth, mellow.
- **Half-diminished (Cm7♭5 / Cø)** — C–E♭–G♭–B♭. Used as the ii in minor keys.

**Sevenths in the chord family of C:** Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, **G7**, Am7, Bm7♭5. Only the **V** is a dominant 7th — and that is why it pulls so strongly to I.

**ii–V–I with sevenths:** **Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7**. Compare it with Dm – G – C: much richer.

**Voicing tips:**

- Left hand plays the **root**; right hand plays the **3rd, 5th and 7th** (or **3rd and 7th** — the notes that define the chord's quality).
- For smooth ii–V–I voice leading, the 7th of one chord moves **down a step** to the 3rd of the next (C in Dm7 → B in G7; F in G7 → E in Cmaj7).

Listen for each type's colour — play them one after another and describe them in a word.

## Key words

- **Seventh chord:** a triad plus the note a seventh above the root
- **Major 7th:** major triad + major seventh
- **Dominant 7th:** major triad + minor seventh — the V7 chord
- **Minor 7th:** minor triad + minor seventh

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

lessons.title: Pedalling
lessons.summary: Using the sustain pedal cleanly: legato pedalling and when not to pedal.
objectives: You will pedal cleanly on chord changes
You will read pedal markings
You will pedal a ballad without blurring
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Legato (syncopated) pedalling:** play the new chord, *then* lift and press the pedal straight after, so the old harmony clears but the sound never breaks. Change the pedal when the harmony changes. Too much pedal blurs; none sounds dry.

## Understand it

The **sustain (damper) pedal** — the right-hand pedal — lifts all the dampers off the strings, so notes keep ringing after you release the keys. Used well, it makes the piano sing, connects notes the hands cannot, and adds resonance. Used badly, it blurs everything into mush.

**Pedal technique:**

- **Heel on the floor**, the ball of the foot on the pedal — the foot pivots at the ankle.
- Press the pedal **fully down** and lift it **fully up** to clear the sound.

**Legato (syncopated) pedalling** — the most important technique:

1. Play the first chord and press the pedal.
2. Play the **next chord**.
3. **Immediately after** the new chord sounds, **lift** the pedal (clearing the old chord) and **press it down again** (catching the new one).

The pedal change comes **just after** the new notes, not at the same time — that is why it is called "syncopated". The result: no gap, no blur.

**Where to change:** **whenever the harmony changes**. Within one chord, the pedal can stay down; across different chords, it must change, or the harmonies overlap and clash.

**Pedal markings:** "Ped." and "✱" (release), or a bracket line underneath the stave showing down, change and up.

**Common faults:** pedalling **too much** (keeping it down through chord changes), pedalling **with** the chord (leaves a gap), and using the pedal to hide uneven fingers. Practise passages **without pedal first**, so fingers are legato on their own.

## Key words

- **Sustain (damper) pedal:** the right pedal that lets strings keep ringing
- **Syncopated pedalling:** changing the pedal just after the new chord
- **Harmony change:** the point where the pedal must change
- **Blur:** notes overlapping when the pedal is held too long

## Read and watch

- [Piano: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/piano/) — Yamaha
- [Piano](https://www.classicfm.com/discover-music/instruments/piano/) — Classic FM

- Pedal a slow ballad

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: all major scales hands together; arpeggios; grand-staff sight-reading; chords of the key; ii–V–I; 12/8 and swing; blues; 7th chords; pedalling.

## Understand it

Term 1 of Year 2 covered a lot: **all major scales hands together**, **arpeggios**, **grand-staff reading**, the **chord family and ii–V–I**, **compound time and swing**, the **12-bar blues**, **seventh chords** and **pedalling**. Revision should be organised.

**Self-test each item** — green, amber or red — then plan the week around the ambers.

**Useful revision techniques:**

- **Random calls** — write each scale and arpeggio on a slip of paper; draw one at random and play it immediately. Tests real readiness, not just the scale you practised last.
- **Key rotation** — play ii–V–I in a different key each day (C, F, G, B♭, D…). Say the chord names aloud.
- **Daily sight-reading** — five minutes of easy grand-staff pieces, never stopping.
- **Theory flashcards** — key signatures, chord spellings (Dm7 = D F A C), note names in both clefs.
- **Pedal check** — play a chord sequence with legato pedalling; record and listen for blurs and gaps.
- **Blues** — play three choruses of 12-bar blues without losing count.

**Fixing problems:**

- **Hands-together scales** fall apart at the thumb crossings — practise the **crossing points** in isolation, slowly.
- **Seventh chords** — spell them before playing.
- **Sight-reading** stalls — choose easier material; the goal is fluency.

Run your prepared piece **every day** as a performance — no stopping.

## Key words

- **Random practice:** testing items in unpredictable order
- **Key rotation:** practising a progression in a new key each day
- **Crossing point:** where the thumb passes in a scale

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

1. Then: Run your test piece

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical:** two scales and an arpeggio; sight-reading; ii–V–I in a key chosen by the examiner; a 12-bar blues; a prepared piece. **Showcase:** perform your piece and a duet or ensemble item.

## Understand it

This term test and showcase assess both **technical command** and **musicianship**.

**The practical:**

- **Two scales and an arpeggio**, hands together — even tempo, correct fingering, smooth crossings.
- **Sight-reading** — use the preparation time: key, time signature, range, rhythms; then a **steady, slow** pulse without stopping.
- **ii–V–I in a key the examiner chooses** — this tests whether you understand the **pattern**, not just one memorised key. Think: "In E♭, ii is Fm7, V is B♭7, I is E♭maj7."
- **12-bar blues** — keep the form, swing the feel, end clearly.
- **A prepared piece** — accurate, with dynamics, articulation, pedalling and shape.

**The showcase** adds an **ensemble or duet** — playing with others:

- **Count in** together; agree the tempo.
- **Listen** to balance — who has the melody at each moment?
- **Watch** your partner for starts, holds and endings.
- **Keep going** together if someone slips — the ensemble matters more than one wrong note.

**Presenting:** introduce your pieces, bow together after ensemble items, thank your partners.

**After the test:** read the feedback carefully. Update your **Year 2 goals** — tick off what you achieved and set the next targets for Term 2 (minor keys, gospel, Afrobeats, choir accompaniment, classical repertoire).

## Key words

- **Musicianship:** musical understanding beyond technique
- **Duet:** music for two performers
- **Ensemble awareness:** listening and adapting to other players

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

In minor, use the **harmonic minor** to build chords: the V becomes major (E in A minor), which pulls strongly home. A minor ii–V–i: Bm7♭5–E7–Am.

## Understand it

Minor keys have a **harmonic problem**: in the natural minor, the V chord is **minor** (Em in A minor), which does not pull strongly home. Composers fixed this centuries ago by **raising the 7th note** (the harmonic minor) when building chords.

**The chord family of A minor (from harmonic minor):**

| i | ii° | III | iv | **V** | VI | vii° |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Am | B° | C (or C+) | Dm | **E** | F | G♯° |

The **V is major (E)** — and as a seventh, **E7** (E–G♯–B–D) — creating a strong pull to Am. In practice, songs mix natural-minor chords (G, Em) with the harmonic-minor V (E7).

**Common minor progressions:**

- **i – iv – V – i**: Am – Dm – E – Am.
- **i – VI – III – VII**: Am – F – C – G (very common in pop and Afrobeats).
- **The minor ii–V–i**: **Bm7♭5 – E7 – Am(7)**. The ii is **half-diminished** (B–D–F–A), the V a dominant 7th. It is the minor-key version of the most important progression in jazz and gospel.

**Melody in minor:** use the **natural minor** for most melody, the **harmonic minor** (G♯) when the V chord is under it, and **melodic minor** for smooth rising lines.

Play the same tune in **A major and A minor** and listen to how completely the mood changes.

## Key words

- **Harmonic minor harmony:** chords built with the raised 7th
- **Major V in minor:** the V chord made major by the raised 7th
- **Half-diminished:** m7♭5 — the ii chord in minor
- **Minor ii–V–i:** iiø7–V7–i

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

lessons.title: Gospel piano I: runs and fills
lessons.summary: Passing chords, walk-ups and the fills that connect phrases in gospel.
objectives: You will play three gospel fills
You will use passing chords between I and IV
You will fill gaps without covering the singer
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Gospel fills happen in the **gaps** between the singer's lines. Learn three: the 1–2–3 walk-up into IV, the pentatonic run down from the 5th, and the 'church chord' (IV/V → I).

## Understand it

Gospel piano is a central sound in Nigerian church music — and in R&B, soul and modern pop. Its **runs and fills** are what make an accompaniment feel alive and responsive to the singer.

**The golden rule: fills go in the gaps.** When the singer sings, the piano supports with chords. When the singer **breathes** or holds a long note at the end of a line, the piano **answers** with a fill. Playing fills over the words fights the singer.

**Three foundational fills:**

1. **The 1–2–3 walk-up into IV** — in C, moving to F: play the bass notes **C – D – E** (or the scale steps in the right hand) on the last beats of the bar, landing on **F** on beat 1. A walking bass leading into the new chord.
2. **The pentatonic run down from the 5th** — a quick descending run on the major pentatonic (G–E–D–C–A–G… in C), ending on a chord tone. Fast, light, flowing.
3. **The "church chord" (IV/V → I)** — play an **F major triad over G in the bass** (F/G), then resolve to **C**. It is a soft, warm version of the V chord, heard constantly at the ends of phrases in gospel.

**Other gospel colours:**

- **Passing chords** — a chord a semitone above or below the target, slid into it.
- **Octave bass** in the left hand for weight.
- **Dynamics with the worship** — sparse and soft in prayer, driving in praise.

**Learn by ear and transcription:** choose a gospel recording, loop one fill, slow it down, copy it, then move it to other keys.

## Key words

- **Fill:** a short musical figure in a gap
- **Walk-up:** a stepwise bass line into a new chord
- **Church chord:** IV/V (e.g. F/G) resolving to I
- **Passing chord:** a brief connecting chord

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Inversions](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/inversions.html) — Ableton Learning Music

```staff C D E F G A B C5
```

```keys C D E F G A B
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Walk-up into IV
- Pentatonic run

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Walk-up into IV
1. Then: Church-chord ending
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Instrument care:** keep pedals clean and check that the sustain pedal works smoothly; dust under the keyboard regularly.

## Make it fit you

- **If you already can:** Use 9th chords and a tritone substitution in a fill.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Afrobeats and amapiano keys
lessons.summary: Modern grooves: Afrobeats syncopation and amapiano's log-drum feel with jazzy chords.
objectives: You will play Afrobeats and amapiano patterns
You will voice m7 and maj9 chords
You will play along to a track
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Afrobeats keys sit on the **3-3-2** feel; amapiano uses slow, jazzy 7th and 9th chords with lots of space, over a log-drum bass. Less is more: leave space for the groove.

## Understand it

**Afrobeats keys** sit on a rhythmic feel often described as **3-3-2**: in a bar of eight quavers (or sixteen semiquavers grouped similarly), the accents fall on **1**, **4** and **7** — **X . . X . . X .** This tresillo-like pattern (shared with much Latin and Caribbean music) gives Afrobeats its rolling, danceable lilt. Keyboard parts:

- Play **short chord stabs** on the 3-3-2 accents, locking with the drums and percussion.
- Use **minor seventh** and **ninth** chords for warmth.
- Keep it **sparse** — the keys are one layer in a busy groove.

**Amapiano** — the South African style that spread across Africa in the late 2010s and 2020s — is quite different:

- **Slow tempo** (roughly 110–115 bpm, but felt as laid-back).
- **Jazzy, lush chords** — sevenths, ninths, elevenths — often held long or played in soft, syncopated patterns.
- **The log drum** — a deep, melodic, pitched bass sound — carries much of the groove; keys must leave it room.
- **Lots of space** — long gaps, repetition, gradual change.

**"Less is more"** is the rule for both: these styles are built on **groove and space**. A keyboard part that fills every beat destroys the feel.

**Practise:**

1. Tap the 3-3-2 rhythm on your knees with a metronome.
2. Play Am7 – Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7 in that rhythm.
3. Play the same chords as long, soft amapiano pads, changing every two bars.
4. Play along with recordings and copy the **rhythm** first.

## Key words

- **3-3-2 rhythm:** accents on 1, 4 and 7 of eight pulses
- **Amapiano:** South African house style with log drum and jazzy chords
- **Log drum:** a deep, pitched synthesised drum sound
- **Space:** deliberate silence that lets the groove breathe

## Read and watch

- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```staff C D E F G A B C5
```

```keys C D E F G A B
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- 3-3-2 chord pattern
- Amapiano pads on Am7–Dm9–Gmaj7–Cmaj7
- Play along to a track

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: 3-3-2 chord pattern
1. Then: Play along to a track
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** modes are scales starting on each note of the major scale. Dorian (from the 2nd) and Mixolydian (from the 5th) are common in pop, funk and gospel.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Program a 4-bar amapiano loop in a DAW and play over it.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Accompanying a choir
lessons.summary: Reading a choir score, giving notes and leading a choir from the piano.
objectives: You will give starting notes
You will read a simple SATB score
You will accompany a choir rehearsal
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Before a choir sings, the pianist **gives the starting notes** (play the chord, then each part's note). Read the SATB score: soprano and alto on the treble, tenor and bass on the bass staff. Follow the conductor — breathe with the choir.

## Understand it

Accompanying a choir is a demanding and respected role — especially in Nigerian churches and schools, where choirs are central.

**Giving the starting notes:** before the choir sings, the pianist sets the **key** and gives each part its **first note**:

1. Play the **tonic chord** (or the opening chord).
2. Play each part's **starting note** separately — soprano, alto, tenor, bass (often top to bottom).
3. Or play a short **introduction** that ends clearly, leading into the first chord.

**Reading an SATB score:**

- **Soprano and alto** on the treble staff (sopranos stems up, altos stems down).
- **Tenor and bass** on the bass staff (tenors stems up, basses stems down). (Some scores give each part its own staff; tenors may read a treble clef with a small 8 below, sounding an octave lower.)
- In **rehearsal**, the pianist often plays **one part** to teach it, or **all four parts** (a "short score" reduction).

**Following the conductor:**

- **Watch the conductor**, not just the music — look up at every phrase.
- **Breathe with the choir** — start phrases together.
- Follow **tempo changes**, holds (*fermatas*), cut-offs.

**Supporting, not dominating:** play **softer** than the choir, **double weak parts** quietly if needed, and drop out where the music is **a cappella**. In rehearsal, be ready to jump to "bar 24, altos only" instantly.

## Key words

- **SATB:** soprano, alto, tenor, bass
- **Starting notes:** the notes given to each part before singing
- **Short score:** four choral parts on two staves
- **Fermata:** a pause or hold, directed by the conductor

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize
- [IMSLP: free scores](https://imslp.org/) — International Music Score Library Project

lessons.title: Classical repertoire
lessons.summary: Learning a short classical piece: style, phrasing and ornaments.
objectives: You will learn a short classical piece
You will shape phrases with dynamics
You will play an ornament (trill or mordent)
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Classical music teaches **control**: even tone, clear phrasing, exact dynamics. Choose a Grade 2–3 piece (for example a Clementi sonatina movement or a Bach minuet). Mark the phrases, practise in sections, and observe every marking.

## Understand it

Classical repertoire — music by composers such as **Bach, Clementi, Mozart, Beethoven, Schumann** and many others — teaches **control**: even tone, clear phrasing, exact rhythm and dynamics. The skills carry into every other style.

**Choosing a piece:** a Grade 2–3 level piece suits most Year 2 players — for example a **Bach minuet** (from the *Notebook for Anna Magdalena Bach*), a **Clementi sonatina** movement, or a short Romantic piece. Many classical scores are free and legal from **IMSLP**, because the music is in the public domain.

**Learning it properly:**

1. **Listen** to good recordings — several, if possible.
2. **Mark the score** in pencil: **phrases** (the musical sentences, usually 2 or 4 bars), **fingering**, difficult spots.
3. **Practise in sections** — two or four bars at a time, hands separately, slowly.
4. **Observe every marking** — dynamics (*p, f, cresc.*), articulation (slurs, staccato), tempo terms (*Allegro, Andante*), ornaments.
5. **Join sections**, then hands together, then build to tempo.

**Style matters:**

- **Baroque (Bach)** — clear, even lines; little or no pedal; each hand an independent voice.
- **Classical (Mozart, Clementi)** — elegant, balanced phrases; light accompaniment (Alberti bass!); clear dynamic contrast.
- **Romantic (Schumann, Chopin)** — expressive, singing melody, more pedal, freer tempo (*rubato*).

Think about **shape**: where does each phrase rise, peak and relax?

## Key words

- **Repertoire:** the pieces a musician learns and performs
- **Phrase:** a musical sentence
- **Public domain:** works free to copy because copyright has expired
- **Rubato:** flexible, expressive tempo

## Read and watch

- [IMSLP: free scores](https://imslp.org/) — International Music Score Library Project
- [Discover music](https://www.classicfm.com/discover-music/) — Classic FM

## Play (40 minutes)

- Section by section, hands separately
- Hands together slowly
- Add dynamics and phrasing

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Section by section, hands separately
1. Then: Add dynamics and phrasing
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Music technology:** a metronome click is your best friend in the studio. Record one take to a click and one without, and compare.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Learn the whole piece and play it from memory.

## This week's assignment

Learn the first half of your classical piece and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Improvisation II: modes and the blues
lessons.summary: Improvising with Dorian and Mixolydian modes over grooves.
objectives: You will play Dorian and Mixolydian
You will improvise over a one-chord vamp
You will build a solo from motifs
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Dorian** (D–E–F–G–A–B–C–D) gives a cool minor sound over Dm7; **Mixolydian** (G–A–B–C–D–E–F–G) fits G7 grooves. Improvise in phrases: question and answer, repeat with a change.

## Understand it

**Modes** are scales made by starting the major scale on a different note. Using only the **white keys**:

| Start | Mode | Sound |
|---|---|---|
| C | **Ionian** (major) | bright |
| D | **Dorian** | minor, but with a raised 6th — cool, soulful |
| E | **Phrygian** | dark, Spanish/Middle-Eastern |
| F | **Lydian** | bright, dreamy, raised 4th |
| G | **Mixolydian** | major with a flat 7th — bluesy, funky |
| A | **Aeolian** (natural minor) | sad |
| B | **Locrian** | unstable, rarely used |

The two most useful for improvising:

- **Dorian** — **D E F G A B C D** over **Dm7**: a minor sound that is cooler and brighter than natural minor because of the **B** (major 6th). Common in funk, gospel, jazz, Afro-fusion.
- **Mixolydian** — **G A B C D E F G** over **G7**: a major sound with a bluesy **F** (flat 7th). Common in rock, funk, highlife and groove-based music.

**The blues** brings the **blues scale** (minor pentatonic + ♭5) and **blue notes** over dominant chords.

**Improvising in phrases:**

- **Question and answer** — a phrase ending "up in the air", answered by one ending home.
- **Repeat with a change** — play an idea, repeat it, then alter the ending.
- **Rhythm first** — a strong rhythmic idea on two notes beats aimless scales.
- **Target chord tones** on strong beats.

Loop Dm7 to G7 (a ii–V vamp) and improvise with D Dorian — it fits both chords.

## Key words

- **Mode:** a scale starting on a different degree of the major scale
- **Dorian:** minor with a raised 6th
- **Mixolydian:** major with a flattened 7th
- **Vamp:** a short repeated chord pattern for improvising over

## Read and watch

- [Modes](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/modes.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- Dm7 vamp with Dorian
- G7 vamp with Mixolydian
- Motif development

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Dm7 vamp with Dorian
1. Then: Motif development
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** use it for ideas — a chord progression, a rhythm, a title — then make them yours at the instrument. Hand in what YOU played. A piece you cannot perform is not your piece.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** dynamics (pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff), crescendo and diminuendo shape music. Mark them in your pieces in pencil.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Improvise over a ii–V–I, changing scale with each chord.

## This week's assignment

Record a two-minute improvisation over a vamp.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Arranging a song for piano
lessons.summary: Turning a lead sheet into a full piano arrangement: intro, verse, chorus, ending.
objectives: You will plan an arrangement
You will vary texture between sections
You will write an intro and an ending
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

An arrangement has **contrast**: a sparse verse, a fuller chorus, an intro taken from the chorus melody, and a clear ending. Choose textures: block chords, broken chords, octaves in the bass, melody in octaves.

## Understand it

An **arrangement** is your own version of an existing song — deciding **what** to play, **where**, and **how**, to make it work as a piano piece (or a piano part in a band).

**Start with the song's structure:** map the sections (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro), the chords and the melody.

**Create contrast** — the most important principle:

- **Verses — sparse**: simple left-hand chords or single notes; melody in the right hand; soft.
- **Chorus — fuller**: bigger chords, octaves in the bass, melody in **octaves** or harmonised; louder.
- **Bridge — different**: a new texture, register or rhythm.
- **Final chorus — biggest**, or a surprise drop to quiet before the end.

**Textures to choose from:**

- **Block chords** — strong, hymn-like.
- **Broken chords / arpeggios** — flowing.
- **Octaves in the bass** — weight and power.
- **Melody in octaves** — the melody stands out above everything.
- **Melody with chords under it** in the right hand, bass in the left — the full "solo piano" sound.

**Intro and ending:**

- **Intro** — often a phrase from the **chorus melody** or the main chord progression, which sets up the song's key and mood.
- **Ending** — a clear finish: repeat the last line slowing down (*ritardando*), a final chord held, or an echo of the intro.

**Write it down** — at least a lead sheet with notes on texture for each section, plus a recording.

## Key words

- **Arrangement:** your own version of a piece, with chosen textures
- **Texture:** how the musical layers are combined
- **Contrast:** differences between sections
- **Ritardando:** gradually slowing down

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [MuseScore handbook](https://musescore.org/en/handbook) — MuseScore

## Play (40 minutes)

- Plan the sections
- Write and play the intro
- Contrast verse and chorus

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Plan the sections
1. Then: Contrast verse and chorus
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Teamwork:** a rehearsal plan saves time: warm-up, run the hardest part first, full run, notes, final run.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add a key change for the final chorus.

## This week's assignment

Arrange one song for solo piano and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.summary: Using a digital keyboard's sounds, MIDI and recording into a DAW.
objectives: You will record a MIDI part
You will change sounds and edit notes
You will layer two parts
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**MIDI** records which keys you pressed, not the sound — so you can change the instrument and fix timing later. Connect a keyboard by USB to a DAW (BandLab, GarageBand), record a part, then quantise lightly.

## Understand it

Modern keyboard players need to understand **music technology** — how keyboards connect to computers, and how to record.

**MIDI** (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) is a language electronic instruments use. A MIDI recording stores **information about what you played** — which key, how hard (**velocity**), when, for how long, pedal on or off — **not the sound itself**. This means you can:

- **Change the instrument** after recording (record on piano, switch to strings).
- **Fix wrong notes** or timing.
- **Change the tempo** without changing the pitch.

**Audio** recording, by contrast, captures the **actual sound** (through a microphone or the keyboard's audio output). You cannot change the instrument later.

**Connecting:** most modern keyboards connect by **USB** directly to a computer, tablet or phone (sometimes with an adapter). In a **DAW** (BandLab, GarageBand, Cakewalk), create a **MIDI/instrument track**, choose a sound, arm the track and record.

**Quantise lightly:** quantising snaps notes to the grid. **Full** quantisation sounds robotic; **light** quantisation (e.g. 50%) or **none** keeps the human feel. Better still — practise until your timing is good.

**Keyboard sounds:** learn the main categories — **acoustic piano, electric piano (Rhodes, Wurlitzer), organ, synth pads, strings, brass** — and when each suits a style.

**Monitoring:** use headphones while recording to avoid other sounds leaking in; keep the volume moderate to protect your hearing.

## Key words

- **MIDI:** data describing notes played, not the sound itself
- **Velocity:** how hard a key is struck, recorded in MIDI
- **Quantise:** snapping notes to the rhythmic grid
- **DAW:** Digital Audio Workstation — recording software

## Read and watch

- [Learning Music: get started](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/) — Ableton
- [Learning Synths](https://learningsynths.ableton.com/) — Ableton
- [Cakewalk by BandLab](https://www.bandlab.com/products/cakewalk) — BandLab

## Play (40 minutes)

- Record chords
- Record a melody on top
- Edit and export

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Record chords
1. Then: Edit and export
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Mindset:** set one SMART goal for the term: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add a bass and drum part to your recording.

## This week's assignment

Record a two-part arrangement in a DAW and share the file.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Ensemble II: leading the band from the keys
lessons.summary: Counting in, signalling changes and keeping the band together.
objectives: You will count in and cue sections
You will play while leading
You will end a song together
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

The keyboard player is often the **music director**: count in clearly, signal the next section a bar early, and cue the ending. Keep your own part simple enough to lead while you play.

## Understand it

In many bands — especially church bands — the **keyboard player is the music director (MD)**: the person who leads the band through the music in real time.

**What leading from the keys involves:**

- **Counting in** — clear, confident, at the right tempo: "One, two, three, four" (or clicks). Think of the song's tempo before counting.
- **Signalling sections one bar early** — the band needs warning. Common signals: **hand signals** (fingers for the section number, a fist for stop), **head nods**, **calling out** ("Chorus!", "Again!", "Bridge!") or **musical cues** (a specific fill that everyone knows means "chorus next").
- **Cueing the ending** — agreed in rehearsal: a raised hand, a held chord, a **ritardando** led by the keys.
- **Following the leader** — in worship, the MD watches the worship leader and translates their intentions to the band: repeat the chorus, go softer, modulate up.
- **Keeping your own part simple** — you cannot lead well while playing your hardest part. Use simple, solid voicings so your attention can be on the band.

**Number charts** (the Nashville Number System) write songs in numbers (1, 4, 5, 6m) instead of letters, so the band can play in any key instantly — very useful when the singer changes key.

**In rehearsal:** agree the arrangement and signals; rehearse **transitions** and **endings** more than the middles of songs.

## Key words

- **Music director (MD):** the musician who leads the band in real time
- **Count-in:** clicks or counts setting the tempo
- **Cue:** a signal to change section or stop
- **Number chart:** chords written as numbers, playable in any key

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

```staff C D E F G A B C5
```

```keys C D E F G A B
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Rehearse cues
- Lead one song
- Swap leaders

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Work on: Rehearse cues
1. Then: Swap leaders
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** 7th chords — major 7 (Cmaj7), minor 7 (Am7), dominant 7 (G7) — are the colours of gospel, jazz and neo-soul.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Lead a song with a key change and a tag ending.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Composition II: a piece in ternary form
lessons.summary: Writing a longer original piece with a modulation and a contrasting middle.
objectives: You will write a 24–32 bar ternary piece
You will modulate in the B section
You will develop a motif
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Ternary form** (A–B–A) with a modulation: the B section moves to a related key (the dominant or relative minor), then returns home. Use a motif and develop it — repeat, sequence, invert.

## Understand it

**Ternary form** — **A B A** — is one of the most satisfying shapes in music: a main section, a contrasting middle, then a return to the start. Many classical pieces, songs and hymns use it.

**The sections:**

- **A** — the main idea, in the **home key**. Ends with a clear cadence (often in the home key).
- **B** — **contrast**: a different mood, texture, rhythm or register — and usually a **different key**.
- **A** (return) — the opening idea again, in the home key; perhaps varied, with a **coda** (an ending section).

**Modulation in the B section** — move to a **related key**:

- The **dominant** (C major → G major) — bright, energetic.
- The **relative minor** (C major → A minor) — darker, more personal.

To get there smoothly, use the new key's **V chord** (D7 → G, or E7 → Am) — it makes the new key sound like home. To return, use the original key's **V** (G7 → C).

**Developing a motif** — make your whole piece from one short idea:

- **Repetition** — play it again.
- **Sequence** — repeat it starting on a different note (higher or lower).
- **Inversion** — turn it upside down (up becomes down).
- **Rhythmic change** — longer or shorter notes.
- **Fragmentation** — use just part of it.

Unity comes from the motif; interest comes from the contrast and development.

Write it out in notation (MuseScore is free) and record it.

## Key words

- **Ternary form:** A–B–A structure
- **Modulation:** changing key within a piece
- **Sequence:** a motif repeated at a different pitch
- **Coda:** a closing section

## Read and watch

- [MuseScore handbook](https://musescore.org/en/handbook) — MuseScore
- [Make melodies](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-melodies/make-melodies.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## Play (40 minutes)

- Write A
- Write B in a new key
- Return and finish

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Write A
1. Then: Return and finish
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Copyright and the business:** royalties are paid to writers when songs are played, streamed or performed. In Nigeria, COSON and MCSN collect them.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Notate it in MuseScore.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

objectives: You will self-test the checklist

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: all major scales and arpeggios; minor harmony; 7th chords and ii–V–I; blues; gospel fills; Afrobeats/amapiano; a classical piece; sight-reading; your arrangement and composition.

## Understand it

The Year 2 assessment covers the whole year. Organise your revision into **five strands**, and touch each one every day.

**1. Technique** — all major scales and arpeggios (and the minor ones learnt), hands together, at a steady tempo. Use random calls.

**2. Harmony** — chord families in several keys; **seventh chords**; **ii–V–I** (major and minor) in keys called at random; 12-bar blues; minor-key progressions.

**3. Styles** — a gospel fill set (walk-up, pentatonic run, church chord); an Afrobeats or amapiano pattern; choir accompaniment (giving notes, following a conductor); a blues chorus.

**4. Reading** — daily sight-reading on the grand staff; theory flashcards.

**5. Pieces** — your **two contrasting pieces** (e.g. a classical piece and a contemporary style) and your **arrangement or composition**.

**Performance readiness:**

- **Run each piece** daily, start to finish, without stopping.
- Record and listen: **balance** (melody vs accompaniment), **pedalling** (no blurs), **dynamics**, **steady tempo**.
- Practise the **starts**, **transitions** and **endings** most.

**Theory checklist** — key signatures and the circle of fifths; chord spelling; modes (Dorian, Mixolydian); compound time and swing; ternary form and modulation.

Rest your hands the day before, and sleep well.

## Key words

- **Strand:** one area of skill in a revision plan
- **Random calls:** testing items in unpredictable order
- **Performance readiness:** being able to play a piece securely under pressure

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

## Play (40 minutes)

- Self-test
- Targeted practice
- Performance run

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Self-test
1. Then: Performance run
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Practice habits:** before the test, practise performing — one take, no stops, as if it were the real thing.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Prepare a third piece in a contrasting style.

## This week's assignment

Follow your revision plan and do one full performance run a day.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

objectives: You will perform under assessment conditions
You will play two contrasting pieces

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical:** scales and arpeggios on request; sight-reading; a progression with 7th chords; two contrasting pieces; your arrangement or composition. **Recital** for families.

## Understand it

The Year 2 assessment and recital show how far you have come: from basic chords and one hand at a time to **hands-together fluency**, **reading both clefs**, **seventh-chord harmony**, **pedalling**, and several styles.

**The practical** — scales and arpeggios on request; sight-reading; a progression with seventh chords (possibly in a called key); two contrasting pieces; your arrangement or composition. Remember: **steady pulse, keep going, use preparation time well**.

**The recital:**

- **Programme for contrast** — e.g. a classical piece, a gospel or Afrobeats arrangement, and your own composition.
- **Introduce each piece** — title, composer or arranger, one sentence of context ("This is my ternary-form piece; the middle section moves to A minor").
- **Check the instrument** — bench height, pedal, and on digital pianos the sound and volume.
- **Stage routine** — walk on, bow, settle, breathe, play, hold the last sound, bow.

**Portfolio:** add recordings of your recital, your arrangement and composition scores, and your practice log.

**Reflection for Year 3** — Year 3 is about **artistry and leadership**: choosing a focus (performer, music director, songwriter/producer, teacher) and a graduation project. Think now:

- Which part of music excites you most?
- What would you like to be able to do by graduation?
- Who could you mentor?

Write down your thoughts — they become your Year 3 plan.

## Key words

- **Recital:** a formal performance of prepared pieces
- **Programme:** the chosen order of pieces
- **Artistic focus:** the direction you choose to specialise in

## Read and watch

- [Piano](https://www.classicfm.com/discover-music/instruments/piano/) — Classic FM
- [MuseScore handbook](https://musescore.org/en/handbook) — MuseScore

- Assessment
- Recital

1. Work on: Assessment
1. Then: Recital
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Use an ear-training app to drill the intervals in this lesson for five minutes. Sing or hum the interval before you answer; an app that only tests recognition trains your eyes, not your ear.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reflection:** write a short letter to yourself for Year 3: what you will keep, what you will change.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play your composition from memory.

## This week's assignment

Write your goals for Year 3 — and the musician you want to be by graduation.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Year 2 builds **fluency across the neck, reading and style**. The instructor checks open chords, barre chords, picking and a song. Players who are ahead take the stretch work every week; those who need more time revisit the Year 1 skills in their plan.

## Understand it

Year 2 builds **fluency across the neck**, **reading** (standard notation and tab) and **style** (blues, gospel, worship, jùjú, highlife, Afrobeats, classical).

**The technique check** — open chords, barre chords, picking and a song — shows what survived the break and what needs work. Most players find barre chords and changes have slowed; that is normal, and comes back quickly with daily practice.

**Setting goals** — specific, measurable, time-bound:

- "Name any note on the 6th and 5th strings within 3 seconds, by week 4."
- "Play E-shape and A-shape barre chords from any called root, cleanly, by week 9."
- "Play a 12-bar blues shuffle and solo for two choruses by week 12."

Write **three goals** — technique, knowledge/reading, and a musical or style goal — and review them at mid-term.

**A practice structure for Year 2:**

1. **Warm-up** (5 min) — chromatic exercise, stretches, a scale.
2. **Technique** (10 min) — the current focus (scale shapes, barre changes, picking).
3. **Knowledge** (5 min) — fretboard notes, reading.
4. **Repertoire/style** (10–15 min) — slow work on hard parts, then a run-through.
5. **Creative** (5 min) — improvise, write, or learn by ear.

**Guitar care:** change strings regularly (every 1–3 months, or when they sound dull or will not stay in tune); wipe strings after playing; keep the guitar in its case away from heat and damp.

## Key words

- **Technique check:** a quick assessment of current skills
- **SMART goal:** Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
- **Practice structure:** a planned order for each session

lessons.title: The notes on the neck
lessons.summary: Finding every note on the 6th and 5th strings, and using them to place barre chords.
objectives: You will name notes on strings 6 and 5
You will place E- and A-shape barre chords by root

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Memorise the natural notes on the low E (E F G A B C D at frets 0 1 3 5 7 8 10) and the A string (A B C D E F G at 0 2 3 5 7 8 10). Fret 12 is the octave. Now any E-shape barre takes its name from the 6th string, any A-shape from the 5th.

## Understand it

Knowing the **notes on the neck** unlocks everything: barre chords in any key, movable scales, reading, and communicating with other musicians ("play an A-shape barre on D").

**Start with the two bass strings:**

- **6th string (low E)**: E (0), F (1), G (3), A (5), B (7), C (8), D (10), E (12).
- **5th string (A)**: A (0), B (2), C (3), D (5), E (7), F (8), G (10), A (12).

Between natural notes are **sharps/flats** — except between **E–F** and **B–C**, which are only one fret apart (a semitone).

**The 12th fret is the octave** — everything repeats from there, so fret 15 is the same note name as fret 3.

**Why it matters for chords:**

- **E-shape barre** chords are named from the **6th string**: barre at fret 5 → **A**; fret 8 → **C**; fret 3 → **G**.
- **A-shape barre** chords (index barres strings 5–1, ring finger barres or fingers play strings 4–2 two frets higher) are named from the **5th string**: fret 3 → **C**; fret 5 → **D**; fret 7 → **E**.

Now any major or minor chord can be played in **two places** — choose the one nearest your hand.

**Learning the notes:**

- Say them aloud as you play up the string.
- **Random quizzes**: name a note, find it on string 6, then string 5. Time yourself.
- **Octave shapes**: a note on string 6 at fret x has its octave on string 4 at fret x+2. Use this to find notes on the D string too.

Five minutes a day for two weeks is enough to know strings 6 and 5 well.

## Key words

- **Natural note:** a note without a sharp or flat
- **Octave shape:** a fixed pattern finding the same note an octave higher
- **E-shape / A-shape barre:** barre chords named from the 6th / 5th string

## Read and watch

- [Explore pitch](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/notes-and-scales/notes-and-scales.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Fretboard note exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **movable scale shape** starts with a root on the 6th string — slide it to change key. Learn the shape with the root under finger 2 (G at fret 3) and with the root on the 5th string.

## Understand it

Open-position scales only work in a few keys. **Movable scale shapes** — patterns using no open strings — work in **every key**: learn the shape once, slide it to a new root.

**How a movable shape works:** the pattern of tones and semitones (T T S T T T S) is fixed by the fingers, so moving the whole shape up or down changes only the **key**. Put the **root** (first note) on the right fret, and the shape does the rest.

**Two shapes to learn first:**

1. **Root on the 6th string, under finger 2** — e.g. **G major** with the root at fret 3: the shape spans frets 2–5 and covers about two octaves. Slide the root to fret 5 → **A major**; fret 8 → **C major**.
2. **Root on the 5th string** — e.g. **C major** with the root at fret 3 on the A string. Slide to fret 5 → **D major**.

Use **one finger per fret** in the position (index on the lowest fret of the box, little finger on the highest), shifting only when the shape needs it.

**Practise:**

- **Up and down**, alternate picking, metronome — start at 60 bpm, two notes per beat.
- **Say the scale degrees** (1, 2, 3…) or note names occasionally — it connects the shape to theory.
- **Find the roots** inside the shape — they are your landing points for melodies and solos.
- **Move the shape** to a new key each day.

The minor scales use the **same shapes** — start from the relative minor's root (the 6th degree).

## Key words

- **Movable shape:** a fingering pattern with no open strings, usable in any key
- **Position:** the area of the neck the hand covers, named by the index finger's fret
- **Scale degree:** a note's number in the scale
- **One finger per fret:** each finger assigned one fret in a position

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons: scales](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Electric guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/electric_guitar/) — Yamaha

## Play (40 minutes)

- Shape from the 6th string
- Shape from the 5th string
- Same shape in three keys

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Shape from the 6th string
1. Then: Same shape in three keys
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Find the song on YouTube and use the playback-speed control (or a free slow-downer app) to take it to 0.5× without changing the pitch. Learn it slowly and correctly, then step the speed back up.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** ledger lines extend the stave above and below; practise reading notes two ledger lines out.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Connect two positions with a slide.

lessons.title: Reading standard notation and tab
lessons.summary: Reading guitar music on the stave and in tablature.
objectives: You will read notes in open position from notation
You will read rhythm from notation
You will sight-read a short melody
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Tab** shows strings and frets but not rhythm; **standard notation** shows pitch and rhythm. Guitar sounds an octave lower than written. Read both: tab for where, notation for when.

## Understand it

Guitar music is written in two ways, often together:

**Tablature (tab)** shows **where** to play: six lines for the six strings (**top line = high E**, bottom line = low E), with **fret numbers** on them. A "3" on the second line from the bottom means fret 3 on the A string.

- **Strength**: instantly shows strings and frets.
- **Weakness**: basic tab shows **no rhythm** — you must know the song or have notation (or rhythm stems) alongside.
- Symbols: **h** (hammer-on), **p** (pull-off), **/ \\** (slide up/down), **b** (bend), **~** (vibrato), **x** (muted).

**Standard notation** shows **pitch and rhythm** on a five-line stave with a treble clef.

- **Guitar music sounds an octave lower than written** — it is written that way so it fits the treble clef without many ledger lines (sometimes shown with a small 8 under the clef).
- Notation shows **when** and **how long**; it does not show **which string** — the same note can be in several places.

**Read both:** **tab for where, notation for when**. Most published guitar books print them together.

**Reading practice:**

- Learn the notes in **first position** on the stave (open E on the 4th line below… up to the high E).
- Clap the **rhythm** first, then play.
- Read a little **every day** — short, easy material builds fluency.

Tools such as MuseScore let you write both notation and tab, and play them back to check.

## Key words

- **Tablature:** notation showing strings and frets
- **Standard notation:** notes on a stave showing pitch and rhythm
- **Octave transposition:** guitar sounds an octave below written pitch
- **Rhythm stems:** rhythm marks added to tab

## Read and watch

- [Customising a tablature staff](https://musescore.org/en/handbook/4/tablature) — MuseScore
- [Music theory lessons: the staff and note values](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- Note-reading drill in open position
- Rhythm reading
- Sight-read a melody

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Note-reading drill in open position
1. Then: Sight-read a melody
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it for four short sight-reading exercises at your level. Check each one BEFORE you play it: are the notes inside the key, do the bars add up to the time signature? Models get notation wrong, and finding the bad bar is the real exercise. Play each sound one ONCE. Sight-reading only improves on music you have not seen before.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** the primary chords are I, IV and V; the secondary chords are ii, iii and vi — all six come from the scale.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Sight-read in the 5th position.

## This week's assignment

Sight-read one short melody every day and log the hardest.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.
