lessons.title: The chord family and ii–V–I
lessons.summary: Every chord in the key and the progressions gospel and jazz rely on.
objectives: You will play all chords in G and C
You will play ii–V–I and I–vi–ii–V
You will find them in songs
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

In G the chords are **G Am Bm C D Em** (and F♯°). With barre shapes you can play them all. ii–V–I in G is Am–D–G; I–vi–ii–V is G–Em–Am–D.

## Understand it

Build a chord on every note of a major scale and you get its **chord family**. In every major key the pattern is the same:

**I** major — **ii** minor — **iii** minor — **IV** major — **V** major — **vi** minor — **vii°** diminished

In **G**: **G – Am – Bm – C – D – Em – F♯°**.

With **open and barre shapes** you can now play all of them:

- **Bm** — the classic beginner barre: A-shape minor barre at fret 2.
- **F♯°** — rarely used in pop; often replaced by D7.

**Thinking in numbers** lets you transpose any song: "I–vi–ii–V" is G–Em–Am–D in G, C–Am–Dm–G in C.

**ii–V–I** — the most important progression in **gospel and jazz**: in G, **Am – D – G**. The roots rise by fourths (A→D→G), creating strong, natural movement. Add sevenths later (Am7 – D7 – Gmaj7).

**I–vi–ii–V** — **G – Em – Am – D** — a classic turnaround that loops back to I, used in doo-wop, soul and gospel.

**Choosing shapes for smooth changes:** use the chord positions closest together. E.g. in G, play **Am** as an open chord and **D** open, or play them as barre chords at frets 5 (Am E-shape) and 5 (D A-shape) — both at the same fret, so changes are tiny.

**Practise:** ii–V–I and I–vi–ii–V in **G, C and D**, first open, then with barre shapes in one position.

## Key words

- **Chord family:** the chords built on each degree of a key
- **ii–V–I:** the key progression of gospel and jazz
- **Turnaround:** a progression leading back to I
- **Roman numerals:** chord labels by scale degree

## Read and watch

- [Play with chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/chords/play-with-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons: diatonic triads](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```chord Am D G Em C
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Chords of the key
- ii–V–I in G and C
- I–vi–ii–V loop

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Chords of the key
1. Then: I–vi–ii–V loop
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Listening:** listen to a full song and map its form: intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, outro. Time each section.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play ii–V–I with barre chords in five keys.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Strumming dynamics and muting
lessons.summary: Palm-muting, chucks and accents for groove.
objectives: You will palm-mute
You will play chucks on 2 and 4
You will build dynamics from verse to chorus
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Palm-muting** rests the picking hand's edge on the strings by the bridge for a tight, chunky sound. A **chuck** (percussive mute) on beats 2 and 4 makes an acoustic sound like it has a snare drum.

## Understand it

**Dynamics and texture** in strumming turn a guitar part from flat to alive. Three tools:

**1. Strumming dynamics**

- **Volume** — strum lighter or harder; strum fewer strings (top three for soft, all six for full).
- **Pick position** — near the neck is warmer and softer; near the bridge is brighter and sharper.
- **Accents** — hit certain strums harder (usually 2 and 4).

**2. Palm muting**

Rest the **edge of your picking hand** (the fleshy side below the little finger) **lightly on the strings right next to the bridge saddle**. Strum or pick: notes sound **short, tight and chunky**. Too far from the bridge, the notes die completely; too light, they ring normally. Find the spot that gives a muted but pitched sound. Used in rock, pop, Afrobeats and worship verses.

**3. The chuck (percussive mute)**

On beats **2 and 4**, strike the strings with the strumming hand while **muting them instantly** — either with the side of the palm landing on the strings, or by lifting the fretting fingers slightly. The result is a percussive "chk" with no pitch — like a **snare drum** on an acoustic guitar. Pattern: **D (chk) D U D (chk) D U** — "boom-chk-a-boom-chk-a".

**Fretting-hand muting:** relax the pressure of the fretting fingers (keep touching the strings) between strums for staccato chords.

Use these to build a song: muted verses, open choruses, chucks for drive.

## Key words

- **Palm muting:** damping strings with the side of the hand by the bridge
- **Chuck:** a percussive muted strum on the backbeat
- **Accent:** a strum played louder than others
- **Staccato chord:** a chord cut short by releasing pressure

## Read and watch

- [Acoustic guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/acoustic_guitar/) — Yamaha
- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## Play (40 minutes)

- Palm-muted eighths
- Chuck pattern
- Verse muted, chorus open

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Palm-muted eighths
1. Then: Verse muted, chorus open
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Body:** tension is the enemy of speed. Check shoulders, wrists and jaw every few minutes; relax and keep playing.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add ghost-strums at 16th-note feel.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Compound time and swing
lessons.summary: 6/8, 12/8 and swing feel on the guitar.
objectives: You will strum in 6/8 and 12/8
You will swing eighth notes
You will play a 12/8 ballad
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

In **6/8** strum down on 1 and 4 with lighter strums between. Swing eighths are long–short. 12/8 ballads are common in gospel and soul.

## Understand it

**Compound time** divides each beat into **three** instead of two.

- **6/8** — two big beats, each split into three quavers: "**1** 2 3 **4** 5 6". Strum **down on 1 and 4** (strong), with **lighter strums** between: "**D** d u **D** d u" or "**D** u u **D** u u". It rolls and sways — common in African and gospel music, folk, ballads and waltz-like songs.
- **12/8** — four big beats, each split into three: the feel of **slow gospel ballads, soul and blues**. Count "**1** & a **2** & a **3** & a **4** & a".

Feel the **big beats** — a 6/8 song is felt in **two**, not six.

**Swing** plays pairs of quavers **long–short**, like the first and last notes of a triplet: "**doo**-ba **doo**-ba". Music marked "Swing" or "Shuffle" is played this way even though it is written as straight quavers. Swing is the heart of **blues, jazz, many gospel songs** and some R&B.

**Straight vs swung:** play the same strumming pattern both ways — straight sounds square and driving; swung sounds relaxed and bouncy.

**Practice:**

- 6/8: G – Em – C – D, two big beats per chord, accenting 1 and 4.
- 12/8: a slow gospel progression (C – Am – F – G) with a gentle triplet strum or picking pattern.
- Swing: a blues shuffle strum with a metronome clicking on 2 and 4.

## Key words

- **Compound time:** beats divided into three
- **6/8:** two dotted-crotchet beats per bar
- **12/8:** four dotted-crotchet beats per bar
- **Swing:** pairs of quavers played long–short

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons: time signatures](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Rhythm exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- 6/8 strumming
- Swing a scale
- 12/8 ballad

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: 6/8 strumming
1. Then: 12/8 ballad
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** compound time (6/8) groups beats in threes — count 1-2-3-4-5-6 with accents on 1 and 4.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Finger-pick the 12/8 ballad.

lessons.title: The 12-bar blues and blues shuffle
lessons.summary: The blues form, the shuffle rhythm and blues licks.
objectives: You will play the shuffle

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

12-bar blues in A: A A A A | D D A A | E D A E. The **shuffle** pattern moves between the 5th and 6th on the bass strings. Solo with the A minor pentatonic plus the ♭5 (the blues scale).

## Understand it

The **12-bar blues** is the foundation of blues, rock and roll, R&B and much rock — and every guitarist should be able to play and solo over it.

**In A:**

| A | A | A | A |
| D | D | A | A |
| E | D | A | E |

(I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V) — the last E (the **turnaround**) leads back to the start. Often played with **seventh chords**: A7, D7, E7.

**The shuffle pattern** — the classic blues rhythm guitar part, on two strings:

- Over **A**: play the open **A string** with the **E string fret 2** (A + E = a "5" power chord), then reach the ring finger to **fret 4** (adding F♯, the 6th) — alternating **5th and 6th**: "A5 – A6 – A5 – A6".
- Move the same shape to the D and G strings for **D**, and to the A and D strings for **E**.
- Play it with a **swing** feel, palm-muted.

**Soloing — the blues scale:** the **A minor pentatonic** (A C D E G) plus the **♭5 (E♭)**: **A C D E♭ E G**. The **blue notes** (C over an A chord, E♭, G) create the tension that defines the blues. Use **bends** (bend C slightly sharp; bend D up to E), **slides** and **vibrato**.

**Phrasing tip:** blues solos often follow the form: a phrase over bars 1–4, the **same phrase** over bars 5–8 (now over D), and a different answering phrase over 9–12. **Call and response** — like the lyrics.

## Key words

- **12-bar blues:** a 12-bar I–IV–V chord pattern
- **Shuffle:** a swung rhythm alternating the 5th and 6th
- **Blues scale:** minor pentatonic plus the flattened 5th
- **Power chord:** root and fifth only, written A5

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Electric guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/electric_guitar/) — Yamaha

lessons.summary: maj7, m7 and 7 shapes — open and barre.
objectives: You will play open and barre 7th chords

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Open: **Cmaj7, Am7, Em7, G7, D7, A7, E7**. Barre: m7 and 7 shapes from the 6th and 5th strings. ii–V–I becomes Am7–D7–Gmaj7.

## Understand it

A **seventh chord** adds the note a **seventh** above the root to a triad. Sevenths give the warmth of gospel, the bite of blues and the sophistication of jazz, R&B and neo-soul.

**The main types (on C):**

- **Major 7th (Cmaj7)** — C E G **B** — soft, dreamy.
- **Dominant 7th (C7)** — C E G **B♭** — bluesy, wants to resolve (to F).
- **Minor 7th (Cm7)** — C E♭ G **B♭** — smooth, mellow.

**Open-position sevenths:**

- **Cmaj7** — like C, but lift the index finger off the B string (open B).
- **Am7** — like Am, but lift the ring finger (open G).
- **Em7** — like Em with the G string fret 2 removed… or add D on the B string fret 3.
- **G7** — like G with F on the high E (fret 1).
- **D7**, **A7**, **E7** — standard shapes from chord charts.

**Barre sevenths:**

- From the 6th string: **E-shape 7** (remove the little finger from the D string), **E-shape m7** (remove from D and lift middle).
- From the 5th string: **A-shape 7**, **A-shape m7**, **A-shape maj7**.

Now you can play any seventh chord by root.

**ii–V–I with sevenths in G:** **Am7 – D7 – Gmaj7**. Compare it with Am – D – G: much richer, and the D7 pulls harder to G.

Play each type and describe its colour in a word — training your ear to hear chord quality.

## Key words

- **Major 7th:** major triad + major seventh
- **Dominant 7th:** major triad + minor seventh
- **Minor 7th:** minor triad + minor seventh
- **Chord quality:** the type of a chord: major, minor, 7th…

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Finger-style places the **melody on the top strings** and the bass with the thumb. Start from the chord shape, find the melody note within or near it, and keep the thumb steady.

## Understand it

A **finger-style arrangement** lets one guitar play **melody, bass and harmony at once** — a complete piece of music on its own.

**The layout:**

- **Melody on the top strings** (high E, B, sometimes G), played with **i, m, a** — usually the highest note at any moment, and the loudest.
- **Bass with the thumb (p)** on the low strings — the root or a steady alternating bass.
- **Harmony** — chord notes filling in between, as the fingers allow.

**How to arrange a melody:**

1. **Choose a key** where the melody sits on the top strings and the chords are open or easy — G, C, D and A are usually best.
2. **Write out the melody** and the chords above it.
3. For each melody note, **find a chord shape** that contains it, or is near it, on the top string. Often the melody note is already part of the chord; sometimes you add a finger.
4. **Keep the thumb steady** — even if the fingers are busy, the bass keeps the time.
5. **Simplify** — when a passage is too hard, drop the harmony and keep **melody + bass**. The melody must always be clear.
6. **Bring out the melody** — play melody notes slightly louder, bass and harmony softer.

**Write it in tab** with rhythm (MuseScore helps), so you remember your choices.

Start with a simple song you know well (a hymn, a folk song) — familiarity helps you hear when the melody is clear.

## Key words

- **Finger-style arrangement:** a guitar version with melody, bass and harmony together
- **Melody note:** the tune note, usually on the top strings
- **Alternating bass:** the thumb switching between bass notes
- **Simplify:** remove notes to keep the melody clear

## Read and watch

- [Classical guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/classical_guitar/) — Yamaha
- [Customising a tablature staff](https://musescore.org/en/handbook/4/tablature) — MuseScore

## Play (40 minutes)

- Thumb bass alone
- Melody alone
- Combine slowly

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Thumb bass alone
1. Then: Combine slowly
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Performance:** practise your stage routine — tune, check, count in, play, finish together — until it is automatic.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add harmonics to your arrangement.

## This week's assignment

Arrange a short melody finger-style and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

Checklist: notes on strings 6 and 5; movable scales; reading; chords of the key; ii–V–I; muting; 12/8 and swing; blues; 7th chords; finger-style.

## Understand it

The Term 1 checklist covers a lot: notes on strings 6 and 5; movable scales; reading notation and tab; the chord family and ii–V–I; strumming dynamics and muting; compound time and swing; the 12-bar blues; seventh chords; finger-style.

**Self-assess** each — green, amber, red — and plan the week around the ambers.

**Revision techniques for guitar:**

- **Note quiz** — a partner (or a random note app) calls notes; find each on strings 6 and 5 within three seconds.
- **Barre chord calls** — "B♭ minor!", "D7 from the 5th string!" — find and play cleanly.
- **Key rotation** — ii–V–I in a different key each day (G, C, D, A, E, F).
- **Scale moves** — play a movable shape in the key called.
- **Blues chorus** — three choruses of shuffle, then two of solo, without losing the form.
- **Reading** — five minutes of notation and tab daily.
- **Finger-style** — your arrangement, slowly, melody clearly louder.

**Fix weak spots with focused practice:**

- Barre chords buzzing → check the index finger's roll and position; practise at fret 5.
- Losing the 12-bar form → count bars aloud; play just the chords with a backing track.
- Slow note finding → octave shapes and daily quizzes.

Run your **prepared piece** daily as a performance.

## Key words

- **Note quiz:** fast recall of fretboard notes
- **Key rotation:** practising in a new key each day
- **Form:** the structure of a piece, e.g. 12 bars

## Understand it

The term test and showcase check **fretboard command** and **musicianship**.

**The practical:**

- **A movable scale** in a key the examiner calls — find the root on string 6 or 5, place the shape, play evenly with alternate picking.
- **Barre chords from called roots** — "F♯ minor", "C from the 5th string". Name the root fret first, then the shape.

- **Sight-reading** — notation and/or tab; scan key, time, rhythms; slow and steady.

**The showcase** adds an **ensemble item**:

- **Different roles** for each guitar (rhythm vs lead; open vs capo).
- **Lock with the rhythm section** — strum with the hi-hat, accents with the snare.
- **Watch** for count-ins, cues and endings.
- **Keep going** together after slips.

**Presentation:** tune before you start; introduce the pieces; bow together.

lessons.title: Minor keys and the minor ii–V–i
lessons.summary: Minor harmony and the harmonic minor sound.
objectives: You will play i–iv–V–i in A and E minor
You will play a minor ii–V–i
You will solo with harmonic minor
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

In A minor, harmony from the harmonic minor gives **E7** as V. The minor ii–V–i is Bm7♭5–E7–Am. Solo over it with A harmonic minor.

## Understand it

In minor keys, the **harmonic minor** (raised 7th) gives the progression a strong pull home, because it makes the **V chord major**.

**In A minor:**

- Natural minor V = **Em** (weak pull).
- Harmonic minor V = **E** (E–G♯–B), or **E7** (E–G♯–B–D) — the G♯ is the **leading note**, a semitone below A, pulling strongly up.

**The minor ii–V–i** — the minor-key version of the most important progression in jazz and gospel:

**Bm7♭5 – E7 – Am(7)**

- **Bm7♭5** (B half-diminished: B–D–F–A) — a tense, dark chord. On guitar: x2323x (root on the 5th string) is a common shape.
- **E7** — open, or a barre.
- **Am** or **Am7** — home.

**Soloing over it with A harmonic minor** (A B C D E F G♯): the **G♯** fits the E7 beautifully and resolves to A over Am. Over Bm7♭5 and Am, the natural minor (G) also works — players often use **G♯ over E7** and **G over the other chords**.

The A harmonic minor sound — with its three-semitone gap F–G♯ — is distinctive: heard in flamenco, Middle-Eastern-influenced music, metal, some gospel and many dramatic film scores.

**Practise:**

- The chord progression with a strumming or picking pattern.
- A harmonic minor in one position, up and down.
- Improvise phrases ending on A over Am, and on G♯ or B over E7.

## Key words

- **Harmonic minor:** minor scale with a raised 7th
- **Half-diminished (m7♭5):** the ii chord in a minor key
- **Minor ii–V–i:** iiø7–V7–i
- **Leading note:** the raised 7th, a semitone below the tonic

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Worship electric guitar uses **volume swells**, delay and simple high voicings that stay out of the keys' way. Gospel rhythm guitar plays short, funky 9th and 13th chord stabs on the off-beats.

## Understand it

Worship and gospel guitar use two very different textures — and great players know when each fits.

**Worship electric guitar (ambient):**

- **Volume swells** — pick a note or chord with the volume knob (or a volume pedal) at zero, then roll it up: the attack disappears and the sound "blooms" like a violin or pad.
- **Delay** — repeats of each note, often set to the song's tempo (e.g. dotted-eighth delay), creating rhythmic echoes.
- **Reverb** — space and atmosphere.
- **Simple, high voicings** — two or three notes high on the neck (often with open strings ringing), so the guitar sits **above** the keys, not on top of them.
- **Less is more** — leave room for the vocals and keys.

**Gospel rhythm guitar (funky):**

- **Short chord stabs** — **9th** and **13th** chords, played staccato on the **off-beats**, locking with the drums and bass.
- **Small voicings** on the top four strings — e.g. a dominant 9 or 13 shape — to stay out of the keyboard's way.
- **Muting** between stabs (release pressure) for a tight, percussive sound.
- **16th-note strumming** with most strums muted and a few accented.

**Working with the keys:** in gospel and worship bands, the **keyboard is usually central** — the guitar complements it. Agree who plays where: keys in the middle register, guitar high; or guitar rhythm stabs while keys hold pads.

## Key words

- **Volume swell:** fading a note in with the volume control
- **Delay:** an effect repeating each note
- **9th / 13th chord:** extended chords adding colour
- **Stab:** a short, accented chord

## Read and watch

- [Electric guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/electric_guitar/) — Yamaha

lessons.title: Afrobeats, juju and highlife guitar II
lessons.summary: Interlocking guitar parts and the West African tradition.
objectives: You will play an interlocking part
You will play in thirds and sixths

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Juju and highlife bands use **two or more guitars interlocking**: one plays a repeating high riff, another plays thirds or sixths, the bass guitar locks with the talking drum. Afrobeats keeps this — short, bright, repeating lines.

## Understand it

Nigerian popular music has some of the world's richest guitar traditions — and the modern Afrobeats guitar sound grew from them.

**Jùjú** — the Yoruba popular music made famous internationally by **King Sunny Adé** (and **Ebenezer Obey**, I. K. Dairo before them) — features:

- **Several guitars interlocking** — each plays a simple, repeating part; together they create a shimmering, complex texture.
- The **talking drum** (dùndún) in conversation with the guitars and vocals; the **bass guitar** often locks with it.
- **Pedal steel guitar** (in King Sunny Adé's band) adding sliding, singing lines.
- **Call-and-response** vocals and praise singing.

**Highlife** guitar — bright, melodic lines in **thirds and sixths**, over I–IV–V harmony, with a lilting, danceable feel.

**Interlocking parts — how they work:**

- **Guitar 1** — a high, repeating **riff** (a few notes, looped).
- **Guitar 2** — **thirds or sixths** in a different rhythm, filling the gaps of guitar 1.
- **Guitar 3 / rhythm** — muted chords on the off-beats.
- **Each part is simple**; the magic is in the **fit**. Players listen to each other more than to themselves.

**Afrobeats** keeps this idea: short, bright, repeating guitar lines, muted between notes, locking with the drums and percussion rather than strumming full chords.

**Exercise:** with a partner, over C – F – G – C, one plays a two-bar high riff, the other plays thirds in the gaps. Swap. Record and listen to how they fit.

## Key words

- **Jùjú:** Yoruba popular music with interlocking guitars and talking drum
- **Interlocking:** separate simple parts fitting into one texture
- **Thirds / sixths:** two notes played together a third or sixth apart
- **Pedal steel:** a guitar played horizontally with a slide

## Read and watch

- [Search: King Sunny Adé](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=king%20sunny%20ade) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Search: jùjú music](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=juju%20music) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Search: highlife](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=highlife) — Google Arts & Culture

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** modes are scales starting on each note of the major scale. Dorian (from the 2nd) and Mixolydian (from the 5th) are common in pop, funk and gospel.

lessons.title: Lead guitar II: vibrato, bends and phrasing
lessons.summary: Making a solo sing: vibrato, accurate bends and phrasing.
objectives: You will play even vibrato
You will bend in tune
You will phrase a solo
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Vibrato** is a controlled wobble of pitch — even and in time. Bends must reach the target pitch: check against the fretted note. Phrase like a singer: breathe between lines.

## Understand it

Year 1 introduced bends and slides. Year 2 makes them **expressive and accurate** — the difference between notes and **phrases that sing**.

**Vibrato** — a controlled, repeated variation in pitch:

- **Even** — the same width each cycle.
- **In time** — many players match vibrato speed to the song's tempo.
- **Width and speed are choices** — narrow and fast is nervous and intense; wide and slow is relaxed and vocal.
- Technique: on electric, rotate the **wrist** (like turning a door handle) so the finger pushes the string slightly up and back, rather than wiggling the finger alone. On classical guitar, rock the finger **along** the string.

**Bends in tune:**

- Know the **target pitch**: a **whole-step bend** must sound the note **two frets higher**; a **half-step bend**, one fret higher.
- **Check**: play the target note first, then bend to match it.
- **Support** the bending finger with the fingers behind it (two or three fingers push together).
- **Release bends** in control; add vibrato **at the top** of a bend for a singing sound.

**Phrasing like a singer:**

- **Breathe** — leave space between phrases.
- **Shape** — phrases rise to a peak and fall.
- **Repeat and vary** — state an idea, then answer it.
- **Dynamics** — pick softer and harder.
- **Target chord tones** at chord changes.

Sing a phrase first, then play it — if you can sing it, it will sound musical.

## Key words

- **Vibrato:** an even, repeated variation in pitch
- **Whole-step bend:** a bend raising the note by two frets' worth
- **Target pitch:** the exact note a bend should reach
- **Phrasing:** shaping musical sentences

## Read and watch

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Nigerian music history:** fuji and apala grew from Yoruba Islamic music; Afrobeat's horns and long grooves came from Fela and Tony Allen. Listen to one track of each.

lessons.title: Classical guitar repertoire
lessons.summary: A short classical study: rest strokes, tone and control.
objectives: You will play rest and free strokes
You will learn a classical study
You will control tone and dynamics
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Classical technique uses **rest strokes** (the finger comes to rest on the next string) for melody and free strokes for arpeggios. Choose a beginner study (for example a Carulli or Sor study).

## Understand it

Classical guitar technique — developed over centuries by composers and players such as **Fernando Sor**, **Mauro Giuliani**, **Matteo Carcassi**, **Ferdinando Carulli**, **Francisco Tárrega** and **Andrés Segovia** — builds **control, tone and independence** that benefit every guitarist.

**Two fundamental strokes:**

- **Rest stroke (apoyando)** — the finger plucks through the string and **comes to rest on the next string** (towards you). Gives a **full, strong, singing tone** — used for **melody** notes.
- **Free stroke (tirando)** — the finger plucks the string and moves **up into the hand**, without touching the next string. Lighter — used for **arpeggios and chords**, where other strings must keep ringing.

**Posture:** the classical guitar sits on the **left leg** (raised with a footstool or a support), neck angled up at about 45°; the right forearm rests on the guitar's edge; wrist slightly arched.

**Nails** — many classical guitarists shape short nails on the picking hand for a clearer tone.

**Choosing a study:** a beginner **study (étude)** by **Carulli** or **Sor** — written to teach a specific technique (arpeggios, melody with bass). Many are free and legal from **IMSLP**, as the music is in the public domain.

**Learning it:**

1. Listen to a recording.
2. Mark **fingerings** (p i m a for the right hand; 1–4 for the left).
3. Practise **slowly**, in sections; use rest strokes for melody where marked.
4. Observe **dynamics** and **tone colour** — play near the bridge (bright) or over the sound hole (warm).

## Key words

- **Rest stroke:** a pluck that comes to rest on the next string
- **Free stroke:** a pluck that clears the next string
- **Study (étude):** a piece written to train a technique
- **Tone colour:** brightness or warmth of sound

## Read and watch

- [Classical guitar: instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/classical_guitar/) — Yamaha
- [IMSLP: free scores](https://imslp.org/) — International Music Score Library Project
- [The Guitar School](https://www.classical-guitar-school.com/) — Classical Guitar School

## Play (40 minutes)

- Rest strokes on scales
- Study, section by section
- Dynamics

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Rest strokes on scales
1. Then: Dynamics
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Music technology:** a metronome click is your best friend in the studio. Record one take to a click and one without, and compare.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Learn the whole study from memory.

## This week's assignment

Learn the first half of your classical study and record it.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Improvisation II: modes
lessons.summary: Dorian and Mixolydian over grooves.
objectives: You will play Dorian and Mixolydian shapes
You will improvise over a vamp
You will develop a motif
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Dorian** over a minor groove (A Dorian over Am7–D) and **Mixolydian** over a dominant groove (A Mixolydian over A7) give funk, gospel and Afro-fusion their sound.

## Understand it

**Modes** are scales made by starting the major scale on a different degree. Each has its own character. Two are especially useful for guitarists:

**Dorian** — the major scale from its **2nd** degree. **A Dorian**: A B C D E **F♯** G A. It is a **minor** scale with a **raised 6th** (F♯ instead of F), giving a cooler, brighter, soulful minor sound.

- Use over **minor grooves**, especially **Am7 – D** (or Am7 – D7) vamps — the F♯ fits the D chord.
- Heard in funk, soul, jazz, gospel, Afro-fusion and Latin music.

**Mixolydian** — the major scale from its **5th** degree. **A Mixolydian**: A B C♯ D E F♯ **G** A. A **major** scale with a **flattened 7th** (G instead of G♯), giving a bluesy, earthy major sound.

- Use over **dominant 7th grooves** — **A7** vamps, or A – G – D (I – ♭VII – IV) progressions.
- Heard in rock, funk, blues, highlife and much Afrobeats.

**Finding them on the guitar:**

- A Dorian = the notes of **G major**, centred on A.
- A Mixolydian = the notes of **D major**, centred on A.
- So you can use **movable major-scale shapes** you already know — just treat a different note as home.

**The key is the target note:** land on **A** and the chord tones (C or C♯, E, G) on strong beats; use the **characteristic note** (F♯ in Dorian, G in Mixolydian) to bring out the mode's colour.

Record a two-chord vamp and improvise for two minutes in each mode.

## Key words

- **Mode:** a scale starting on a different degree of the major scale
- **Dorian:** minor with a raised 6th
- **Mixolydian:** major with a flattened 7th
- **Characteristic note:** the note that gives a mode its colour

## Read and watch

- [Modes](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/modes.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- Dorian vamp
- Mixolydian vamp
- Motif development

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Dorian vamp
1. Then: Motif development
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** use it for ideas — a chord progression, a rhythm, a title — then make them yours at the instrument. Hand in what YOU played. A piece you cannot perform is not your piece.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Reading:** dynamics (pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff), crescendo and diminuendo shape music. Mark them in your pieces in pencil.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Switch modes as the chord changes.

## This week's assignment

Record a two-minute improvisation over a vamp.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Arranging for two guitars
lessons.summary: Splitting a song between rhythm and lead, open and capo.
objectives: You will split a song into two parts
You will use a capo for a second voicing
You will write an intro riff
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Divide roles: one guitar open chords low, the other a **capo shape** higher (for example capo 5 with D shapes for a song in G). Add a melody line or riff for the intro.

## Understand it

Two guitars playing the **same chords in the same place** sound thick and muddy, and any small timing difference becomes obvious. A good **two-guitar arrangement** gives each its own **role, register and rhythm**.

**Divide by register:**

- **Guitar 1** — open chords, low and full (e.g. G shapes in G).
- **Guitar 2** — a **capo** shape higher: for a song in G, **capo 5 with D shapes** (D shape at capo 5 sounds as G; A shape sounds as D; C shape sounds as F… choose shapes that give the song's chords). Or barre/triad shapes high on the neck. The same harmony, brighter and in a different range.

**Divide by rhythm:**

- Guitar 1 strums steady eighths; guitar 2 plays **arpeggios** or **off-beat stabs**.
- Or guitar 1 finger-picks, guitar 2 plays a **melody or riff**.

**Divide by role:**

- **Intro** — guitar 2 plays a **melody or riff** (often from the chorus) over guitar 1's chords.
- **Verses** — one guitar only, or both sparse.
- **Choruses** — both full.
- **Solo section** — one plays lead, the other holds the rhythm.

**Write the arrangement down** — a chart showing who plays what in each section, with tab for riffs.

**Rehearse together**: listen for clashes (both playing the same notes in the same range), timing (lock strums together) and balance. Record it and check that both parts are heard.

## Key words

- **Register:** how high or low the notes sit
- **Capo voicing:** chord shapes played higher with a capo
- **Part writing:** deciding each instrument's role
- **Clash:** two parts fighting in the same range or rhythm

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Customising a tablature staff](https://musescore.org/en/handbook/4/tablature) — MuseScore

## Play (40 minutes)

- Plan parts
- Capo voicing
- Intro riff

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Plan parts
1. Then: Intro riff
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Teamwork:** a rehearsal plan saves time: warm-up, run the hardest part first, full run, notes, final run.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add a harmony line in thirds.

## This week's assignment

Arrange and record a two-guitar version of a song with a partner.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Music technology: amps, pedals and recording
lessons.summary: Your signal chain and recording guitar into a DAW.
objectives: You will set up a signal chain
You will record guitar into a DAW
You will layer two takes
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Signal chain: **guitar → tuner → drive → modulation → delay/reverb → amp**. Record with an audio interface (direct) or a mic on the amp. Record a clean DI so you can change the tone later.

## Understand it

Electric guitar sound is shaped by a **signal chain** — the path from strings to speaker.

**A typical pedalboard order:**

**guitar → tuner → drive/distortion → modulation (chorus, phaser) → delay → reverb → amp**

- **Tuner** first, so it gets a clean signal (and can mute for silent tuning).
- **Drive / overdrive / distortion** — adds grit and sustain by clipping the signal. Overdrive is warm and light; distortion heavy.
- **Modulation** — chorus (shimmer, thickness), phaser, flanger.
- **Delay** — echoes, timed to the song.
- **Reverb** — space, room, hall.

Drive before time effects keeps echoes clean; reversing it makes echoes distorted and messy. (Rules can be broken for effect.)

**Amps** — the amp's **gain** controls distortion; **master volume** controls loudness; **EQ** (bass, middle, treble) shapes tone. Start with everything at 12 o'clock and adjust by ear.

**Recording guitar:**

- **DI (direct injection)** — plug into an **audio interface** and record the dry signal. Use **amp-simulation** software in the DAW to shape the tone.
- **Mic the amp** — a dynamic mic (like the SM57) close to the speaker cone, slightly off-centre.
- **Record a clean DI as well** as the amp sound — then you can **re-amp** or change the tone later without replaying.

Set input levels so peaks sit around −12 to −6 dBFS — never clipping. Protect your hearing: practise and record at moderate volume.

## Key words

- **Signal chain:** the path the sound takes from guitar to speaker
- **Overdrive / distortion:** effects that add grit by clipping the signal
- **DI:** direct injection — recording the guitar's signal straight in
- **Re-amping:** sending a recorded DI through an amp later

## Read and watch

- [Recording and mixing techniques](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques) — Sound On Sound
- [Audio insights and guides](https://www.shure.com/en-US/insights) — Shure
- [Deafness and hearing loss: safe listening](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/deafness-and-hearing-loss) — World Health Organization

## Play (40 minutes)

- Set the chain
- Record rhythm
- Record lead over it

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Set the chain
1. Then: Record lead over it
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Mindset:** set one SMART goal for the term: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add bass and drums in the DAW.

## This week's assignment

Record a two-part guitar arrangement and share the file.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.summary: Locking with drums and bass, leaving space, leading a band.
objectives: You will lock to the drummer
You will play under a singer
You will lead a song
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Lock your strumming to the hi-hat and your accents to the snare. Signal sections a bar early, agree endings, and watch the drummer for tempo.

## Understand it

A band sounds tight when its rhythm section **locks** — drums, bass, keys and guitars feeling the beat in exactly the same place.

**Locking guitar to the drums:**

- **Strumming with the hi-hat** — if the hi-hat plays eighths, strum eighths with it; if it plays sixteenths, your pendulum moves in sixteenths.
- **Accents with the snare** — beats 2 and 4 — or with the drummer's accents in the groove.
- **Watch the drummer** for tempo, fills and section changes. The drummer's fill usually signals "next section".

**Signalling and structure:**

- **Signal sections a bar early** — a nod, a raised hand, a called word ("Chorus!").
- **Agree the endings**: a hit together on beat 1; a held chord ended by a cue; a fade.
- **Know the form** — how many bars per section, how many repeats.

**Playing with the bass:**

- Let the bass own the low notes — use **higher voicings** and avoid hammering the low E string under the bass line.
- Match the bass's rhythmic feel.

**Volume and tone:**

- If you cannot hear the singer, you are too loud.
- Choose a tone that sits **in the mix** — a little less bass and a bit more mid than when playing alone.

**Rehearsal habits:** rehearse transitions and endings most; record rehearsals and listen back; fix one thing at a time.

## Key words

- **Locking:** playing in exactly the same rhythmic place as the drums
- **Fill (drums):** a drum figure signalling a section change
- **Voicing:** the choice of notes and register for a chord
- **Mix:** the balance of all the instruments together

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E F G A B
```

## Play (40 minutes)

- Rehearse cues
- Lead one song
- Swap leaders

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Rehearse cues
1. Then: Swap leaders
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Search for a backing track in this key ("C major backing track 70bpm") and play along. Playing to someone else's time is a different skill from playing alone, and it is the one a band needs.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Theory:** 7th chords — major 7 (Cmaj7), minor 7 (Am7), dominant 7 (G7) — are the colours of gospel, jazz and neo-soul.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Lead a song with a key change.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.summary: A song with verse, pre-chorus, chorus and bridge.
objectives: You will write a four-section song
You will use contrasting chords for the bridge
You will record a demo
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Extend your songwriting with a **pre-chorus** (builds tension) and a **bridge** (new chords, new perspective). Try a modulation for the last chorus.

## Understand it

In Year 1 you wrote verse–chorus songs. Year 2 adds two sections that give songs **shape and journey**, and a technique to lift the end.

**The pre-chorus** — a short section (usually 2–4 lines) between the verse and chorus that **builds tension**:

- **New chords** — often starting on IV or vi, ending on V (which pulls into the chorus).
- **Rising melody** — climbing towards the chorus's opening note.
- **Increasing energy** — fuller strumming, rhythm building, sometimes a break just before the chorus.

**The bridge** — a contrasting section, usually once, before the final chorus:

- **New chords** — chords not used elsewhere (e.g. starting on IV or vi).
- **New perspective** in the lyrics — a twist, a realisation, a question, looking at the story from another angle.
- **Different melody and feel** — it refreshes the listener's ear, so the last chorus feels new.

**Modulation for the last chorus** — moving **up a semitone or a tone** for the final chorus lifts the energy dramatically. Simplest method: play the **V chord of the new key** just before it (to go from G to A, play E or E7, then start the chorus in A). With a capo, move it up one or two frets!

**Typical full form:** Intro – Verse – Pre-chorus – Chorus – Verse – Pre-chorus – Chorus – Bridge – (Chorus in new key) – Outro.

Record demos, play them for others, and revise — songwriting is rewriting.

## Key words

- **Pre-chorus:** a short section building tension into the chorus
- **Bridge:** a contrasting section before the final chorus
- **Modulation:** changing key
- **Demo:** a rough recording of a song idea

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Make melodies](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-melodies/make-melodies.html) — Ableton Learning Music

- Record a demo

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Write the pre-chorus
1. Then: Record a demo
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Copyright and the business:** royalties are paid to writers when songs are played, streamed or performed. In Nigeria, COSON and MCSN collect them.

- **If you already can:** Add a harmony vocal or a second guitar part.

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: neck notes; movable scales; reading; chords of the key and 7ths; blues; worship/gospel textures; interlocking parts; lead techniques; classical study; your song.

## Understand it

Year 2 revision covers ten areas. Plan a week that touches each at least twice, weighted to your weakest.

**Checklist:**

1. **Neck notes** — strings 6 and 5, instant recall.
2. **Movable scales** — major and minor shapes in called keys.
3. **Reading** — notation and tab, daily.
4. **Chords** — the chord family in G, C, D; barre and seventh chords from any root.
5. **Progressions** — ii–V–I (major and minor); I–vi–ii–V.
6. **Blues** — shuffle and solo, keeping the form.
7. **Textures** — worship swells and high voicings; gospel 9th/13th stabs; muting and chucks.
8. **Interlocking parts** — highlife/jùjú/Afrobeats riffs with a partner.
9. **Lead techniques** — vibrato, accurate bends, phrasing; modes.
10. **Repertoire** — your classical study, your arrangement, your song.

**Testing methods:**

- **Random calls** (notes, chords, keys) from a partner or a list.
- **Record yourself** in the prepared pieces and judge tone, timing, dynamics.
- **Play for someone** — even once — before the assessment.

**Physical care:** short, frequent sessions; warm up; rest when the hand tires. Change strings a few days before the recital so they stretch and settle.

## Key words

- **Random calls:** testing items in unpredictable order
- **Weighted revision:** spending most time on weakest areas
- **Self-recording:** recording to judge your own playing

## Read and watch

- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

## Play (40 minutes)

- Self-test
- Targeted practice
- Performance run

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Self-test
1. Then: Performance run
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Practice habits:** before the test, practise performing — one take, no stops, as if it were the real thing.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Prepare a third piece in another style.

## This week's assignment

Follow your revision plan; one full run a day.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Year 2 assessment and recital
lessons.summary: The year's assessment and a recital.
objectives: You will perform under assessment conditions
You will play two contrasting pieces
You will present your own song
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical:** scales on request; barre and 7th chords; sight-reading; two contrasting pieces; your song. **Recital** for families.

## Understand it

The Year 2 assessment and recital show your growth from open chords to a guitarist who knows the neck, reads, plays in many styles, and leads parts in a band.

**The practical** — scales on request, barre and seventh chords, sight-reading, two contrasting pieces, and your song. Remember: **clean and steady first**, use preparation time, never restart.

**The recital:**

- **Choose contrasting pieces** — e.g. the classical study, a highlife or Afrobeats piece, a blues, and your own song.
- **Introduce each piece** briefly — what it is and something interesting about it.
- **Gear check** — fresh strings (settled), tuner, spare strings, picks, capo, cable (for electric), a strap.
- **Stage routine** — set up calmly, tune, introduce, breathe, play, finish, bow.

**Portfolio:** recordings from the recital; your arrangement and song (tab/notation and lyric sheet); your practice log.

**Looking ahead to Year 3** — the focus becomes **artistry and leadership**. You will choose a direction (**performer**, **music director**, **songwriter/producer** or **teacher**), plan a graduation project, and mentor younger players. Start thinking:

- Which style feels most like **you**?
- Do you enjoy **leading**, **creating**, **performing** or **teaching** most?
- What would you like to have achieved by graduation?

Write your thoughts down — they shape your Year 3 plan.

## Key words

- **Recital:** a formal performance of prepared pieces
- **Gear check:** preparing instrument and equipment before performing
- **Artistic direction:** the area you choose to develop

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

## Learn (30 minutes)

Year 3 is about **artistry and leadership**: you choose a focus (performer, music director, songwriter/producer or teacher), plan a graduation project, and mentor younger members. Today: a technique check, a listening session of musicians you admire, and a first project plan.

## Understand it

Year 3 shifts from **learning skills** to **becoming a musician with your own voice** — and to **leading** others.

**Choose a focus** for the year. Each leads to a different graduation project:

- **Performer** — a 20-minute recital that shows your range and identity.
- **Music director** — leading a band or choir through a performance.
- **Songwriter / producer** — an EP of three recorded original tracks.
- **Teacher** — a unit taught to Year 1 members, with evidence of their progress.

You can do all of these later in life; choosing one now lets you go deep.

**Finding your musical identity:**

- **Listen widely and deliberately.** Make a list of ten recordings that move you. What do they share — a groove, a harmony, a type of voice, a feeling?
- **Notice your instincts.** When you improvise or arrange, what do you naturally do? That is the start of a style.
- **Combine influences.** Most distinctive artists blend two or three traditions — highlife with jazz, gospel with Afrobeats, classical with neo-soul.

**Plan the project now**, with a timeline back from graduation: research and repertoire choice, development, rehearsal, feedback, final preparation. Use SMART goals and check them each term.

**Mentoring** is part of Year 3: explaining something to a beginner is the best test of whether you understand it.

## Key words

- **Musical identity:** the combination of influences and instincts that makes your playing yours
- **Graduation project:** the year's main piece of work, in your chosen focus
- **Mentoring:** guiding a less experienced player

lessons.title: Advanced technique I: speed with control
lessons.summary: Building speed safely with a metronome and burst practice.
objectives: You will use burst practice
You will raise tempo by clean steps

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Burst practice:** play a short group fast, stop, relax, repeat — then join groups. Raise the metronome 4 bpm only after three clean repetitions. Speed is relaxation plus accuracy.

## Understand it

Speed is not a separate skill from accuracy — it is **accuracy plus relaxation**. Tension is what limits speed: a tight hand cannot move quickly or for long.

**Burst practice** (also called chunking):

1. Take a short group of notes — 3 to 5 — from a fast passage.
2. Play the group **fast**, then **stop** and **relax** completely.
3. Repeat until the burst is clean and easy.
4. Join two bursts; then three; then the whole passage.

The brain learns the movement as one gesture rather than many separate notes.

**Metronome discipline:**

- Find the tempo where the passage is **perfect**.
- Play it **three times clean** in a row.
- Raise the tempo by **4 bpm**. Repeat.
- When mistakes appear, drop back 8–10 bpm and rebuild.
- Practise slightly **above** performance tempo, so the real tempo feels comfortable.

**Other tools:**

- **Rhythmic variations** — play an even passage in dotted rhythms (long-short, then short-long). It trains each finger transition.
- **Minimal motion** — fingers close to the keys or strings; no wasted lift.
- **Breathe** and check shoulders, jaw and wrists for tension.

Short, focused sessions beat long tired ones — practising fast while fatigued trains sloppiness.

## Key words

- **Burst practice:** playing short groups fast, then relaxing
- **Tension:** unnecessary muscle effort that limits speed
- **Rhythmic variation:** practising even notes in uneven rhythms

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Extensions stack thirds above the 7th: **9, 11, 13**. Altered dominants (7♭9, 7♯9, 7♯5) add tension that resolves to I. Gospel and neo-soul live here.

## Understand it

**Extended chords** keep stacking thirds above the 7th:

- **9th** — the 2nd an octave up (C9: C E G B♭ D; Cmaj9: C E G B D).
- **11th** — the 4th an octave up (often used on minor chords: Cm11).
- **13th** — the 6th an octave up (C13: C E G B♭ D A; often played without the 11th).

In practice, players **leave notes out**: the **root** (the bass player has it), the **5th** (adds little colour). The **3rd and 7th** define the chord; the extension adds colour. A C13 might be voiced simply as **B♭–E–A** over a C bass.

**Altered dominants** add tension to the V chord by sharpening or flattening the 5th and 9th:

- **7♭9** (G7♭9: G B D F A♭) — dark, dramatic.
- **7♯9** (G7♯9: G B D F A♯) — the bluesy "Hendrix chord".
- **7♯5** (augmented) — restless, rising.

The more tension on V, the sweeter the resolution to I.

**Where they live:** gospel (13ths, 7♭9 walk-ups, 9ths everywhere), neo-soul (minor 9ths and 11ths), jazz, R&B and Afro-fusion.

**Practise:** ii–V–I as **Dm9 – G13 – Cmaj9**, then with **G7♭9**. Listen to how each colour changes the emotion.

## Key words

- **Extended chord:** a chord with 9ths, 11ths or 13ths added
- **Altered dominant:** a V chord with sharpened or flattened 5th or 9th
- **Shell voicing:** a voicing using mainly the 3rd and 7th

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Transposing** means playing the same song in another key — think in numbers (I, IV, V) not letters. **Modulating** uses a pivot chord or the new key's V to move smoothly.

## Understand it

**Transposition** means playing the same music in a different key — essential when a singer needs it higher or lower.

**Think in numbers, not letters.** A song that is "1 – 5 – 6m – 4" is C–G–Am–F in C, D–A–Bm–G in D, and B♭–F–Gm–E♭ in B♭. If you know the song as numbers, any key is the same song. Many church and session musicians learn every song this way (the Nashville Number System).

**Modulation** means changing key **during** a piece. Common methods:

- **Via the new key's V** — play the dominant (7th) chord of the new key, then arrive. To go from C to D: play **A7**, then D.
- **Pivot chord** — a chord that belongs to both keys. C major and G major share Am, C, Em, G. Use one as the hinge: C – Am (as vi of C, then reinterpreted as ii of G) – D7 – G.
- **Direct ("truck driver") modulation** — simply jump up a semitone or tone, usually for the last chorus. Dramatic and common in gospel and pop.

**Practise:**

1. Learn a song in numbers.
2. Play it in three keys.
3. Add a modulation up a tone for the last chorus using the new key's V.

Transposing on the spot is a professional skill that makes you valuable to every singer and band.

## Key words

- **Transpose:** play music in a different key
- **Modulate:** change key within a piece
- **Pivot chord:** a chord shared by two keys, used to move between them
- **Number system:** writing chords as scale degrees

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Music direction: rehearsing a band
lessons.summary: Running an effective rehearsal and arranging for a band.
objectives: You will plan a rehearsal
You will give clear instructions

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

A music director: **plans** (set list, keys, arrangements), **communicates** (number charts, cues), **listens** (balance, tempo) and **encourages**. Rehearse transitions, not just songs.

## Understand it

A **music director (MD)** turns a group of players into a band. The job has four parts:

**1. Plan**

- **Set list** — the songs, their order, keys and tempos.
- **Arrangements** — intro, sections, repeats, dynamics, endings, who plays what.
- **Charts** — clear lead sheets or number charts for every player.
- **Rehearsal plan** — what to work on, in what order, with timings.

**2. Communicate**

- **Number charts** so the band can follow key changes.
- **Clear cues** — agreed hand signals or calls for sections, repeats, builds, drops and endings.
- **Short, specific instructions** — "Bass, play only roots in verse 1", not "make it better".

**3. Listen**

- **Balance** — can you hear the singer? Is anything too loud?
- **Tempo** — is the band rushing in the chorus or dragging in the bridge?
- **Tightness** — are hits and endings together?

**4. Encourage**

- Name what is working, specifically. Correct one thing at a time.
- Keep energy up; end rehearsals on a good run.

**Rehearse transitions, not just songs.** Bands usually know the middles of songs; they fall apart at **starts, section changes and endings**. Loop these: "From the last line of the verse into the chorus — again."

## Key words

- **Music director:** the person who leads a band's musical decisions
- **Set list:** the planned order of songs
- **Transition:** the move from one section or song to the next

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Afro-fusion** blends Afrobeats, highlife, R&B and jazz; **neo-soul** uses extended chords, laid-back timing and lush voicings. Study one track's part note-for-note, then create your own.

## Understand it

**Afro-fusion** blends Afrobeats with highlife, R&B, reggae/dancehall, jazz and soul — the sound of artists who move between styles while keeping a West African rhythmic core. **Neo-soul** (from the 1990s onward) brought jazz harmony and loose, laid-back grooves to soul and R&B.

**What they share and what to study:**

- **Extended chords** — minor 9ths and 11ths, major 9ths, 13ths (week 3).
- **Laid-back timing** — notes placed slightly **behind** the beat. It feels relaxed and heavy. It is deliberate: practise playing just behind a metronome without dragging the tempo.
- **Lush voicings** — spread chords, close clusters, moving inner voices.
- **Groove first** — repetitive two- or four-bar loops with small variations.
- **Space** — what you leave out matters as much as what you play.

**The study method (transcribe, then create):**

1. Choose **one track** and **one part** (the keys, or the guitar).
2. Learn it **note-for-note** by ear, slowing the track if needed. Copy the **rhythm and feel**, not only the notes.
3. Analyse: what chords? Which voicings? Where is it behind the beat?
4. **Create your own** part over the same progression, using what you learned.

This is how musicians absorb a style — through the ear and the hands, not just from explanations.

## Key words

- **Afro-fusion:** Afrobeats blended with other styles
- **Neo-soul:** soul music with jazz harmony and laid-back grooves
- **Behind the beat:** playing slightly late on purpose for a relaxed feel

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

1. Then: Write an original part

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **jazz standard** (for example 'Autumn Leaves') is mostly ii–V–I chains. **Comping** is rhythmic chord accompaniment; the head is the melody, then solos, then the head again.

## Understand it

A **jazz standard** is a well-known tune that jazz musicians share and play in their own ways — many come from 1920s–1950s musical theatre and popular song. Their harmony is built largely from **chains of ii–V–I**, which is why learning standards is the best training in harmony there is.

**"Autumn Leaves"** is a classic first standard: it alternates a **major ii–V–I** and its **relative minor ii–V–i**:

- In G minor / B♭ major: **Cm7 – F7 – B♭maj7 – E♭maj7 – Am7♭5 – D7 – Gm**.

**How a jazz performance is organised:**

1. **The head** — the melody played once (or twice) through.
2. **Solos** — each soloist improvises over the **same chord sequence** (one time through is a **chorus**).
3. **The head again**, then an ending.

**Comping** (from "accompanying" / "complementing") — playing the chords **rhythmically and sparingly** behind the melody or soloist:

- Short chords, off the beat, leaving space.
- **Shell voicings** (3rd and 7th) or rootless voicings so the bass is free.
- **Listen and respond** to the soloist — it is a conversation.

**Practise:** learn the chord sequence until you can play it without reading; comp along with a recording; then improvise over it using **chord tones** (1, 3, 5, 7 of each chord) on the strong beats.

## Key words

- **Jazz standard:** a widely known tune in the jazz repertoire
- **Head:** the tune's melody, played at the start and end
- **Chorus (jazz):** one time through the chord sequence
- **Comping:** rhythmic chordal accompaniment

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

1. Then: Head and solo

## Learn (30 minutes)

Prepare: tempo, key, click, chart. Record a **guide**, then real takes. Do three good takes and comp the best parts. Keep notes on what each take was.

## Understand it

A recording session rewards **preparation**: studio time is limited, and every problem fixed before you arrive saves an hour.

**Before the session:**

- **Tempo** (bpm) and **key** decided and written down.
- **Chart** — the arrangement with sections and bar counts.
- **Click track** — practise with it; recording to a click lets parts be edited together later.
- **Instrument ready** — fresh (settled) strings, tuned, intonation checked; for keys, sounds chosen and saved.
- **Warm up** before you arrive.

**The process:**

1. **Guide track** — a quick rough recording of the whole song (often guitar or keys plus a guide vocal), so everyone knows where they are.
2. **Real takes** — the actual parts, one instrument at a time, usually starting with the rhythm section.
3. **Several good takes** — record three or more full takes of your part.
4. **Comping** — choosing the best sections from several takes and joining them.

**Keep notes** on each take: "Take 2 — great verse, chorus rushed", "Take 3 — best feel". In a long session, nobody remembers which take was which.

**Headphone mix** — ask for what you need to play well (more click, more vocal, less of yourself).

Listen to playback critically: tuning, timing, tone, feel. If something is wrong, re-record now — "fix it in the mix" rarely works.

## Key words

- **Click track:** a metronome heard in headphones while recording
- **Guide track:** a rough recording that others record over
- **Take:** one recorded performance
- **Comping:** combining the best parts of several takes

## Read and watch

- [Recording and mixing techniques](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques) — Sound On Sound
- [Production tips and tutorials](https://www.izotope.com/en/learn.html) — iZotope

- Set up
- Takes
- Comp and export

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Set up
1. Then: Comp and export
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Music technology:** mixing basics — balance levels first, then pan, then EQ; leave effects for last.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Mix the track: levels, pan, EQ, reverb.

## This week's assignment

Record and share a finished track of a song from your repertoire.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Mentoring: teaching a beginner
lessons.summary: Planning and teaching a 20-minute lesson to a Year 1 member.
objectives: You will plan a 20-minute lesson
You will teach one skill
You will give specific feedback
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Good teaching: **one goal**, demonstrate, let them try, correct one thing, praise specifically, repeat. Check understanding by asking them to show you, not tell you.

## Understand it

Teaching someone else is one of the fastest ways to deepen your own understanding — you discover what you only *thought* you knew. Good teaching follows a simple cycle:

1. **One goal** — a small, specific target for the lesson: "Change from C to G in time", not "get better at guitar".
2. **Demonstrate** — show it slowly, then at normal speed. Let them hear the target.
3. **Let them try** — hands on the instrument quickly; do not talk for long.
4. **Correct one thing** — the most important problem only. Five corrections at once overwhelm a beginner.
5. **Praise specifically** — "Your thumb is behind the neck now — that's why the chord rings" teaches more than "well done".
6. **Repeat** — practise until it is reliable, then set the next small step.

**Check understanding by asking them to show you, not tell you.** "Do you understand?" almost always gets "yes". "Show me the change from C to G" reveals the truth.

**Other principles:**

- **Patience** — remember how hard it was for you.
- **Encourage practice habits** — short daily practice, a log.
- **Adapt** — every learner is different; if one explanation fails, try another (a picture, a comparison, slower).
- **Safeguarding** — follow the Club's rules for working with younger members: in shared spaces, with staff aware.

Keep brief notes after each lesson: goal, progress, next step.

## Key words

- **Teaching cycle:** goal, demonstrate, try, correct, praise, repeat
- **Specific praise:** naming exactly what was done well
- **Check for understanding:** asking a learner to show, not tell

- **If you already can:** Teach a small group of three.

**Today's session, to scale:**


## Warm-up (10 minutes)

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: speed with control; extended chords; transposition and modulation; music direction; one modern and one jazz style; a recorded track. **Project check:** is your plan on schedule?

## Understand it

Mid-year is the moment to check two things: **your skills** and **your project**.

**Skills checklist** — rate each green, amber or red:

- Speed with control (burst practice, metronome progress).
- Extended and altered chords — can you voice them in several keys?
- Transposition on the spot; modulation by the V of the new key.
- Music direction — clear cues, structured rehearsals.
- One modern style (Afro-fusion/neo-soul) and one jazz standard.
- A recorded track from the session.

**Project check** — answer honestly:

- **Is the plan on schedule?** Compare your timeline with where you are.
- **What is done** and what is evidence of it (recordings, charts, lesson notes)?
- **What is at risk?** Time, people, equipment, a piece that is too hard?
- **What needs to change?** Cut scope, simplify a piece, book rehearsals earlier.

A project that is behind can almost always be saved if you notice **now** — and almost never if you notice in the last month.

**Revise for the term test** with mixed practice: technique at tempo, an extended-chord progression in a called key, transposing a song, directing a short section, and your prepared piece.

## Key words

- **Project check:** a review of progress against the plan
- **Scope:** how much the project includes
- **Risk:** something that could stop the plan succeeding

objectives: You will perform under test conditions

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical:** technique at tempo; an extended-chord progression; transpose a song on request; direct a short section; perform a prepared piece in a style of your choice.

## Understand it

The Year 3 term test assesses **artistry and leadership**, not just correctness.

**What it includes:**

- **Technique at tempo** — scales, arpeggios or technical passages at a demanding speed, clean and relaxed.
- **An extended-chord progression** — e.g. ii–V–I with 9ths and 13ths, possibly in a key the examiner calls. Think in numbers and voice-lead smoothly.
- **Transpose a song on request** — play a known song in a new key without preparation. Use the number system.
- **Direct a short section** — lead other players: count in, cue sections, fix one problem, run it again.
- **A prepared piece in a style of your choice** — performed with conviction and personal character.

**What examiners look for at this level:**

- **Control** — tempo, dynamics, tone, all deliberate.
- **Understanding** — you can explain your choices.
- **Communication** — with the audience and with other players.
- **Recovery** — calm handling of anything that goes wrong.

**On the day:** warm up properly, tune carefully, breathe, and make decisions with confidence. Ask for clarification if a request is unclear — professionals do.

Afterwards, use the feedback to adjust your graduation project plan.

## Key words

- **Artistry:** personal, convincing musical expression
- **Conviction:** playing with commitment and intention
- **Transposition on sight:** changing key without preparation

lessons.title: Showcase: your musical identity
lessons.summary: A performance that shows who you are as a musician.
objectives: You will perform a short set
You will introduce your music
You will receive audience feedback
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Perform a short set (two or three pieces) that shows your **focus** and your voice: a cover reimagined, an original, and something that stretches you. Introduce each one.

## Understand it

This showcase is a **short set** — two or three pieces — that says who you are as a musician.

**Building the set:**

1. **A cover reimagined** — a known song in your own arrangement: a new groove (ballad to Afro-groove), new harmony (reharmonised with extended chords), or a new texture. The audience recognises it; your version shows your identity.
2. **An original** — your composition or song.
3. **Something that stretches you** — a piece at the edge of your ability or in a new style.

**Order matters:** start with something confident to settle in; put the most demanding piece in the middle; end with the strongest.

**Introductions** — one or two sentences each: what it is, and why you chose it or what you did with it. Speaking connects you with the audience.

**Presence:**

- Walk on and set up calmly; tune; adjust the seat or strap.
- Pause before starting; let the audience settle.
- Commit to every choice — an interpretation played with conviction convinces.
- Acknowledge applause between pieces; thank the audience and any band members at the end.

**Record it** — it belongs in your portfolio, and watching it afterwards teaches you more than any feedback.

## Key words

- **Set:** a planned group of pieces performed together
- **Reimagined cover:** your own new version of an existing song
- **Running order:** the sequence of pieces in a set

lessons.title: Advanced technique: octaves, chords and the four-octave scale
lessons.summary: Octaves, rapid chord changes and four-octave scales and arpeggios.
objectives: You will play octave passages relaxed
You will play four-octave scales at 100 bpm
