lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Octaves come from a loose wrist bouncing from the elbow, not tight fingers. Four-octave scales need an even thumb crossing at speed. Play chords from the arm's weight so loud never means hard.

## Understand it

Advanced repertoire demands three techniques that all depend on **using the arm, not forcing the fingers**.

**Octaves:**

- Hand shaped with thumb and finger 5 (or 4 on black keys) spanning the octave; the fingers between relaxed, not stretched stiff.
- The motion comes from a **loose wrist bouncing**, driven by the **forearm and elbow** — not from tense fingers pressing.
- Practise slowly with a light touch, staying close to the keys; increase speed with burst practice.
- **Rest** if the hand aches — octave work tires small hands; never push through pain.

**Four-octave scales:**

- The challenge is **even thumb crossings at speed** — the thumb must move early and smoothly, without a bump or accent.
- The **arm travels** smoothly along the keyboard; the elbow leads the hand.
- Practise in **rhythmic groups** (accenting every 4th note, then every 3rd) and with burst practice; use the metronome ladder.

**Big chords from the arm:**

- **Arm weight**, released into the keys from a relaxed shoulder, gives a full, rich sound. **Loud never means hard** — hitting with tense fingers makes a harsh tone and risks injury.
- Prepare the **hand shape** above the keys before the chord, then drop.
- Listen for **balance** within the chord — usually the top note sings.

Warm up before technical work, and keep sessions short and focused.

## Key words

- **Octave technique:** playing octaves with a loose wrist and arm
- **Arm weight:** the arm's weight released into the keys
- **Thumb crossing:** passing the thumb under smoothly in scales

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Ear III: transcription
lessons.summary: Transcribing a full song section: melody, bass, chords.
objectives: You will transcribe a bass line
You will identify chord qualities
You will write out a chorus
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Work in layers: **bass first** (it tells you the chords), then the chord quality, then the melody. Slow the track (most players can at 75% without changing pitch).

## Understand it

**Transcription** — working out music from a recording — is how players have learned styles for generations. It trains the ear, the hands and your understanding of how music is built.

**Work in layers:**

1. **Structure** — map the sections and count the bars.
2. **Bass line first** — the lowest notes usually tell you the **roots** of the chords. Sing it, then find it.
3. **Chord quality** — over each root: major or minor? Is there a 7th? A 9th? Try options until it matches.
4. **Melody** — sing a phrase, find the first note, then each interval.
5. **Details** — fills, voicings, rhythm hits, articulation.

**Tools and habits:**

- **Slow the track down** — most players can work comfortably at 75% speed with pitch preserved (many apps and YouTube's speed control do this).
- **Loop** short sections — two bars at a time.
- **Sing before you play** — if you can sing it, you can find it.
- **Use headphones** — bass lines and inner voices are much clearer.
- **Write it down** — chord chart, notation or tab — so the work is not lost.

**Check your transcription** by playing along with the recording at full speed: anything that clashes is wrong. Start with simple songs and build up; speed comes with practice.

## Key words

- **Transcription:** working out and writing down music from a recording
- **Layering:** transcribing one element at a time
- **Loop:** repeating a short section for study

## Read and watch

- [Ear training exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

**Instrument care:** learn the basics of keyboard setup — splits, layers and saving patches for a gig.

lessons.title: Reharmonisation and arranging
lessons.summary: Creating your own version of a song by changing its harmony and feel.
objectives: You will reharmonise a song
You will change its feel
You will keep the melody recognisable
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Reharmonise by **substituting** (vi for I, ii–V for V), **changing feel** (ballad to Afro-groove), or **adding passing chords**. Keep the melody recognisable.

## Understand it

**Reharmonisation** means changing the chords under a melody while keeping the melody the same. It is how arrangers make a familiar song feel new.

**Techniques:**

- **Substitution** — replace a chord with one that shares notes and function:
  - **vi for I** (Am instead of C) — softer, more emotional.
  - **iii for I** (Em for C).
  - **ii–V for V** (Dm7–G7 instead of G7) — more movement.
  - **Tritone substitution** in jazz (D♭7 for G7).
- **Passing chords** — a quick chord between two main ones (a diminished chord, or a chord a semitone above or below the target).
- **Extensions** — turn triads into 7ths, 9ths and 13ths.
- **Changing the bass** — slash chords and a moving bass line (C – C/B – Am – Am/G).
- **Changing the feel** — the same chords as a ballad, an Afro-groove, a gospel 12/8, a swing.

**The rule: keep the melody recognisable.** Check every new chord against the melody note on top of it — the melody note should be a chord tone or a pleasing extension, not a harsh clash (unless you want one).

**Arranging process:** sing the melody; try alternative chords bar by bar; record versions; keep what serves the song's emotion. Write the final arrangement as a lead sheet.

## Key words

- **Reharmonisation:** new chords under an existing melody
- **Chord substitution:** replacing a chord with one of similar function
- **Passing chord:** a brief connecting chord
- **Tritone substitution:** replacing V7 with the dominant a tritone away

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

lessons.title: Music business essentials
lessons.summary: Royalties, contracts, gigs and building your profile.
objectives: You will explain royalties
You will draft a simple gig agreement

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Know the basics: **performance and mechanical royalties**, work-for-hire vs. ownership, a simple gig agreement (date, fee, time, equipment), and a profile (bio, photo, recordings). Never sign a contract you don't understand — ask a trusted adult or lawyer.

## Understand it

Musicians who understand the business keep more of what they earn and avoid bad deals.

**Copyright** — when you create an original song or recording, you own copyright in it automatically. There are usually **two copyrights** in recorded music:

- The **composition** (melody and lyrics) — owned by the **songwriters** (and their publishers).
- The **sound recording (master)** — owned by whoever paid for or made the recording (the artist or a label).

**Royalties** — money earned when music is used:

- **Performance royalties** — when music is played publicly or broadcast (radio, TV, venues, streaming). Collected by collective management organisations.
- **Mechanical royalties** — when the composition is reproduced (sales, downloads, streams).
- **Sync fees** — for use in film, adverts, games.

**Work-for-hire vs ownership:** if you are paid to play on someone's record as a session musician, you are usually paid a **fee** and own nothing. If you co-write the song, you should be credited as a **songwriter** — agree splits in writing **at the time**.

**A simple gig agreement** (even a WhatsApp message counts as evidence): **date, times, location, fee, deposit, what equipment is provided, sound check time, cancellation terms**.

**Your profile (EPK):** a short bio, a good photo, links to recordings and videos, contact details.

**Never sign a contract you do not understand.** Ask a trusted adult, a teacher, or a lawyer.

## Key words

- **Copyright:** the legal right of creators over their work
- **Master:** the original sound recording
- **Royalty:** payment for use of music
- **Split:** the agreed share of a song between co-writers

## Read and watch

- [Copyright](https://www.wipo.int/copyright/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization
- [About Creative Commons licences](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/) — Creative Commons
- [About MusicBrainz (open music metadata)](https://musicbrainz.org/doc/About) — MusicBrainz

- Write your bio

1. Work on: Royalties discussion
1. Then: Write your bio
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to turn this week's material into a 20-minute daily practice plan, then change it to fit your actual week. A plan you will not follow is worse than a shorter one you will.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Business:** a press kit has a short bio, a photo, two recordings and contacts. Draft yours.

- **If you already can:** Build a simple press kit online.

objectives: You will extend and cut a song on cue
You will play underscore
You will score a short video
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Event playing needs **flexibility**: extend a song, cut to an ending on a signal, play underscore softly while people speak. Music for video follows the picture: mood, timing and silence.

## Understand it

Much paid music work is **functional** — music that serves an event, a service or a picture. It needs **flexibility, listening and restraint**.

**Worship and events:**

- **Extend a song** — keep a section looping (a chorus, a vamp) for as long as needed: a prayer, a procession, an altar call.
- **Cut to an ending on a signal** — agree a cue so the band can end cleanly from any point.
- **Underscore** — play softly and simply while someone speaks: no busy fills, nothing that competes with the voice.
- **Transitions between songs** — a pad, a held chord, a modulation, so there is no awkward silence.
- **Read the room** — the leader or MC sets the mood; the music follows.
- **Repertoire** — be ready for requests: popular wedding songs, highlife classics, praise medleys, national anthems.

**Music for media (video, adverts, film):**

- **Follow the picture** — the music changes when the scene changes. Mark the **timings** (in seconds) of key moments.
- **Mood** — support the emotion of the images; do not fight it.
- **Silence** is a tool — music that stops can be more powerful than music that continues.
- **Leave room for dialogue** — avoid busy melodies in the voice's frequency range under speech.
- **Rights** — only use music you own or have licensed.

Practise: take a two-minute video clip and score it with your instrument, matching three key moments.

## Key words

- **Underscore:** soft music played under speech or action
- **Vamp:** a short section repeated as long as needed
- **Cue point:** a moment in a video that the music marks

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Copyright](https://www.wipo.int/copyright/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization

1. Then: Score a 30-second clip

**Today's session, to scale:**

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Year 3 members form the graduation band: each **leads** one song (their project) and supports the others. Agree the running order, charts and rehearsal plan.

## Understand it

The graduation band brings Year 3 members together: each player **leads one song** (often from their project) and **supports** everyone else's.

**Getting organised:**

- **Running order** — which songs, in which order, with keys, tempos and lengths. Balance moods and styles; put strong songs at the start and end.
- **Charts** — every song has a clear chart (lead sheet or number chart) shared with everyone before rehearsals, in a shared folder.
- **Roles per song** — who leads, who sings, who solos, who counts in.
- **Rehearsal plan** — a schedule with which songs on which day, and a full run-through date well before the performance.

**Leading your song:**

- Explain the arrangement simply: "Intro is the chorus chords twice, then verse."
- Give **clear cues** during rehearsal and performance.
- Listen and fix **one thing at a time**.

**Supporting others' songs:**

- Learn your parts **before** rehearsal.
- Play **for the song** — keep it simple when you are not featured.
- Watch the song leader; accept their decisions in their song.

**Band habits:** arrive on time and set up quickly; tune together; keep phones away; write notes on your chart; record rehearsals and listen back.

## Key words

- **Running order:** the sequence of songs in a performance
- **Song leader:** the player who directs a particular song
- **Rehearsal schedule:** the plan of what is rehearsed when

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Projects take one of four forms: a **recital** (20 minutes), an **EP** (three recorded tracks), a **directed performance** (you lead a band or choir), or a **teaching portfolio** (a unit taught to Year 1, with evidence). Today: instructor check-in and rehearsal.

## Understand it

Development is where the graduation project takes real shape. Each form has its own milestones:

- **Recital (20 minutes)** — a balanced programme (contrasting styles, tempos and moods), all pieces learnt, introductions written, transitions planned. Time the whole programme.
- **EP (three recorded tracks)** — songs written and arranged; demos recorded; musicians booked; recording plan (where, when, who); then tracking, mixing and artwork.
- **Directed performance** — repertoire chosen for the group's level; charts prepared; rehearsal schedule; your cues and arrangement decisions documented.
- **Teaching portfolio** — a unit plan (goals, sequence of lessons), lesson notes, evidence of learner progress (before-and-after recordings), and your reflection.

**Today's work:**

1. **Check the plan** — what must be finished by week 20 (rehearsal and feedback)? By week 23?
2. **List the remaining tasks** with dates and who is involved.
3. **Identify the hardest part** and work on it first.
4. **Make evidence as you go** — recordings, charts, notes, photos. Your portfolio is built from them.

**Get early feedback** — play a rough version for your instructor or a peer now, while there is time to change direction.

## Key words

- **Milestone:** a key point in the project timeline
- **Evidence:** recordings and documents showing the work
- **Unit plan:** a sequence of lessons with goals

## Read and watch

- [SMART goals](https://www.mindtools.com/a4wo118/smart-goals) — Mind Tools
- [Recording and mixing techniques](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques) — Sound On Sound

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

A full run under performance conditions, then **feedback**: two things that work, one change. Act on the change this week.

## Understand it

A full run **under performance conditions** reveals what practice hides: stamina, transitions, nerves, equipment problems, timing.

**Performance conditions means:**

- **The whole thing, start to finish**, without stopping — including introductions and changes between pieces.
- **In the real space** if possible, with the real equipment.
- **An audience** — even a few classmates.
- **Timed** — does it fit the slot?
- **Recorded** — video if possible.

**Feedback format: two things that work, one change.**

- **Two strengths** — specific ("The modulation into the last chorus lifted the room"), so you keep doing them.
- **One change** — the single most important improvement, so it can actually be done in a week.

Asking for only one change is deliberate: a list of ten problems is overwhelming and nothing gets fixed properly.

**When receiving feedback:** listen, write it down, say thank you, ask questions to understand — do not defend. Then **decide** and **act**.

**Act on the change this week** — plan specific practice for it, and test it in a mini-run before the next session. Watch your recording for anything nobody mentioned (posture, introductions, tuning between pieces).

## Key words

- **Performance conditions:** rehearsing exactly as the real performance will be
- **Actionable feedback:** a specific change that can be made
- **Run-through:** performing everything without stopping

## Read and watch

- [Giving feedback](https://www.mindtools.com/a0edu3n/giving-feedback) — Mind Tools
- [Presentation skills](https://www.skillsyouneed.com/presentation-skills.html) — SkillsYouNeed

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Review: keys and the circle of fifths; scales and modes; chords from triads to extensions; progressions and form; intervals and chords by ear; transposition. A short quiz finds the gaps.

## Understand it

Three years of theory and aural skills, reviewed. A short quiz shows the gaps; this summary helps you fill them.

**Keys and the circle of fifths** — order of sharps (F C G D A E B) and flats (B E A D G C F); finding a key from its signature; relative minors (three semitones below the major).

**Scales and modes** — major (T T S T T T S); natural, harmonic and melodic minor; major and minor pentatonic; blues scale; the modes — Ionian, **Dorian** (minor, raised 6th), Phrygian, Lydian, **Mixolydian** (major, flat 7th), Aeolian, Locrian.

**Chords** — triads (major, minor, diminished, augmented); sevenths (maj7, 7, m7, m7♭5, dim7); extensions (9, 11, 13); altered dominants (7♭9, 7♯9); inversions and slash chords; sus chords.

**Progressions and form** — I–IV–V–I, I–V–vi–IV, ii–V–I (major and minor), 12-bar blues; binary, ternary, verse–chorus with pre-chorus and bridge; modulation by the new key's V or a pivot chord.

**Aural** — intervals (with reference songs); chord qualities; finding roots by bass line; transcribing short phrases.

**Transposition** — thinking in numbers.

**Fill gaps with short daily drills** — online ear-training and theory exercises give instant feedback. Ten minutes a day beats one long session.

## Key words

- **Circle of fifths:** the keys arranged by fifths, adding sharps or flats
- **Chord quality:** the type of chord: major, minor, dominant…
- **Aural skills:** recognising musical elements by ear

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Lead a sectional with a **warm-up, one skill, one song**. Give each player one piece of specific praise and one target. Write a short report for their instructor.

## Understand it

A **sectional** is a rehearsal for one part of a larger group — e.g. all the Year 1 players of your instrument. Leading one is a real leadership task.

**A simple, effective structure:**

1. **Warm-up** (5–10 minutes) — something everyone can do, that prepares for the skill: a scale, a chord change drill, a rhythm game.
2. **One skill** (15–20 minutes) — a single, clear target, taught with the teaching cycle: demonstrate, everyone tries, correct one thing, repeat.
3. **One song** (15–20 minutes) — apply the skill in music, so the session ends with something played together.

**Managing a group:**

- **Clear instructions**, given once, short. Demonstrate rather than explain.
- **Count-ins** so everyone starts together.
- **Watch everyone** — move around; notice who is struggling quietly.
- **Keep everyone playing** — avoid long periods of one person playing while others wait.
- **Positive atmosphere** — mistakes are normal; make it safe to try.

**Individual attention:** give **each player** one piece of **specific praise** and **one target** for the week.

**Write a short report** for their instructor: what you covered, how the group did, and a line per player (strength and target). Reports like this are how musical leaders communicate in schools, churches and bands.

## Key words

- **Sectional:** a rehearsal for one section of a group
- **Group management:** organising and engaging a group of learners
- **Instructor report:** a short written summary for the teacher

**Today's session, to scale:**


## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Final checks: running order, charts, equipment, tuning, outfits, timings, introductions. Run the whole programme once; rest your hands the day before.

## Understand it

Final preparation is about **removing every possible surprise**, so that on the day you only have to play.

**The checklist:**

- **Running order** — final, written, shared with everyone involved (band, sound, MC).
- **Charts** — printed or on a tablet, in order, with spares.
- **Equipment** — instrument serviced (strings settled, keyboard working), cables, tuner, capo, picks, stands, power, adaptors, batteries; spares of anything that can fail.
- **Tuning plan** — when and how you will tune between pieces.
- **Outfits** — decided, ready, comfortable to play in.
- **Timings** — arrival, sound check, start, your slot length.
- **Introductions** — written and practised aloud.
- **Logistics** — transport, who carries what, contact numbers.

**Run the whole programme once**, under performance conditions, a few days before. Then only touch-up practice: hard passages slowly, starts and endings.

**Rest your hands the day before** — light practice only. Muscles and tendons need recovery; tiredness causes mistakes. Sleep well; sleep also consolidates what you have practised.

**Mental preparation:** visualise the performance going well, from walking on to bowing. Plan your breathing routine for before you start.

## Key words

- **Running order:** the final sequence of the performance
- **Contingency:** a backup plan for something going wrong
- **Recovery:** rest that lets the body perform at its best

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Scales and arpeggios in this week's key, slowly then at tempo
- One minute of relaxed finger exercises

## Learn (30 minutes)

Perform your project for families, mentors and the Club. Submit your **portfolio**: recordings from Years 1, 2 and 3, your compositions or arrangements, your mentoring reports and a reflection.

## Understand it

Graduation is the culmination of three years: performing your project for families, mentors and the Club, and submitting a portfolio that tells your musical story.

**The performance** — everything you have prepared: arrive early, sound-check, warm up, follow your routine, introduce your work, play with conviction, acknowledge the audience and everyone who supported you.

**The portfolio** should include:

- **Recordings from Years 1, 2 and 3** — the progression is the most powerful evidence there is.
- **Your compositions and arrangements** — scores, lead sheets or tab, with recordings.
- **Your graduation project** evidence — programme, recordings, charts, lesson plans or EP.
- **Mentoring reports** — the sessions you led and the progress of those you taught.
- **A reflection** (one to two pages):
  - Where you started and where you are now.
  - The moments that changed your playing.
  - What you learnt about practice, performance, leadership and yourself.
  - Your next goals — further study, a band, church music, teaching, production, music as a career or a lifelong passion.

**Organise it** — a folder with clear file names and an index document; backed up in two places.

**Thank the people** who made it possible — instructors, mentors, family, fellow musicians. Then keep playing: the habits you have built will carry you for life.

## Key words

- **Portfolio:** an organised record of your work and progress
- **Reflection:** a written review of learning and next steps
- **Graduation:** the completion of the programme

## Read and watch

- [File naming conventions](https://datamanagement.hms.harvard.edu/plan-design/file-naming-conventions) — Harvard Medical School Data Management
- [Back up your data](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/top-tips-for-staying-secure-online/always-back-up-your-most-important-data) — UK National Cyber Security Centre

## Play (40 minutes)

- Graduation recital
- Portfolio

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Graduation recital
1. Then: Portfolio
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** Record yourself on your phone and listen back before anyone else hears it. AI can tell you about timing and tuning; it cannot tell you whether it moved anybody. That part is yours and your teacher's.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Graduation:** NGG is a beginning. Write your next step: an exam grade, a band, a church or school role, a course, or a release.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Plan your first step after NGG with a date.

## This week's assignment

Submit your portfolio and a one-page reflection: who you were in Year 1, who you are now, and where you go next.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

**Today's session, to scale:**


## Warm-up (10 minutes)

## Learn (30 minutes)

Year 3 is about **artistry and leadership**: you choose a focus (performer, music director, songwriter/producer or teacher), plan a graduation project, and mentor younger members. Today: a technique check, a listening session of musicians you admire, and a first project plan.

## Understand it

Year 3 shifts from **learning skills** to **becoming a musician with your own voice** — and to **leading** others.

**Choose a focus** for the year. Each leads to a different graduation project:

- **Performer** — a 20-minute recital that shows your range and identity.
- **Music director** — leading a band or choir through a performance.
- **Songwriter / producer** — an EP of three recorded original tracks.
- **Teacher** — a unit taught to Year 1 members, with evidence of their progress.

You can do all of these later in life; choosing one now lets you go deep.

**Finding your musical identity:**

- **Listen widely and deliberately.** Make a list of ten recordings that move you. What do they share — a groove, a harmony, a type of voice, a feeling?
- **Notice your instincts.** When you improvise or arrange, what do you naturally do? That is the start of a style.
- **Combine influences.** Most distinctive artists blend two or three traditions — highlife with jazz, gospel with Afrobeats, classical with neo-soul.

**Plan the project now**, with a timeline back from graduation: research and repertoire choice, development, rehearsal, feedback, final preparation. Use SMART goals and check them each term.

**Mentoring** is part of Year 3: explaining something to a beginner is the best test of whether you understand it.

## Key words

- **Musical identity:** the combination of influences and instincts that makes your playing yours
- **Graduation project:** the year's main piece of work, in your chosen focus
- **Mentoring:** guiding a less experienced player

lessons.title: Advanced technique I: speed with control
lessons.summary: Building speed safely with a metronome and burst practice.
objectives: You will use burst practice
You will raise tempo by clean steps
You will stay relaxed at speed
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Burst practice:** play a short group fast, stop, relax, repeat — then join groups. Raise the metronome 4 bpm only after three clean repetitions. Speed is relaxation plus accuracy.

## Understand it

Speed is not a separate skill from accuracy — it is **accuracy plus relaxation**. Tension is what limits speed: a tight hand cannot move quickly or for long.

**Burst practice** (also called chunking):

1. Take a short group of notes — 3 to 5 — from a fast passage.
2. Play the group **fast**, then **stop** and **relax** completely.
3. Repeat until the burst is clean and easy.
4. Join two bursts; then three; then the whole passage.

The brain learns the movement as one gesture rather than many separate notes.

**Metronome discipline:**

- Find the tempo where the passage is **perfect**.
- Play it **three times clean** in a row.
- Raise the tempo by **4 bpm**. Repeat.
- When mistakes appear, drop back 8–10 bpm and rebuild.
- Practise slightly **above** performance tempo, so the real tempo feels comfortable.

**Other tools:**

- **Rhythmic variations** — play an even passage in dotted rhythms (long-short, then short-long). It trains each finger transition.
- **Minimal motion** — fingers close to the keys or strings; no wasted lift.
- **Breathe** and check shoulders, jaw and wrists for tension.

Short, focused sessions beat long tired ones — practising fast while fatigued trains sloppiness.

## Key words

- **Burst practice:** playing short groups fast, then relaxing
- **Tension:** unnecessary muscle effort that limits speed
- **Rhythmic variation:** practising even notes in uneven rhythms

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Harmony III: extended and altered chords
lessons.summary: 9ths, 11ths, 13ths and altered dominants.
objectives: You will voice 9th, 11th and 13th chords

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Extensions stack thirds above the 7th: **9, 11, 13**. Altered dominants (7♭9, 7♯9, 7♯5) add tension that resolves to I. Gospel and neo-soul live here.

## Understand it

**Extended chords** keep stacking thirds above the 7th:

- **9th** — the 2nd an octave up (C9: C E G B♭ D; Cmaj9: C E G B D).
- **11th** — the 4th an octave up (often used on minor chords: Cm11).
- **13th** — the 6th an octave up (C13: C E G B♭ D A; often played without the 11th).

In practice, players **leave notes out**: the **root** (the bass player has it), the **5th** (adds little colour). The **3rd and 7th** define the chord; the extension adds colour. A C13 might be voiced simply as **B♭–E–A** over a C bass.

**Altered dominants** add tension to the V chord by sharpening or flattening the 5th and 9th:

- **7♭9** (G7♭9: G B D F A♭) — dark, dramatic.
- **7♯9** (G7♯9: G B D F A♯) — the bluesy "Hendrix chord".
- **7♯5** (augmented) — restless, rising.

The more tension on V, the sweeter the resolution to I.

**Where they live:** gospel (13ths, 7♭9 walk-ups, 9ths everywhere), neo-soul (minor 9ths and 11ths), jazz, R&B and Afro-fusion.

**Practise:** ii–V–I as **Dm9 – G13 – Cmaj9**, then with **G7♭9**. Listen to how each colour changes the emotion.

## Key words

- **Extended chord:** a chord with 9ths, 11ths or 13ths added
- **Altered dominant:** a V chord with sharpened or flattened 5th or 9th
- **Shell voicing:** a voicing using mainly the 3rd and 7th

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music

lessons.title: Modulation and transposition
lessons.summary: Changing key smoothly and playing songs in any key a singer needs.
objectives: You will transpose a song to three keys

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Transposing** means playing the same song in another key — think in numbers (I, IV, V) not letters. **Modulating** uses a pivot chord or the new key's V to move smoothly.

## Understand it

**Transposition** means playing the same music in a different key — essential when a singer needs it higher or lower.

**Think in numbers, not letters.** A song that is "1 – 5 – 6m – 4" is C–G–Am–F in C, D–A–Bm–G in D, and B♭–F–Gm–E♭ in B♭. If you know the song as numbers, any key is the same song. Many church and session musicians learn every song this way (the Nashville Number System).

**Modulation** means changing key **during** a piece. Common methods:

- **Via the new key's V** — play the dominant (7th) chord of the new key, then arrive. To go from C to D: play **A7**, then D.
- **Pivot chord** — a chord that belongs to both keys. C major and G major share Am, C, Em, G. Use one as the hinge: C – Am (as vi of C, then reinterpreted as ii of G) – D7 – G.
- **Direct ("truck driver") modulation** — simply jump up a semitone or tone, usually for the last chorus. Dramatic and common in gospel and pop.

**Practise:**

1. Learn a song in numbers.
2. Play it in three keys.
3. Add a modulation up a tone for the last chorus using the new key's V.

Transposing on the spot is a professional skill that makes you valuable to every singer and band.

## Key words

- **Transpose:** play music in a different key
- **Modulate:** change key within a piece
- **Pivot chord:** a chord shared by two keys, used to move between them
- **Number system:** writing chords as scale degrees

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Music technology:** microphones — dynamic for loud sources and stage, condenser for studio voice and acoustic instruments.

## Make it fit you

- **If you already can:** Transpose at sight when a singer calls a key.

lessons.title: Music direction: rehearsing a band
lessons.summary: Running an effective rehearsal and arranging for a band.
objectives: You will plan a rehearsal
You will give clear instructions

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

A music director: **plans** (set list, keys, arrangements), **communicates** (number charts, cues), **listens** (balance, tempo) and **encourages**. Rehearse transitions, not just songs.

## Understand it

A **music director (MD)** turns a group of players into a band. The job has four parts:

**1. Plan**

- **Set list** — the songs, their order, keys and tempos.
- **Arrangements** — intro, sections, repeats, dynamics, endings, who plays what.
- **Charts** — clear lead sheets or number charts for every player.
- **Rehearsal plan** — what to work on, in what order, with timings.

**2. Communicate**

- **Number charts** so the band can follow key changes.
- **Clear cues** — agreed hand signals or calls for sections, repeats, builds, drops and endings.
- **Short, specific instructions** — "Bass, play only roots in verse 1", not "make it better".

**3. Listen**

- **Balance** — can you hear the singer? Is anything too loud?
- **Tempo** — is the band rushing in the chorus or dragging in the bridge?
- **Tightness** — are hits and endings together?

**4. Encourage**

- Name what is working, specifically. Correct one thing at a time.
- Keep energy up; end rehearsals on a good run.

**Rehearse transitions, not just songs.** Bands usually know the middles of songs; they fall apart at **starts, section changes and endings**. Loop these: "From the last line of the verse into the chorus — again."

## Key words

- **Music director:** the person who leads a band's musical decisions
- **Set list:** the planned order of songs
- **Transition:** the move from one section or song to the next

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music

lessons.title: Styles workshop: Afro-fusion and neo-soul
lessons.summary: Modern African and soul styles in depth.
objectives: You will transcribe a part from an Afro-fusion or neo-soul track
You will play with laid-back timing
You will write your own part
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Afro-fusion** blends Afrobeats, highlife, R&B and jazz; **neo-soul** uses extended chords, laid-back timing and lush voicings. Study one track's part note-for-note, then create your own.

## Understand it

**Afro-fusion** blends Afrobeats with highlife, R&B, reggae/dancehall, jazz and soul — the sound of artists who move between styles while keeping a West African rhythmic core. **Neo-soul** (from the 1990s onward) brought jazz harmony and loose, laid-back grooves to soul and R&B.

**What they share and what to study:**

- **Extended chords** — minor 9ths and 11ths, major 9ths, 13ths (week 3).
- **Laid-back timing** — notes placed slightly **behind** the beat. It feels relaxed and heavy. It is deliberate: practise playing just behind a metronome without dragging the tempo.
- **Lush voicings** — spread chords, close clusters, moving inner voices.
- **Groove first** — repetitive two- or four-bar loops with small variations.
- **Space** — what you leave out matters as much as what you play.

**The study method (transcribe, then create):**

1. Choose **one track** and **one part** (the keys, or the guitar).
2. Learn it **note-for-note** by ear, slowing the track if needed. Copy the **rhythm and feel**, not only the notes.
3. Analyse: what chords? Which voicings? Where is it behind the beat?
4. **Create your own** part over the same progression, using what you learned.

This is how musicians absorb a style — through the ear and the hands, not just from explanations.

## Key words

- **Afro-fusion:** Afrobeats blended with other styles
- **Neo-soul:** soul music with jazz harmony and laid-back grooves
- **Behind the beat:** playing slightly late on purpose for a relaxed feel

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music

- Play along
- Write an original part

1. Work on: Transcribe
1. Then: Write an original part

**Body:** long rehearsals need breaks — five minutes every 30 protects your hands, ears and focus.

lessons.title: Styles workshop: jazz standards
lessons.summary: Reading a jazz lead sheet and comping through a standard.
objectives: You will comp through a standard
You will play the head
You will solo over one chorus
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

A **jazz standard** (for example 'Autumn Leaves') is mostly ii–V–I chains. **Comping** is rhythmic chord accompaniment; the head is the melody, then solos, then the head again.

## Understand it

A **jazz standard** is a well-known tune that jazz musicians share and play in their own ways — many come from 1920s–1950s musical theatre and popular song. Their harmony is built largely from **chains of ii–V–I**, which is why learning standards is the best training in harmony there is.

**"Autumn Leaves"** is a classic first standard: it alternates a **major ii–V–I** and its **relative minor ii–V–i**:

- In G minor / B♭ major: **Cm7 – F7 – B♭maj7 – E♭maj7 – Am7♭5 – D7 – Gm**.

**How a jazz performance is organised:**

1. **The head** — the melody played once (or twice) through.
2. **Solos** — each soloist improvises over the **same chord sequence** (one time through is a **chorus**).
3. **The head again**, then an ending.

**Comping** (from "accompanying" / "complementing") — playing the chords **rhythmically and sparingly** behind the melody or soloist:

- Short chords, off the beat, leaving space.
- **Shell voicings** (3rd and 7th) or rootless voicings so the bass is free.
- **Listen and respond** to the soloist — it is a conversation.

**Practise:** learn the chord sequence until you can play it without reading; comp along with a recording; then improvise over it using **chord tones** (1, 3, 5, 7 of each chord) on the strong beats.

## Key words

- **Jazz standard:** a widely known tune in the jazz repertoire
- **Head:** the tune's melody, played at the start and end
- **Chorus (jazz):** one time through the chord sequence
- **Comping:** rhythmic chordal accompaniment

## Read and watch

- [Seventh chords](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/advanced-topics/seventh-chords.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Play (40 minutes)

- Chord chart
- Comp
- Head and solo

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Chord chart
1. Then: Head and solo

lessons.title: Recording session
lessons.summary: Recording a professional-quality track: preparation, takes and editing.
objectives: You will record to a click
You will comp the best take
You will export a clean track
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Prepare: tempo, key, click, chart. Record a **guide**, then real takes. Do three good takes and comp the best parts. Keep notes on what each take was.

## Understand it

A recording session rewards **preparation**: studio time is limited, and every problem fixed before you arrive saves an hour.

**Before the session:**

- **Tempo** (bpm) and **key** decided and written down.
- **Chart** — the arrangement with sections and bar counts.
- **Click track** — practise with it; recording to a click lets parts be edited together later.
- **Instrument ready** — fresh (settled) strings, tuned, intonation checked; for keys, sounds chosen and saved.
- **Warm up** before you arrive.

**The process:**

1. **Guide track** — a quick rough recording of the whole song (often guitar or keys plus a guide vocal), so everyone knows where they are.
2. **Real takes** — the actual parts, one instrument at a time, usually starting with the rhythm section.
3. **Several good takes** — record three or more full takes of your part.
4. **Comping** — choosing the best sections from several takes and joining them.

**Keep notes** on each take: "Take 2 — great verse, chorus rushed", "Take 3 — best feel". In a long session, nobody remembers which take was which.

**Headphone mix** — ask for what you need to play well (more click, more vocal, less of yourself).

Listen to playback critically: tuning, timing, tone, feel. If something is wrong, re-record now — "fix it in the mix" rarely works.

## Key words

- **Click track:** a metronome heard in headphones while recording
- **Guide track:** a rough recording that others record over
- **Take:** one recorded performance
- **Comping:** combining the best parts of several takes

## Read and watch

- [Recording and mixing techniques](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques) — Sound On Sound
- [Production tips and tutorials](https://www.izotope.com/en/learn.html) — iZotope

- Comp and export

1. Then: Comp and export
1. Record one take and listen back

- **If you already can:** Mix the track: levels, pan, EQ, reverb.

lessons.title: Mentoring: teaching a beginner
lessons.summary: Planning and teaching a 20-minute lesson to a Year 1 member.
objectives: You will plan a 20-minute lesson
You will teach one skill
You will give specific feedback
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Good teaching: **one goal**, demonstrate, let them try, correct one thing, praise specifically, repeat. Check understanding by asking them to show you, not tell you.

## Understand it

Teaching someone else is one of the fastest ways to deepen your own understanding — you discover what you only *thought* you knew. Good teaching follows a simple cycle:

1. **One goal** — a small, specific target for the lesson: "Change from C to G in time", not "get better at guitar".
2. **Demonstrate** — show it slowly, then at normal speed. Let them hear the target.
3. **Let them try** — hands on the instrument quickly; do not talk for long.
4. **Correct one thing** — the most important problem only. Five corrections at once overwhelm a beginner.
5. **Praise specifically** — "Your thumb is behind the neck now — that's why the chord rings" teaches more than "well done".
6. **Repeat** — practise until it is reliable, then set the next small step.

**Check understanding by asking them to show you, not tell you.** "Do you understand?" almost always gets "yes". "Show me the change from C to G" reveals the truth.

**Other principles:**

- **Patience** — remember how hard it was for you.
- **Encourage practice habits** — short daily practice, a log.
- **Adapt** — every learner is different; if one explanation fails, try another (a picture, a comparison, slower).
- **Safeguarding** — follow the Club's rules for working with younger members: in shared spaces, with staff aware.

Keep brief notes after each lesson: goal, progress, next step.

## Key words

- **Teaching cycle:** goal, demonstrate, try, correct, praise, repeat
- **Specific praise:** naming exactly what was done well
- **Check for understanding:** asking a learner to show, not tell

## Read and watch

- [Giving feedback](https://www.mindtools.com/a0edu3n/giving-feedback) — Mind Tools

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Checklist: speed with control; extended chords; transposition and modulation; music direction; one modern and one jazz style; a recorded track. **Project check:** is your plan on schedule?

## Understand it

Mid-year is the moment to check two things: **your skills** and **your project**.

**Skills checklist** — rate each green, amber or red:

- Speed with control (burst practice, metronome progress).
- Extended and altered chords — can you voice them in several keys?
- Transposition on the spot; modulation by the V of the new key.
- Music direction — clear cues, structured rehearsals.
- One modern style (Afro-fusion/neo-soul) and one jazz standard.
- A recorded track from the session.

**Project check** — answer honestly:

- **Is the plan on schedule?** Compare your timeline with where you are.
- **What is done** and what is evidence of it (recordings, charts, lesson notes)?
- **What is at risk?** Time, people, equipment, a piece that is too hard?
- **What needs to change?** Cut scope, simplify a piece, book rehearsals earlier.

A project that is behind can almost always be saved if you notice **now** — and almost never if you notice in the last month.

**Revise for the term test** with mixed practice: technique at tempo, an extended-chord progression in a called key, transposing a song, directing a short section, and your prepared piece.

## Key words

- **Project check:** a review of progress against the plan
- **Scope:** how much the project includes
- **Risk:** something that could stop the plan succeeding

## Read and watch

lessons.summary: Practical assessment of the first Year 3 term.
objectives: You will perform under test conditions

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Practical:** technique at tempo; an extended-chord progression; transpose a song on request; direct a short section; perform a prepared piece in a style of your choice.

## Understand it

The Year 3 term test assesses **artistry and leadership**, not just correctness.

**What it includes:**

- **Technique at tempo** — scales, arpeggios or technical passages at a demanding speed, clean and relaxed.
- **An extended-chord progression** — e.g. ii–V–I with 9ths and 13ths, possibly in a key the examiner calls. Think in numbers and voice-lead smoothly.
- **Transpose a song on request** — play a known song in a new key without preparation. Use the number system.
- **Direct a short section** — lead other players: count in, cue sections, fix one problem, run it again.
- **A prepared piece in a style of your choice** — performed with conviction and personal character.

**What examiners look for at this level:**

- **Control** — tempo, dynamics, tone, all deliberate.
- **Understanding** — you can explain your choices.
- **Communication** — with the audience and with other players.
- **Recovery** — calm handling of anything that goes wrong.

**On the day:** warm up properly, tune carefully, breathe, and make decisions with confidence. Ask for clarification if a request is unclear — professionals do.

Afterwards, use the feedback to adjust your graduation project plan.

## Key words

- **Artistry:** personal, convincing musical expression
- **Conviction:** playing with commitment and intention
- **Transposition on sight:** changing key without preparation

- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

lessons.title: Showcase: your musical identity
lessons.summary: A performance that shows who you are as a musician.
objectives: You will perform a short set
You will introduce your music

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Perform a short set (two or three pieces) that shows your **focus** and your voice: a cover reimagined, an original, and something that stretches you. Introduce each one.

## Understand it

This showcase is a **short set** — two or three pieces — that says who you are as a musician.

**Building the set:**

1. **A cover reimagined** — a known song in your own arrangement: a new groove (ballad to Afro-groove), new harmony (reharmonised with extended chords), or a new texture. The audience recognises it; your version shows your identity.
2. **An original** — your composition or song.
3. **Something that stretches you** — a piece at the edge of your ability or in a new style.

**Order matters:** start with something confident to settle in; put the most demanding piece in the middle; end with the strongest.

**Introductions** — one or two sentences each: what it is, and why you chose it or what you did with it. Speaking connects you with the audience.

**Presence:**

- Walk on and set up calmly; tune; adjust the seat or strap.
- Pause before starting; let the audience settle.
- Commit to every choice — an interpretation played with conviction convinces.
- Acknowledge applause between pieces; thank the audience and any band members at the end.

**Record it** — it belongs in your portfolio, and watching it afterwards teaches you more than any feedback.

## Key words

- **Set:** a planned group of pieces performed together
- **Reimagined cover:** your own new version of an existing song
- **Running order:** the sequence of pieces in a set

lessons.summary: Arpeggio sweeps, legato runs and hybrid picking.
objectives: You will sweep a three-string arpeggio

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

**Sweep picking** plays an arpeggio with one smooth pick motion across strings, muting each note as you go. **Legato** uses hammer-ons and pull-offs for flowing runs. **Hybrid picking** uses pick and fingers together for country and gospel lines.

## Understand it

Three advanced techniques extend what the guitar can do.

**Sweep picking** — playing an **arpeggio** across several strings with **one continuous pick motion**, like a slow strum, but each note sounding separately:

- The pick **falls through** the strings in one direction (down when ascending in pitch towards the high strings, up when descending).
- The **fretting hand** frets each note only while it sounds, then **lifts or mutes** it — so the notes do not ring together like a chord. This is the hard part.
- Start **very slowly** on three-string shapes (e.g. a minor triad on G, B and E strings).

**Legato** — flowing runs using mainly **hammer-ons and pull-offs**, picking only the first note on each string (or even fewer). Smooth and fluid; it needs **strong, accurate fretting fingers** and even volume between picked and slurred notes.

**Hybrid picking** — using the **pick** (held between thumb and index) **plus the middle and ring fingers** to pluck strings. It allows:

- Bass with the pick and melody notes with the fingers at once.
- Skipping strings cleanly.
- Country "chicken picking", funk and modern pop and Afrobeats lines.

**Practice principles:** slow, clean, relaxed; metronome ladder; burst practice; muting unused strings with both hands. Speed comes only after accuracy.

## Key words

- **Sweep picking:** an arpeggio played with one continuous pick motion
- **Legato:** smooth runs using hammer-ons and pull-offs
- **Hybrid picking:** pick and fingers used together

lessons.title: Ear III: transcription
lessons.summary: Transcribing a full song section: melody, bass, chords.
objectives: You will transcribe a bass line
You will identify chord qualities
You will write out a chorus
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Work in layers: **bass first** (it tells you the chords), then the chord quality, then the melody. Slow the track (most players can at 75% without changing pitch).

## Understand it

**Transcription** — working out music from a recording — is how players have learned styles for generations. It trains the ear, the hands and your understanding of how music is built.

**Work in layers:**

1. **Structure** — map the sections and count the bars.
2. **Bass line first** — the lowest notes usually tell you the **roots** of the chords. Sing it, then find it.
3. **Chord quality** — over each root: major or minor? Is there a 7th? A 9th? Try options until it matches.
4. **Melody** — sing a phrase, find the first note, then each interval.
5. **Details** — fills, voicings, rhythm hits, articulation.

**Tools and habits:**

- **Slow the track down** — most players can work comfortably at 75% speed with pitch preserved (many apps and YouTube's speed control do this).
- **Loop** short sections — two bars at a time.
- **Sing before you play** — if you can sing it, you can find it.
- **Use headphones** — bass lines and inner voices are much clearer.
- **Write it down** — chord chart, notation or tab — so the work is not lost.

**Check your transcription** by playing along with the recording at full speed: anything that clashes is wrong. Start with simple songs and build up; speed comes with practice.

## Key words

- **Transcription:** working out and writing down music from a recording
- **Layering:** transcribing one element at a time
- **Loop:** repeating a short section for study

## Read and watch

- [Ear training exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net

objectives: You will reharmonise a song
You will change its feel
You will keep the melody recognisable
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Reharmonise by **substituting** (vi for I, ii–V for V), **changing feel** (ballad to Afro-groove), or **adding passing chords**. Keep the melody recognisable.

## Understand it

**Reharmonisation** means changing the chords under a melody while keeping the melody the same. It is how arrangers make a familiar song feel new.

**Techniques:**

- **Substitution** — replace a chord with one that shares notes and function:
  - **vi for I** (Am instead of C) — softer, more emotional.
  - **iii for I** (Em for C).
  - **ii–V for V** (Dm7–G7 instead of G7) — more movement.
  - **Tritone substitution** in jazz (D♭7 for G7).
- **Passing chords** — a quick chord between two main ones (a diminished chord, or a chord a semitone above or below the target).
- **Extensions** — turn triads into 7ths, 9ths and 13ths.
- **Changing the bass** — slash chords and a moving bass line (C – C/B – Am – Am/G).
- **Changing the feel** — the same chords as a ballad, an Afro-groove, a gospel 12/8, a swing.

**The rule: keep the melody recognisable.** Check every new chord against the melody note on top of it — the melody note should be a chord tone or a pleasing extension, not a harsh clash (unless you want one).

**Arranging process:** sing the melody; try alternative chords bar by bar; record versions; keep what serves the song's emotion. Write the final arrangement as a lead sheet.

## Key words

- **Reharmonisation:** new chords under an existing melody
- **Chord substitution:** replacing a chord with one of similar function
- **Passing chord:** a brief connecting chord
- **Tritone substitution:** replacing V7 with the dominant a tritone away

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Music business essentials
lessons.summary: Royalties, contracts, gigs and building your profile.
objectives: You will explain royalties
You will draft a simple gig agreement
You will write a short artist bio
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Know the basics: **performance and mechanical royalties**, work-for-hire vs. ownership, a simple gig agreement (date, fee, time, equipment), and a profile (bio, photo, recordings). Never sign a contract you don't understand — ask a trusted adult or lawyer.

## Understand it

Musicians who understand the business keep more of what they earn and avoid bad deals.

**Copyright** — when you create an original song or recording, you own copyright in it automatically. There are usually **two copyrights** in recorded music:

- The **composition** (melody and lyrics) — owned by the **songwriters** (and their publishers).
- The **sound recording (master)** — owned by whoever paid for or made the recording (the artist or a label).

**Royalties** — money earned when music is used:

- **Performance royalties** — when music is played publicly or broadcast (radio, TV, venues, streaming). Collected by collective management organisations.
- **Mechanical royalties** — when the composition is reproduced (sales, downloads, streams).
- **Sync fees** — for use in film, adverts, games.

**Work-for-hire vs ownership:** if you are paid to play on someone's record as a session musician, you are usually paid a **fee** and own nothing. If you co-write the song, you should be credited as a **songwriter** — agree splits in writing **at the time**.

**A simple gig agreement** (even a WhatsApp message counts as evidence): **date, times, location, fee, deposit, what equipment is provided, sound check time, cancellation terms**.

**Your profile (EPK):** a short bio, a good photo, links to recordings and videos, contact details.

**Never sign a contract you do not understand.** Ask a trusted adult, a teacher, or a lawyer.

## Key words

- **Copyright:** the legal right of creators over their work
- **Master:** the original sound recording
- **Royalty:** payment for use of music
- **Split:** the agreed share of a song between co-writers

## Read and watch

- [Copyright](https://www.wipo.int/copyright/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization
- [About Creative Commons licences](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/) — Creative Commons
- [About MusicBrainz (open music metadata)](https://musicbrainz.org/doc/About) — MusicBrainz

## Play (40 minutes)

- Royalties discussion
- Draft an agreement
- Write your bio

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Royalties discussion
1. Then: Write your bio
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to turn this week's material into a 20-minute daily practice plan, then change it to fit your actual week. A plan you will not follow is worse than a shorter one you will.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Business:** a press kit has a short bio, a photo, two recordings and contacts. Draft yours.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Build a simple press kit online.

## This week's assignment

Write your artist bio and a one-page gig agreement template.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Music for worship, events and media
lessons.summary: Playing for services, weddings and events; music for video.
objectives: You will extend and cut a song on cue
You will play underscore
You will score a short video
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Event playing needs **flexibility**: extend a song, cut to an ending on a signal, play underscore softly while people speak. Music for video follows the picture: mood, timing and silence.

## Understand it

Much paid music work is **functional** — music that serves an event, a service or a picture. It needs **flexibility, listening and restraint**.

**Worship and events:**

- **Extend a song** — keep a section looping (a chorus, a vamp) for as long as needed: a prayer, a procession, an altar call.
- **Cut to an ending on a signal** — agree a cue so the band can end cleanly from any point.
- **Underscore** — play softly and simply while someone speaks: no busy fills, nothing that competes with the voice.
- **Transitions between songs** — a pad, a held chord, a modulation, so there is no awkward silence.
- **Read the room** — the leader or MC sets the mood; the music follows.
- **Repertoire** — be ready for requests: popular wedding songs, highlife classics, praise medleys, national anthems.

**Music for media (video, adverts, film):**

- **Follow the picture** — the music changes when the scene changes. Mark the **timings** (in seconds) of key moments.
- **Mood** — support the emotion of the images; do not fight it.
- **Silence** is a tool — music that stops can be more powerful than music that continues.
- **Leave room for dialogue** — avoid busy melodies in the voice's frequency range under speech.
- **Rights** — only use music you own or have licensed.

Practise: take a two-minute video clip and score it with your instrument, matching three key moments.

## Key words

- **Underscore:** soft music played under speech or action
- **Vamp:** a short section repeated as long as needed
- **Cue point:** a moment in a video that the music marks

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Copyright](https://www.wipo.int/copyright/en/) — World Intellectual Property Organization

- Score a 30-second clip

1. Work on: Cue practice
1. Then: Score a 30-second clip
1. Record one take and listen back

- **If you already can:** Score a 60-second clip with two moods.

lessons.summary: Rehearsing the band that will play your graduation projects.
objectives: You will lead your project song
You will support others

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Year 3 members form the graduation band: each **leads** one song (their project) and supports the others. Agree the running order, charts and rehearsal plan.

## Understand it

The graduation band brings Year 3 members together: each player **leads one song** (often from their project) and **supports** everyone else's.

**Getting organised:**

- **Running order** — which songs, in which order, with keys, tempos and lengths. Balance moods and styles; put strong songs at the start and end.
- **Charts** — every song has a clear chart (lead sheet or number chart) shared with everyone before rehearsals, in a shared folder.
- **Roles per song** — who leads, who sings, who solos, who counts in.
- **Rehearsal plan** — a schedule with which songs on which day, and a full run-through date well before the performance.

**Leading your song:**

- Explain the arrangement simply: "Intro is the chorus chords twice, then verse."
- Give **clear cues** during rehearsal and performance.
- Listen and fix **one thing at a time**.

**Supporting others' songs:**

- Learn your parts **before** rehearsal.
- Play **for the song** — keep it simple when you are not featured.
- Watch the song leader; accept their decisions in their song.

**Band habits:** arrive on time and set up quickly; tune together; keep phones away; write notes on your chart; record rehearsals and listen back.

## Key words

- **Running order:** the sequence of songs in a performance
- **Song leader:** the player who directs a particular song
- **Rehearsal schedule:** the plan of what is rehearsed when

## Read and watch

- [Team working skills](https://www.skillsyouneed.com/ips/team-working.html) — SkillsYouNeed

lessons.summary: Building your project: arrangement, rehearsal, recording.
objectives: You will present your project progress
You will fix the biggest risk
You will rehearse
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Projects take one of four forms: a **recital** (20 minutes), an **EP** (three recorded tracks), a **directed performance** (you lead a band or choir), or a **teaching portfolio** (a unit taught to Year 1, with evidence). Today: instructor check-in and rehearsal.

## Understand it

Development is where the graduation project takes real shape. Each form has its own milestones:

- **Recital (20 minutes)** — a balanced programme (contrasting styles, tempos and moods), all pieces learnt, introductions written, transitions planned. Time the whole programme.
- **EP (three recorded tracks)** — songs written and arranged; demos recorded; musicians booked; recording plan (where, when, who); then tracking, mixing and artwork.
- **Directed performance** — repertoire chosen for the group's level; charts prepared; rehearsal schedule; your cues and arrangement decisions documented.
- **Teaching portfolio** — a unit plan (goals, sequence of lessons), lesson notes, evidence of learner progress (before-and-after recordings), and your reflection.

**Today's work:**

1. **Check the plan** — what must be finished by week 20 (rehearsal and feedback)? By week 23?
2. **List the remaining tasks** with dates and who is involved.
3. **Identify the hardest part** and work on it first.
4. **Make evidence as you go** — recordings, charts, notes, photos. Your portfolio is built from them.

**Get early feedback** — play a rough version for your instructor or a peer now, while there is time to change direction.

## Key words

- **Milestone:** a key point in the project timeline
- **Evidence:** recordings and documents showing the work
- **Unit plan:** a sequence of lessons with goals

## Read and watch

- [SMART goals](https://www.mindtools.com/a4wo118/smart-goals) — Mind Tools
- [Recording and mixing techniques](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques) — Sound On Sound

## Play (40 minutes)

- Check-in
- Fix the risk
- Rehearse

## Practise at home (20 minutes a day)

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Check-in
1. Then: Rehearse
1. Record one take and listen back

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Teamwork:** in a recording session time is money — arrive prepared, tuned and warmed up; take direction gracefully.

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Add a second element (e.g. a recorded track alongside the recital).

## This week's assignment

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Graduation project: rehearsal and feedback
lessons.summary: A full run of your project and peer feedback.
objectives: You will do a full run
You will give and receive feedback
You will act on one change
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

A full run under performance conditions, then **feedback**: two things that work, one change. Act on the change this week.

## Understand it

A full run **under performance conditions** reveals what practice hides: stamina, transitions, nerves, equipment problems, timing.

**Performance conditions means:**

- **The whole thing, start to finish**, without stopping — including introductions and changes between pieces.
- **In the real space** if possible, with the real equipment.
- **An audience** — even a few classmates.
- **Timed** — does it fit the slot?
- **Recorded** — video if possible.

**Feedback format: two things that work, one change.**

- **Two strengths** — specific ("The modulation into the last chorus lifted the room"), so you keep doing them.
- **One change** — the single most important improvement, so it can actually be done in a week.

Asking for only one change is deliberate: a list of ten problems is overwhelming and nothing gets fixed properly.

**When receiving feedback:** listen, write it down, say thank you, ask questions to understand — do not defend. Then **decide** and **act**.

**Act on the change this week** — plan specific practice for it, and test it in a mini-run before the next session. Watch your recording for anything nobody mentioned (posture, introductions, tuning between pieces).

## Key words

- **Performance conditions:** rehearsing exactly as the real performance will be
- **Actionable feedback:** a specific change that can be made
- **Run-through:** performing everything without stopping

## Read and watch

- [Giving feedback](https://www.mindtools.com/a0edu3n/giving-feedback) — Mind Tools
- [Presentation skills](https://www.skillsyouneed.com/presentation-skills.html) — SkillsYouNeed

## Play (40 minutes)

- Full run
- Feedback
- Revise

1. Warm up with this week's scale
1. Work on: Full run
1. Then: Revise
1. Record one take and listen back
1. **With a tool —** Use an ear-training app to drill the intervals in this lesson for five minutes. Sing or hum the interval before you answer; an app that only tests recognition trains your eyes, not your ear.

## Essentials (10 minutes)

**Planning:** your final project needs a plan with dates: choose, arrange, rehearse, record, perform.

- **If this is new to you:** halve the tempo, practise hands (or strings) separately, and master one part before adding the next. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Invite an outside listener and act on their feedback.

## This week's assignment

Make the agreed change and do two more full runs at home.

> Practise slowly first. Speed comes from playing it right, not from playing it fast.

lessons.title: Theory and aural review
lessons.summary: A final review of the three years' theory and aural skills.
objectives: You will complete a theory review
You will complete an aural review
You will fix one gap
lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Review: keys and the circle of fifths; scales and modes; chords from triads to extensions; progressions and form; intervals and chords by ear; transposition. A short quiz finds the gaps.

## Understand it

Three years of theory and aural skills, reviewed. A short quiz shows the gaps; this summary helps you fill them.

**Keys and the circle of fifths** — order of sharps (F C G D A E B) and flats (B E A D G C F); finding a key from its signature; relative minors (three semitones below the major).

**Scales and modes** — major (T T S T T T S); natural, harmonic and melodic minor; major and minor pentatonic; blues scale; the modes — Ionian, **Dorian** (minor, raised 6th), Phrygian, Lydian, **Mixolydian** (major, flat 7th), Aeolian, Locrian.

**Chords** — triads (major, minor, diminished, augmented); sevenths (maj7, 7, m7, m7♭5, dim7); extensions (9, 11, 13); altered dominants (7♭9, 7♯9); inversions and slash chords; sus chords.

**Progressions and form** — I–IV–V–I, I–V–vi–IV, ii–V–I (major and minor), 12-bar blues; binary, ternary, verse–chorus with pre-chorus and bridge; modulation by the new key's V or a pivot chord.

**Aural** — intervals (with reference songs); chord qualities; finding roots by bass line; transcribing short phrases.

**Transposition** — thinking in numbers.

**Fill gaps with short daily drills** — online ear-training and theory exercises give instant feedback. Ten minutes a day beats one long session.

## Key words

- **Circle of fifths:** the keys arranged by fifths, adding sharps or flats
- **Chord quality:** the type of chord: major, minor, dominant…
- **Aural skills:** recognising musical elements by ear

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

- Gap fixing

lessons.summary: Leading a 20-minute session for Year 1 or 2 members.
objectives: You will lead a sectional

lessons.body:
**Today's session, to scale:**

```steps 10 Warm-up | 30 Learn | 40 Play | 10 Essentials
```

## Warm-up (10 minutes)

- Chromatic warm-up across all six strings, alternate picking
- Chord changes from last week, one minute

## Learn (30 minutes)

Lead a sectional with a **warm-up, one skill, one song**. Give each player one piece of specific praise and one target. Write a short report for their instructor.

## Understand it

A **sectional** is a rehearsal for one part of a larger group — e.g. all the Year 1 players of your instrument. Leading one is a real leadership task.

**A simple, effective structure:**

1. **Warm-up** (5–10 minutes) — something everyone can do, that prepares for the skill: a scale, a chord change drill, a rhythm game.
2. **One skill** (15–20 minutes) — a single, clear target, taught with the teaching cycle: demonstrate, everyone tries, correct one thing, repeat.
3. **One song** (15–20 minutes) — apply the skill in music, so the session ends with something played together.

**Managing a group:**

- **Clear instructions**, given once, short. Demonstrate rather than explain.
- **Count-ins** so everyone starts together.
- **Watch everyone** — move around; notice who is struggling quietly.
- **Keep everyone playing** — avoid long periods of one person playing while others wait.
- **Positive atmosphere** — mistakes are normal; make it safe to try.

**Individual attention:** give **each player** one piece of **specific praise** and **one target** for the week.

**Write a short report** for their instructor: what you covered, how the group did, and a line per player (strength and target). Reports like this are how musical leaders communicate in schools, churches and bands.

## Key words

- **Sectional:** a rehearsal for one section of a group
- **Group management:** organising and engaging a group of learners
- **Instructor report:** a short written summary for the teacher

lessons.summary: The last full run and the details of the graduation day.
objectives: You will run the full programme
You will check every detail
